label: HB 9108
title: AN ACT REVISING THE ANIMAL WELFARE ACT, STRENGTHENING ANIMAL WELFARE STANDARDS BY ESTABLISHING AN ANIMAL WELFARE BUREAU UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act (RA) No. 8485 or the Animal Welfare Act of 1998 was a laudable landmark legislation which laid the groundwork for animal rights protection in the Philippines. It was subsequently amended by Republic Act No. 10631, but in the more than two (2) decades since its original passage, there remains numerous legal and institutional gaps which prevent the law from being implemented efficiently and comprehensively. Firstly, the penalties and fines provided for under the old law are inadequate, if not outdated, that they do not reflect the severity of the offenses. As such, the seemingly minimal penalties also fail to deter the commission of abusive acts to animals. Worse, since some violative acts are even committed by people of authority within the government, such as barangay officials and animal pound personnel, their acts and omissions should warrant maximum penalties. In the spirit of moving towards a more progressive and modernized Animal Welfare law, supportive institutional arrangements should be put in place like an Animal Welfare Bureau under a proper national government agency like the Department of Agriculture to be coordinated with counterparts at the local government level. For senior citizens, having pets have proven to have positive effects since it keeps them physically active and engaged in their day-to-day life. The special interaction they provide not only keeps away loneliness and feelings of isolation, the companionship they provide keep our older persons mentally and emotionally stimulated, thus preventing the early on-set of dementia. As sentient beings, animals, be they domesticated pets, farm-raised for food, or working/service animals, do not deserve to be treated with cruelty or be needlessly subject to harmful practices, regardless or cultural or economic justifications. It is high time that we learn to treat them humanely, if not genuinely protect them as fellow living things. In view thereof, immediate approval of this bill is requested. title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE ANIMAL WELFARE STANDARDS IN THE PHILIPPINES, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE ANIMAL WELFARE BUREAU UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE, THEREBY REPEALING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8485, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10631, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 8485 or known as the The Animal Welfare Act of 1998’s purpose is to protect and promote the welfare of all animals in the Philippines by supervising and regulating the establishment and operations of all facilities utilized for breeding, maintaining, keeping, treating or training of all animals either as objects of trade or as household pets. With the increasing reports of animal cruelty in news and social media, there is a need for stronger enforcement of existing animal welfare laws. As some provisions of the current law have proven insufficient in preventing abuse and ensuring compliance, this measure seeks to enhance the protection and welfare of animals in the Philippines. The proposed legislation aims to address the urgent need to strengthen animal welfare standards by creating the Animal Welfare Bureau, which will be considered as an attached agency with the Department of Agriculture, and impose stricter penalties for violations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly requested. RICARDO S. CRUZ JR. label: HB 10895
title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The persistent prevalence of egregious animal abuse highlights the critical limitations of our current animal welfare penal framework. Under the current regime of Republic Act No. 8485, as amended by Republic Act No. 10631, the relatively light penalties allow even the most sadistic abusers to escape incarceration by availi ng themselves of probation under Presidential Decree No. 968. This loophole effectively undermines the law’s deterrent value and leaves the public crying out for real judicial accountability. This measure directly addresses this gap by establishing a distinct statutory classification for Aggravated Animal Cruelty. By enumerating specific, severe malicious acts, including extreme physical torture, mass poisoning, and exploitation for profit, and elevating their penalties to prisién mayor (six years and one day to eight years), this Bill pushes these offenses beyond the six-year statutory threshold for probation. Consequently, this mandatory, non-probationary sentencing structure ensures that both repeat offenders and first-time perpetrators of heinous animal abuse face certain, actual confinement in a national penitentiary. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. PH CONRAD “DOK' BONG” M. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is one of 18 mega-biodiverse countries in the world, containing two- thirds of the earth’s biodiversity and between 70% and 80% of the world’s plant and animal species. The Philippines ranks fifth in the number of plant species and maintains 5% of the world’s flora.1 Its biodiversity, composed of various flora and fauna, provides resources to meet basic needs for human survival, promotes economic development and offers environmental services. Unfortunately, our country is also a biodiversity hotspot. We continue to lose our forests to commercial exploitation and habitat destruction. Our waters are threatened by chemical pollution, fisheries operations, habitat alteration, and global climate change. This bill seeks to create an Environmental Protection and Enforcement Bureau (EPEB) under the Department of Environment and Natural Resources to give more teeth to the Constitutional mandate to protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology. It also seeks to strengthen the enforcement of environmental laws and regulations in order to truly preserve our incomparably rich biodiversity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is most earnestly sought. LUIS RAYMUND “LRAY” F. VILLAFUERTE, JR. MIGUEL LUIS R. VILLAFUERTE TSUYOSHI ANTHONY G. The Philippines is a biodiversity hotspot as it contains two-thirds of the world's biodiversity in its isolated archipelagic topography, which makes it extremely vulnerable to threats and exploitation of iis natural resources. Forest covers, mangrove areas, and our reefs, which house our endemic flora and fauna, are depleting daily and will continue to decrease if we do not actively protect it. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. MARIA LOURDES NANCY S. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is playing a notoriously substantial role in the illegal trade, not only as a poaching area and transshipment point, but the country has also increasingly become an end destination for exotic pets. Even at the height of the COVID-19 quarantine measures, the illegal trade of wildlife went on in online forums or social media pages. On top of this, illegal logging is still being reported in the field. The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) estimated that the total value of wildlife trafficking alone is at 50 billion pesos, and illegal logging data if aggregated, could even be higher. The estimates do not include trafficking done through the Philippines. With increasing habitat destruction from conversion through logging and encroachment to poaching and the illegal transshipment of wildlife, there are increasing risks of encountering zoonotic diseases due to the degradation of habitats, which will increase human-wildlife interactions. In addition, weak enforcement of pollution laws for environmental threats such as wastewater, solid waste, hospital waste, and hazardous waste, as well as an infraction of protected area laws, rules and regulations have brought numerous issues with tremendous economic problems. This measure seeks to support the initiative within the DENR to professionalize and institutionalize law enforcement in the agency by creating the Enviromnental Protection and Enforcement Bureau (EPEB) through congressional action. Through the EPEB, DENR can strengthen its environmental law enforcement capacity and its synergy with other agencies having environmental law enforcement duties. The EPEB will allow the DENR to target the syndicates responsible for wildlife and timber trafficking. In terms of pollution control and the law on hazardous materials, the EPEB can improve its capabilities to detect and stop these violations, especially those involving hospital wastes and discharges by pollutive industries. The EPEB will utilize advanced skills training on crime scene forensics, intelligence, surveillance, and investigation, DNA, and other criminalistics to go after high-profile perpetrators and build up cases on entire networks of traffickers rather than just the low-level poachers. The forensics lab contained in the proposed measure will cover the entire range of needs of the DENR to address violations of most, if not all, environmental laws, including logging, wildlife poaching, toxic contaminations, pollution, and hazardous materials and wastes. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT CREATING THE ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AND ENFORCEMENT BUREAU (EPEB) UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF ENVIRONMENT AND NATURAL RESOURCES (DENR), DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 16 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution declares: “The State shall protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature.” Far from being a mere policy aspiration, this provision imposes an enforceable legal obligation on the State. This principle was firmly established in the landmark case of Oposa v. Factoran (G.R. No. 101083, July 30, 1993), where the Supreme Court recognized the government’s duty to safeguard the environment not only for the present generation but also for those yet to come. However, despite the existence of various laws, including the Philippine Clean Air Act of 1999 (R.A. No. 8749), Philippine Clean Water Act of 2004 (R.A. No. 9275), Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000 (R.A. No. 9003), Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act (R.A. No. 9147), and the Expanded National Integrated Protected Areas System Act of 2018 (R.A. No. 11038), the country continues to face grave environmental challenges, such as illegal logging, destructive mining, biodiversity loss, hazardous waste dumping, and rampant wildlife trafficking. At present, enforcement responsibilities within the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) are dispersed across multiple offices, resulting in problems with coordination, operational delays, and low prosecution and conviction rates for environmental offenders. This fragmentation has created significant gaps between law and implementation, weakening the effectiveness of these laws. To address these long-standing deficiencies, this bill proposes the creation of the Environmental Protection and Enforcement Bureau (EPEB), a specialized, well-resourced enforcement Bureau under the DENR. The EPEB shall consolidate all environmental enforcement functions into a single, accountable agency, empowered to conduct investigations, apprehend violators, initiate prosecutions, and coordinate with the National Prosecution Service, the Office of the Ombudsman, and other law enforcement bodies. It shall have the authority to issue cease-and-desist orders and abate environmental violations in urgent situations. The EPEB will be equipped with modern forensic laboratories to support the scientific investigation of environmental crimes. This will address a critical gap in past enforcement efforts, where the lack of scientifically sound evidence has often hindered successful prosecutions. To ensure professionalism and continuous capacity-building, the measure also establishes an Environmental and Natural Resources Law Enforcement Academy, which will train all Bureau enforcers and personnel and provide standardized training to local governments and relevant national agencies. This bill further extends Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation (SLAPP) protection to enforcers, complainants, and witnesses, shielding them from retaliatory lawsuits that aim to silence environmental defenders. The creation of the EPEB signifies a transformative shift in how environmental protection is approached: from reactive compliance to proactive enforcement and from fragmented authority to unified command. In the face of accelerating ecological degradation and growing threats to environmental defenders, the immediate passage of this measure is both urgent and necessary. It gives life to the constitutional right to a balanced and healthful ecology and affirms the intergenerational responsibility of protecting the environment. MARLYN L. title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE STOCKPILING OF STRATEGIC AND CRITICAL DRUGS AND MEDICINES, VACCINES, DEVICES, AND MATERIALS FOR THE PUBLIC HEALTH EMERGENCIES, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE HEALTH PROCUREMENT AND STOCKPILING BUREAU UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The COVID-19 global pandemic has seen a lot of lapses in terms of healthcare in the country. There has been a lack in terms of facilities, medicines, professionals, and other lapses which are currently being addressed by the government. The State recognizes that there is a need to protect the welfare of every Filipino. This protection includes the guarantee to every Filipino that resources would be made available to them by the State in times of need and one of the lapses that can be seen during the COVID-19 is the lack of sufficient medicine and its supply. The lack of available medicines made it difficult for healthcare professionals to address the needs of the patients; with some patients even needing their relatives to go around the metro in search for the medicines they so desperately need. The purpose of this measure is to ensure the preparedness of the government in terms of medicine supply when there is a public health emergency. This measure permits the government to stockpile strategic medicines and supplies which are deemed important to overcome the public health emergency. This bill was first filed by Rep. Helen Tan. Without the successful passage of the bill, this measure is being refiled in the 19th Congress. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HARRIS CHRISTOPHER M. title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE STOCKPILING OF STRATEGIC AND CRITICAL DRUGS AND MEDICINES, VACCINES, DEVICES, AND MATERIALS FOR PUBLIC HEALTH EMERGENCIES, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE HEALTH PROCUREMENT AND STOCKPILING BUREAU UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This proposed measure seeks to protect public health and safety by stockpiling essential and critical drugs, medicines, vaccines, devices, and materials to effectively and swiftly address public health emergencies. This bill creates the Health Procurement and Stockpiling Bureau (HPSB) as a body under the Department of Health (DOH) to provide a transparent, fair, proactive, and innovative procurement service to stockpile, conserve, and facilitate the release of life-saving pharmaceuticals, vaccines, devices, and materials in times of public health emergencies. Among other salient responsibilities, the HPSB is responsible for developing plans, policies, and programs on procurement management, taking the procurement process following the Government Procurement Reform Act, advising the Secretary of Health on matters about the procurement of goods and services, infrastructure and consultancy services, managing the Bureau's response activities during a public health emergency, conducting procurement monitoring visits, providing technical assistance to DOH field offices on procurement matters, identifying and stockpiling strategic and critical drugs and medicines, vaccines, devices, and materials needed for public health emergencies, maintaining a buffer supply of these items to ensure the availability of these items, facilitating the provision of potentially life-saving pharmaceuticals, and acting as the supply-chain manager to ensure the rotation and replenishment of stocks. Hence, this representation seeks the passage of this measure. RUDYS CAESAR G. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 2019 report by the Global Preparedness Monitoring Board (GPMB), an independent monitoring and advocacy body that aims to assess the world’s ability to protect itself from health emergencies and identify critical gaps to preparedness across multiple perspectives, warns that humankind is stumbling toward the 21st- century equivalent of the 1918 influenza pandemic, which affected one-third of the world’s population and killed approximately 50 million people. Based on the report, only one third of countries have the capacities required under the International Health Regulations (IHR) and that the great majority of national health systems would be unable to handle a large influx of patients infected with a respiratory pathogen capable of easy transmissibility and high mortality. The Joint External Evaluation (JEE) of IHR Core Capacities of the Republic of the Philippines reveals that “While the Philippines has developed capabilities in various programme areas for public health emergency preparedness and response, there are still challenges in achieving a harmonized approach for implementation of the IHR. Several identified challenges are not only relevant to IHR implementation but are common across the health sector and include the implementation of policies and regulations; effective coordination between national and local levels and among sectors, and investments in institutional capacities.” Accordingly, to capitalize on the momentum generated by the JEE in the Philippines, one of the overarching priority recommendations of the JEE team is to foster the institutional capacity of the health sector to lead the prevention, detection and response to public health events and emergencies. The 2024 GPMB report underscores that pandemics are no longer rare shocks but enduring global threats driven by increased mobility, urbanization, climate change, and human encroachment on ecosystems. The report identifies fifteen (15) key pandemic risk drivers across five domains—social, technological, environmental, economic, and political—using a “STEEP” framework. These drivers, such as social inequity, digital misinformation, urban crowding, environmental degradation, and weak governance, interact over time and amplify vulnerabilities. Current outbreaks, including H5N1 and mpox, illustrate that without early intervention and comprehensive mitigation, localized health crises can rapidly escalate into pandemics. The report emphasizes that preparedness must evolve beyond lessons from COVID-19. The future of pandemic threats will differ significantly and demand adaptive planning, region-specific risk assessments, and integrated, flexible health systems. A key tenet is that anticipatory planning and real-time response capacities are essential, not optional. This bill, which was approved by the House and transmitted to the Senate during the 18th Congress, aims to protect public health by addressing the problem of access to critical drugs and medicines, vaccines, devices, and materials in times of public health emergencies by mandating the procurement and stockpiling of critical and strategic pharmaceuticals and medical devices as well as the supply of raw materials. It is hoped that through this proposal, problems on the lack of access to strategic and critical drugs and medicines, vaccines, devices, and materials in times of national need may now be adequately addressed. Hence, immediate passage of this bill is earnestly being sought. Keith Micah “Atty. Mike” D.L. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE All lands of the public domain, waters, minerals, coal, petroleum, mineral oils, all forces of potential energy, fisheries, forests or timber, wildlife, fora and fauna, and other natural resources are owned by the State. With the exception of agricultural lands, all other natural resources shall not be alienated. Thus, there is a need for rational, optimal and sustainable settlements development, consistent with the principles of environmental management and equitable access to land and security. This bill proposes to provide the national framework for a rational, holistic, and just allocation, utilization, management, and development of the country's land to ensure their optimum use, consistent with the principle of sustainable development. Moreover, the bill will include mandatory consultations from the regional, provincial, city and municipal level. Overall, the goal of this proposed legislation is to harmonize existing plans, rules and regulations governing the allocation, utilization, development and management of land resources. title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A NATIONAL LAND USE POLICY, PROVIDING THE IMPLEMENTING MECHANISMS, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE NATIONAL LAND USE COMMISSION, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE All lands of the public domains, waters, minerals, coal, petroleum, mineral oils, all forces of potential energy, fisheries, forests or timber, wildlife, flora and fauna, and other natural resources are owned by the State. With the exception of agricultural lands, all other natural resources shall not be alienated. Thus, there is a need for rational, optimal, and sustainable settlements development, consistent with the principles of environmental management and equitable access to land security. This bill proposes to provide the national framework for a rational, holistic, and just allocation, utilization, management, and development of the country’s land to ensure their optimum use, consistent with the principle of sustainable development. Moreover, the bill will include mandatory consultations from the regional, provincial, city and municipal level. Overall, the goal of this proposed legislation is to harmonize existing plans, rules and regulations governing the allocation, utilization, development and management of land resources. This proposed bill also provides guidelines in the following major areas: forest lands and watersheds, coastal zones, settlements development areas, protected areas under the National Integrated Area System, agricultural lands, energy resource lands, industrial development areas, tourism development areas, infrastructure development area, and agro-industrial development area. Moreover, land use and physical planning shall at all times adhere to the principles that promote and ensure: (a) Sustainable management and utilization of natural resources; (b) Maintenance and preservation of environmental integrity and stability specifically the perpetual protection of permanent forests and watershed and ecosystem services for the attainment of food, water and energy sufficiency; (c) Disaster risk-reduction and climate change resiliency; (d) Protection of prime agricultural lands for food security in basic commodities with emphasis on self-sufficiency in rice and corn; (e) Water security through sustainable development and management of water resources towards water security; (f) Provision of adequate and efficient settlements, transportation and infrastructure development in support of urban, peri-urban, and rural linkages towards regional development and inclusive growth; (g) Harmony between the rights and the varied interests of every Filipino within the framework of people empowerment, decentralization, social justice, and equity; (h) Respect for and protection of the sustainable traditional resource rights of the Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples (ICCs/IPs) to their ancestral domains to ensure their economic, social, and cultural well-being as well as recognition of the applicability of customary laws and sustainable traditional resource use and management, knowledge, and practices in ancestral domains in compliance with free and prior informed consent of ICCs/IPs; (i) Protection of the rights of basic sectors to equitable access to the country’s land; (j) Protection, preservation, and development of the country’s historical, cultural, archaeological, and built heritage resources for the deeper understanding of our history and culture as a people; (k) Attainment of energy security and self-sufficiency; (1) A whole-of-society and whole-of-government orientation, through which thrusts and strategies espoused by different actors and sectors are heard and brought together to achieve complex and interrelated goals, is encouraged and adopted as a basic parameter in achieving efficiency in land use and allocation, within the framework of ecological development and equity; (m) Promotion of the integrated approach to land use and urban transport planning to effectively manage growth in urban areas and ensure that the capacity of transport facilities can accommodate the demand for movement of passengers and goods to, from, and within the centers of socioeconomic activities; title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A NATIONAL LAND USE POLICY, PROVIDING THE IMPLEMENTING MECHANISMS, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE NATIONAL LAND USE COMMISSION, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A national land use law or policy is long-overdue. For decades, the Philippines has lacked a unified, national framework to guide land use and management. While several laws address specific land-related issues, there remains no overarching policy that integrates and harmonizes these into a coherent land use strategy. This bill seeks to establish a comprehensive and sustainable framework for managing the country's land and natural resources. Its passage is crucial in addressing the growing challenges of environmental degradation, urban congestion, food insecurity, and disaster vulnerability in the Philippines. At present, land use planning in the country is fragmented and governed by overlapping policies and regulations administered by different government agencies. This results in conflicting land uses, inefficient allocation of land resources, and unregulated development. This bill seeks to establish a National Land Use Commission which will serve as the highest policy making body on land use and resolve land use policy conflicts between or among agencies, branches, or levels of the government. It shall also coordinate efforts towards the development of integrated land use plans at the national, regional, provincial. and municipal/city levels, and monitor the implementation of all land use plans including relevant policies. Efforts to pass a national land use act date back to as early as the 9th Congress. Great stride was made, however, during the 19tt Congress when a version of the bill was passed on Third Reading by the Lower Chamber. This version of the bill is the said Third Reading version. This version is the result of the efforts of both the legislative and executive branches of government to come up with a version acceptable to all. It is the joint effort by all relevant stakeholders to finally see a national land use bill to fruition. The importance of a National Land Use Policy cannot be overemphasized. It will provide a sustainable and equitable use of our land and ensure its proper allocation. It will serve as a guide to both national and local planners and address issues of food insecurity, climate change and disaster risks, among others. Considering the importance of this piece of legislation, it’s immediate passage is earnestly sought. FRANCISCQ T. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Under the Regalian doctrine, all lands and all other natural resources belong to the state. This principle is articulated in Section 2, Article XII of the 1987 Constitution which provides: "Sec. 2. All lands of the public domain, waters, minerals, coal, petroleum, and other mineral oils, all forces of potential energy, fisheries, forests or timber, wildlife, flora and fauna, and other natural resources are owned by the State. With the exception of agricultural lands, all other natural resources shall not be alienated." The proposed National Land Use Act (NLUA) proposes a State action to declare a national public policy framework plan that would define policies guiding utilization versus preservation, and indicative uses of land and its resources, from the National government down to the local government units (LGU). There should be orderly allocation of land and its natural use, be it for agricultural, residential, commercial, industrial or mixed use. As a consequence of heavy industrialization and uncontrolled urbanization around the world, the globe has become warmer, oceans are overfished, forests denuded, and the Philippines today is on the hottest spot of the globe. Thus, the Philippines is more prone to natural disasters, particularly typhoons, floods, landslides, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, and tsunamis, lying as it does astride the typhoon belt, in the active volcanic region known as the "Pacific Ring of Fire," and in the geologically unstable region between the Pacific and Eurasian tectonic plates. The Philippines also suffers 1 major human-caused environmental degradation aggravated by a high annual population growth rate, including loss of agricultural lands, deforestation, soil erosion, air and water pollution, improper disposal of solid and toxic wastes, loss of coral reefs, mismanagement and abuse of coastal resources, and overfishing. Climate change is an urgent and serious calamity faced by the nations today. C.J. Puno states: "Climate change represents the most serious, most pervasive environmental threat that the world faces. The issues are not merely scientific; climate change spans political, social, and economic dimensions; crosses national boundaries and reaches beyond the present degeneration. It will aggravate the complex problems of development that we struggle with today like poverty, food, security, and water availability that threaten to ignite large-scale political and social upheavals." [“Redefining Humanity: Seeking Environmental Justice in a World Without Restraint”, Chief Justice Puno] Thus, this bill proposes to come up with an overall framework for rational allocation, disposition, sustainable use and management of land resources, and to prevent the premature conversion of inalienable lands and of agricultural lands to other uses. The proposed measure is also aligned with our commitment to the 17 Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 11, on making cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable; SDG 13 on taking urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts; and SDG 15 on protecting, restoring and promoting sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems, sustainably managing forests, combating desertification, and halting and reversing land degradation and halting biodiversity loss. With this measure, Comprehensive Land Use Plans will be formulated following a combined bottom-up and top-down approach, and a Land Use Policy Council (LUPC) will be created under the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (DepDev). The Council is responsible, among others, for preparing, periodically reviewing, and updating the national framework for physical planning which shall provide the general long-term framework for the spatial development directions and policy guidelines on settlement development, production land use, protection land use and infrastructure development for the entire country and sub-national levels. The National Land Use Act is also identified as legislative agenda of the updated Philippine Development Plan 2017-2022, as it is an essential part of three major thrusts: a) Building safe, resilient and sustainable communities; b) Ensuring ecological integrity, clean and health environment; and c) Expanding economic opportunities In agriculture, forestry, and fisheries and ensuring food security. With a total land area of about 298,170 km2 (29,817,000 hectares), and a total forest cover of 7,226,394 hectares as of 2020, the Philippines has a rich bank of natural resources which should be managed properly as an instrument of economic development, with due regard to environmental sustainability and the realities of climate change. If we hope to conserve our forest cover and inalienable natural resources, if we are to preserve our agricultural lands for self- 2 sufficiency in food production, and if we are to prepare our land to the devastating effects of global warming and climate change, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. This measure was already approved on Third and Final Reading by both houses during the Nineteenth Congress. REP. LANI MERCADO - REVILLA , MSLG, DM (hc) Representative 2 District of Cavite nd REP. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill was approved by the House of Representatives during the 19th Congress. Land is the most tangible and limited resource of any country. It is similarly the most valuable commodity prized by its citizenry and most controversial because not every person can have access to land. In the Philippines, the country’s 30 million hectares of land is shared by the country’s more than 80 million Filipinos. However, not all Filipinos have access to these lands much more own any land. Thus, it is imperative that our country’s land resources are effectively and equitably managed not only by the State and its agencies but also by its people for the sake of generations to come. Because land is a major resource of a country and its people, the utilization of our land resources for national and local development is crucial to maximize the benefits derived from utilization, management and ownership of land. The responsibility of ensuring that the benefits accruing to the country’s land resources rests with the national and local governments. In the case of the national government, it is the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) that is mandated to administer, conserve, protect and manage almost 15.88 million hectares of forestlands or 52.9% of the country’s total land area. Likewise, the DENR, through the Land Management Bureau (LMB), is further mandated to dispose and issue tittles to another 6 million hectares of untitled lands that have been released and classified as alienable and disposable (A&D) lands. On the other hand, the Land Registration Authority (LRA) is responsible for the registration of issued titles released by the DENR or judicially decreed lands totaling another 6 million hectares. However, both agencies operate on totally different system of records, information and document management systems and are guided by outdated legal mandates (e.g. Public Land Act of 1936, Land Registration Act of 1902 and Property Registration Decree of 1978) that are not anymore attuned to present day conditions of land administration in the Philippines. On the other hand, local government units (LGUs) are the key field managers of land resources for both public and private lands. Whilst the DENR and LRA have specific mandates on the over-all administration of public and private lands, LGUs exercise direct administration, preservation, utilization and allocation of land uses and resources at the local levels. In this regard, LGUs have a big stake in the effective and efficient management of land resources in their localities because a large part of the local revenues generated by LGUs in their localities come from income from real property taxes and land related transactions such as transfer taxes. A joint study by the Bureau of Local Government Finance (BLGF) and the National Tax Research Center (NTRC) of the Department of Finance, reported that for the period 2000- 2005, LGUs lost some PhP 9.5 billion yearly due to poor collection efficiency of local property taxes. Among key reasons cited for the poor collection of RPT among LGUs are inefficient 1 collection systems, understated values of assessed real properties compared to real market values and local economic development. It is no wonder that many LGUs are dependent on national revenue transfers, particularly the yearly internal revenue allotments (IRA), because RPT collection which should be the main source of local revenues is a mere 12.5% of the total revenues generated by LGUs. It is fervently prayed and admonished that the proposed National Land Use and Management Act be urgently and readily passed into law so that our future generations of Filipinos will not have to suffer the negligence and distress suffered by our parents and ancestors. We can remedy this malady. In view of the foregoing, immediate approval of this measure is earnestly requested. RUFUS B. RODRIGUEZ MAXIMO B. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines faces longstanding and overlapping issues related to land use, including land registration, agrarian reform, ancestral domain, agricultural modernization, mining, taxation, urban development, housing, and local governance. While many of these are addressed by existing laws, rapid population growth and competing demands on limited resources require a more integrated and strategic approach. The current land-related laws often conflict and lack coordination, resulting in inefficient land use, premature conversion of agricultural lands, and missed opportunities for sustainable development. The absence of a unified framework limits the capacity of national and local governments to make informed, balanced decisions on land allocation. It is vital to systematically integrate and harmonize existing laws, regulatory policies, and planning guidelines related to land use. Such integration is critical to the formulation of a comprehensive and coherent land use framework that will establish definitive parameters for land utilization and ensure the effective implementation and monitoring of land use plans across all levels of governance. This bill aims to establish a unified and strategic framework for the rational allocation, sustainable utilization, and effective management of land resources to support diverse ecological and economic functions. It further seeks to regulate and prevent the untimely conversion of agricultural lands to non-agricultural purposes, thereby preserving their productive value. Furthermore, the proposed measure seeks to define the indicative uses of land and other physical resources across all territorial levels—from the national down to the regional, provincial, city, and municipal levels. This strategic planning instrument will serve as the primary reference and guiding framework for local government units (LGUs) in the preparation, alignment, and implementation of their respective comprehensive land use and development plans. It will ensure consistency with national priorities and the rational distribution of land uses, enabling more coherent spatial planning and resource allocation across jurisdictions. This measure also highlights the indispensable role of land as a finite and strategic resource in driving inclusive and sustainable national development. It emphasizes the need for an organized, equitable, and forward-looking approach to land allocation for various functional uses. As such, the passage of this bill is urgently and strongly recommended to lay the foundation for a more rational, resilient, and inclusive land governance system that supports long-term national development goals. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines constitutional mandates that all public domains, forests, watersheds, coastal zones, protected areas, agricultural lands, and other natural resources—are owned by the State and must be managed sustainably. Yet, recent events have demonstrated a disturbing pattern of abuse and mismanagement across these vital ecosystems. In the Sierra Madre Mountain range, notorious for its critical role as a watershed barrier protecting Metro Manila, illegal logging, slash-and-burn farming, and residential encroachment continue to degrade at least 1,400 hectares annually despite existing protections.1 Similarly, the Kaliwa watershed project threatened ancestral lands and endangered species, drawing widespread criticism from environmental groups and Indigenous communities alike. 2 Within protected landscapes such as the Upper Marikina River Basin and the Masungi Georeserve, developers have defied cease-and-desist orders, leading to illegal quarrying, armed intrusions, and even violent attacks on park rangers—a stark indicator of governance failures in safeguarding National Integrated Protected Areas System (NIPAS) zones.3 Agricultural lands, especially in regions like Central Luzon and Mindoro, are increasingly converted into industrial estates and subdivisions, undermining national food security and violating the mandate to reserve prime farmlands for agricultural use. 1 https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1233008 2 https://thedefiant.net/to-save-the-sierra-madre-the-kaliwa-dam-project-must-be-scrapped 3 https://www.philstar.com/nation/2025/04/08/2434369/check-illegal-reclamation-denr-asked These examples reveal an alarming pattern – the uncoordinated allocation and development of public lands have not only degraded ecosystems but eroded public trust and exacerbated vulnerabilities to climate change and natural disaster. In response, the proposed National Land Use Act seeks to establish an integrated, ridge-to-reef, ecosystem-based planning framework under national oversight, with mandatory consultations across regional, provincial, city, and municipal governments. The bill aims to harmonize conflicting laws and local plans, protect watersheds, forests, coastal areas, agricultural lands, and ancestral domains of Indigenous Peoples, and ensure development is environmentally sound, equitable, resilient, and informed by data. The passage of this legislation is a vital step toward fulfilling our constitutional responsibility to manage land and natural resources sustainably, protect our environment from further degradation, and ensure future generations inherit a resilient and just Republic. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ATTY. GERVILLE “JINKY BITRICS” R. This Commission shall serve as the highest policy-making body on land use and resolve land use policy conflicts between or among agencies, branches, or levels of the government. It shall coordinate efforts towards the development of integrated land use plans at the national, regional, provincial, and municipal/city levels, and monitor the implementation of all land use plans, including relevant policies. The passage of this bill has been a priority measure of the four past Presidents of the Philippines. Similar measures were also approved on third and final reading during the 15'", 16", 17" and 19'" Congresses of the House of Representatives but were unfortunately not enacted into law. This Representation, as a former Senator, also co-authored the same bill with Senator Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan during the 18" Congress but it remained pending at the committee level. Needless to say, the enactment of a National Land Use Act is overdue as efforts to pass this significant legislation already span over three decades. Through this measure, aside from integrating and harmonizing our conflicting laws, policies, principles and guidelines on land use and physical planning, we are upholding social justice and promoting sustainable development for the benefit of our country and people. As a background, land use planning is the process of regulating the use of land in an effort to promote more desirable social and environmental outcomes as well as a more efficient use of resources. Goals of land use planning may include environmental conservation, restraint of urban sprawl, minimization of transport costs, prevention of land use conflicts, and a reduction in exposure to pollutants. By and large, the uses of land determine the diverse socioeconomic activities that occur in a specific area, the patterns of human behavior they produce, and their impact on the environment. In urban planning, land use planning seeks to order and regulate land use in an efficient and ethical way, thus preventing land use conflicts. Governments use land use planning to manage the development of land within their jurisdictions. In doing so, the governmental unit can plan for the needs of the community while safeguarding natural resources. To this end, it is the systematic assessment of land and water potential, alternatives for land use, and economic and social conditions in order to select and adopt the best land use options.1 Often one element of a comprehensive plan, a land use plan provides a vision for the future possibilities of development in neighborhood, districts, cities, or any defined planning area. The unchecked use of land makes the Philippines even more susceptible to natural disasters. It is a tropical country that has been historically prone to harsh weather conditions and calamities. The 2016 World Risk Index report even ranked it 3rd among 171 countries most vulnerable to natural hazards. It has since improved its ranking for 2018 by coming in 69th over 173 countries. The main aspects analyzed in the study are exposure, susceptibility, coping capacity, and adaptive capacity. When speaking of exposure, the study looks into the degree of threat that earthquakes, cyclones or typhoons, floods, droughts, and sea level rise have on the population. Balancing these dangers out are some competencies in public infrastructure (susceptibility), government and disaster preparedness (coping capacity), and ecosystem protection (adaptive capacity). Exposure is unavoidable, as the country notoriously experiences typhoons and floods on an annual basis. It can, however, improve on its public infrastructure, land use, and ecosystem protection. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, being an archipelagic country endowed with vast but finite land and natural resources, faces immense pressure to harmonize the competing demands of production, settlement, protection, and infrastructure development. The lack of a coherent national land use policy has resulted in fragmented land use decisions, unregulated conversion of agricultural lands, encroachment into protected areas, increased exposure to climate-induced disasters, and conflicts among stakeholders. Article XII, Section 2 of the 1987 Constitution provides that all lands of the public domain and natural resources are owned by the State, and mandates their judicious management for the benefit of the Filipino people. Further, Article II, Section 16 declares the State’s responsibility to protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature. Despite these mandates, the absence of an institutionalized framework for land use allocation continues to hinder equitable, sustainable, and efficient development. This bill seeks to institutionalize a National Land Use Policy that will serve as the guiding legal and policy framework for the rational and sustainable management and development of the country’s land and physical resources. By classifying land into four main categories—Protection, Production, Settlements Development, and Infrastructure Development—the measure aims to harmonize spatial planning across all levels of government while promoting ecological integrity, food and water security, climate change resilience, and inclusive growth. This legislative proposal creates the National Land Use Commission (NLUC) under the Office of the President, which shall act as the highest policy-making body on land use. The NLUC will ensure coordination, standardization, and integration among agencies and local government units in the preparation, implementation, and monitoring of land use and physical framework plans. Supporting this structure are Regional, Provincial, and City/Municipal Land Use Policy Councils that will operationalize the land use planning process at the appropriate levels using the ridge- to-reef or watershed ecosystem management approach. The measure strengthens land governance by defining clear procedures and responsibilities for planning, mapping, data management, and inter-LGU coordination. It mandates the preparation of a National Physical Framework Plan (NPFP) and aligns it with regional and local plans such as the Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP), thereby addressing the inconsistencies and overlaps that have long plagued land allocation and development processes. Moreover, this bill introduces safeguards and enforcement mechanisms to protect prime agricultural lands, ancestral domains, critical watersheds, and protected areas from illegal conversion and incompatible uses. It provides mechanisms for the reversion of exhausted mineral and energy lands, encourages land consolidation for agro-industrial development, and upholds the rights of Indigenous Cultural Communities (ICCs/IPs) through recognition of their own land use plans in accordance with RA 8371. Additionally, the bill enforces accountability through incentives for compliant LGUs, and imposes penalties for illegal land conversion, non-implementation of CLUPs, and improper reclassification of protected agricultural areas. The proposed measure likewise includes transitory provisions to ensure a smooth transition and full alignment of existing land use plans with the standards set forth by the NLUC. With the increasing threats of climate change, rapid urbanization, and food insecurity, the need for an integrated land use policy has become even more urgent. This bill envisions a future where land is not only seen as a commodity, but as a vital resource managed for the collective welfare of present and future generations. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. EMILIO BERNARDINO L. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The enactment of this bill envisioned the National Land Use Act (NaLUA) to develop a coherent and strategic framework for the formulation, implementation, and monitoring of national and sub-national land use policies in the Philippines. This proposed measure aims to harmonize existing mechanisms and regulations governing the allocation, utilization, development, and management of the country’s land and physical resources. Land use misgovernance has long been a persistent challenge in the Philippines. Across the country’s approximately 30 million hectares of land, multiple sectors— agriculture, industry, environmental conservation, human settlements, and cultural preservation—compete for finite space and resources. A study undertaken by Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) senior research fellow, Adoracion M. Navarro (2023), underscores that decisions concerning the allocation and enjoyment of use or developmental rights over land have far-reaching implications for industrial productivity, food security, settlement safety, environmental protection, public health, and the nghts of indigenous peoples. Land use conflicts often arise when decisions made in one sector adversely impact others, primarily due to the absence of rational, science-based policies and enforceable standards for land use planning and governance. Further compounding the issue is the fragmented implementation of land use planning at the local level. Many local government units (LGUs) operate with outdated, incomplete, or entirely lacking Comprehensive Land Use Plans (CLUPs) and Provincial Development and Physical Framework Plans (PDPFPs). This planning gap has significant implications for national development, as uncoordinated or inconsistent land use decisions at the LGU level undermine efforts to pursue integrated, inclusive, and sustainable development across the country. The lack of a unified, legally binding national land use policy has led to overlapping institutional mandates, disjointed land allocation, and unregulated land conversions that threaten food security, ecological balance, and disaster resilience. The bill recognizes the urgency of institutionalizing a national land use policy that aligns spatial planning with the country's long-term development goals concerning land resource planning and governance. It also takes into account the longstanding political, economic, and sectoral interests that have historically impeded the passage of this legislation. By establishing clear guidelines for land classification and prioritization, delineating roles and responsibilities across levels of government, and promoting the use of data-driven, participatory planning processes, the proposed National Land Use Act seeks to unify fragmented efforts and ensure that land is governed as a strategic, finite, and vital national resource. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Land is a finite and invaluable resource that must be managed equitably and sustainably for present and future generations of Filipinos. The Philippines has over 30 million hectares of land that can be shared by a population exceeding 110 million, yet not all Filipinos enjoy secure access to or ownership of land. This imbalance that is made worse by overlapping sectoral policies contributes to inefficient land allocation, environmental degradation, and rising inequality. At present, forestlands fall under the jurisdiction of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources, while alienable and disposable lands are managed by the Land Management Bureau, reflecting a fragmented system of governance that urgently calls for a unified, rational framework for national land use planning. ! The proposed National Land Use Act seeks to establish such a framework by institutionalizing a holistic, just, and science-based system for the sustainable management of land and water resources. It rests on the principles of environmental integrity and social justice, while recognizing the social function of land. The measure also emphasizes accountability among landowners to develop and conserve their lands responsibly, while empowering local government units (LGUs) to exercise stronger stewardship over their respective jurisdictions in partnership with national agencies. The passage of this Act is both a strategic and moral imperative. By establishing a comprehensive land use policy, the State can prevent further environmental degradation, ensure food security, protect vulnerable 1 Navarro, Adoracion (December 2023), The Need for a National Land Use Act in the Philippines, Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS). Available at https://pidswebs pids.gov.ph/CDN/document/pidsdps2340. pdf. communities from displacement and disasters, and balance urban, rural, agricultural, and ecological development. It institutionalizes inclusivity, accountability, and sustainability in land management, while affirming the constitutional mandate to promote equitable access to natural resources for the common good. title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A NATIONAL LAND USE AND MANAGEMENT POLICY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Land is a finite resource that underpins every dimension of national development — from food security, housing, and industry, to culture, disaster resilience, and climate adaptation. Yet, for decades, the Philippines has lacked a comprehensive and forward-looking framework to govern the allocation and use of land. The result has been fragmented planning, unchecked conversion, inefficient land markets, and severe vulnerability to natural hazards and climate change. The 1987 Constitution provides that all lands of the public domain, waters, minerals, coal, petroleum, and other natural resources are owned by the State, and that their utilization must promote equitable distribution, sustainability, and the common good. It also mandates the protection of prime agricultural lands, the rights of indigenous peoples to ancestral domains, and the obligation of the State to ensure a balanced and healthful ecology. This bill institutionalizes a National Land Use and Management Policy that is science- based, data-driven, and climate-resilient. It recognizes that sound land use planning requires more than static maps and outdated regulations; it requires probabilistic hazard mapping, geospatial analysis, ecosystem accounting, and evidence-informed decision-making. Land allocation under anne uF * fey this measure shall be continuously updated with real-time data, to minimize exposure to hazards and maximize long-term productivity. The bill also establishes mixed-use and compact development as the default principle in settlements planning. By integrating residential, commercial, institutional, and public spaces into cohesive communities, the State can reduce sprawl, shorten commutes, promote walkability, and lower carbon emissions. Transit-oriented development around transport corridors shall be prioritized to ensure sustainable growth. Critically, the bill introduces a land value capture framework. When public investment in infrastructure, transport, or zoning upgrades increases land values, a portion of that increase must accrue to the public, rather than being captured entirely by private landowners. Mechanisms such as betterment levies, incremental property taxation, and transfer of development rights will ensure that gains in land value are reinvested into socialized housing, resilient infrastructure, and climate adaptation programs. The measure also safeguards prime agricultural lands, watersheds, biodiversity, and cultural heritage through ecosystem-based management, while enabling responsible production, tourism, and industrial development in designated areas. It harmonizes the responsibilities of the national government, local government units, and communities under a clear, transparent, and accountable framework. By institutionalizing this Act, the Philippines will finally establish a comprehensive National Land Use Commission to rationalize policies, harmonize planning, resolve conflicts, and measure outcomes. This approach is both forward-looking and inclusive: it respects indigenous peoples’ rights, empowers LGUs, and requires meaningful participation of civil society and stakeholders. In sum, this bill transforms land from a source of conflict and inefficiency into a platform for inclusive growth, disaster resilience, ecological integrity, and intergenerational equity. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is on a promising economic trajectory. Growth is stable, investments are rising, industries are innovating, and our people are demonstrating confidence in sustainable development. But as we pursue this momentum, we face a critical question: are we using our land—our most finite and valuable resource—wisely? Uncoordinated land use has led to environmental degradation, worsening floods, housing backlogs, food insecurity, and the loss of green spaces. Competing interests for agriculture, industry, housing, infrastructure, and conservation have long operated in silos, often resulting in conflict, inefficiency, and irreversible damage. This bill seeks to change that. The proposed National Land Use Act (NLUA) establishes a clear and unified policy framework to govern the allocation, utilization, and management of land resources across the country. It institutionalizes land use planning at all levels of government— anchored on sustainability, risk reduction, and inclusive development. By ensuring that land is allocated according to its most suitable and strategic use, we protect ecosystems, secure food production areas, promote equitable housing, guide urban growth, and build resilience against climate change. Proper land use is the cornerstone of environmental protection, public health, infrastructure development, and disaster preparedness. To sustain our gains and plan for a livable future, we must legislate now what should have been in place decades ago. The immediate passage of this measure is therefore earnestly sought. ATTY. A national land use plan is an effective tool in harmonizing laws specific to each sector sans overlapping mandates, resolves existing land conflicts, enable sustainable development and inclusive growth. The framework that a national land use plan provides, ensures that competing uses of land are managed rationally because for the longest time, the non-institutionalization of a national level framework for land use and the non-harmonization of sector-specific laws on the utilization of land resources resulted to land use misgovernance in the country. Industrial productivity, food and tenurial security, environment protection, public health and indigenous people’s rights are on top of the list of affected by many decisions on the allocation and enjoyment of use or development rights related to land resources. A national level land use governance policy can help resolve land use conflicts first and foremost given that in the Philippines, one of the most pressing concerns is to minimize land use conflicts. A well implemented national land use plan can support greater and sustainable value addition to the economy because it enables the State to optimize land use and the potential short- to medium-term impacts are the orderly settlement of the years-old land use conflict, prevention of future conflicts, resulting to a potential medium- to long-term impacts on higher productive and sustainable socio-economic development. For the record, the efforts to enact a national land use plan has been going on for almost three (3) decades since the 9th Congress until today. In view of the foregoing, passage of this measure is earnestly sought. SITTIE SHAHARA “BAI DIMPLE” I. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Land is a finite and irreplaceable resource. In the Philippines, the absence of a unified and comprehensive national land use framework has resulted in overlapping land uses, conflicting policies among government agencies, environmental degradation, unplanned urban expansion, and the persistent vulnerability of communities to natural hazards. At present, land use planning is fragmented across various sectoral laws and institutional mandates, leading to inefficiencies and unsustainable development outcomes. Rapid population growth, industrial expansion, increased demand for settlements, agricultural land conversion, and the impacts of climate change further heighten the urgency of establishing a coherent and integrated national land use policy. Without a clear framework that harmonizes competing land use demands, the country risks worsening food insecurity, environmental decline, displacement of vulnerable communities, and the loss of vital ecological buffers. This bill seeks to institutionalize a National Land Use Policy (NLUP) that will provide a rational, holistic, and science-based approach to allocating and managing the country’s land resources. It aims to ensure the highest and best use of land in accordance with the principles of sustainable development, disaster risk reduction, climate resilience, environmental protection, equity, and inclusive growth. To effectively implement this national framework, the bill creates the National Land Use Commission (NLUC)—a central policy-making, coordinating, and monitoring body mandated to harmonize land-related policies, integrate sectoral land use plans, and guide national and local governments in the preparation and enforcement of land use plans. The Commission shall also serve as the primary institution ensuring that land classification, allocation, and utilization are consistent with the national policy and long- term development goals. Through this measure, the State shall clearly delineate land for protection, production, settlements, and infrastructure development, balancing economic growth with environmental integrity and social well-being. It likewise strengthens the capacities of local government units by providing technical standards and ensuring that local land use plans are aligned with national priorities. This bill already passed third reading in the previous Congress and in view of the urgent need to address long-standing issues in land management and to secure a safer, more resilient, and sustainable future for our people, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A NATIONAL LAND USE POLICY, PROVIDING THE IMPLEMENTING MECHANISMS, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE NATIONAL LAND USE COMMISSION, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Land use in the Philippines is currently governed by a patchwork of sectoral laws and local plans (environment, agriculture, housing, forestry, mining, zoning ordinances, etc.), resulting in conflicting classifications, inefficient allocation, and unsustainable land conversion. This has led to numerous problems such as deforestation, loss of agricultural lands, unplanned urban sprawl, and increased vulnerability to natural hazards. To address these long-standing issues, the proposed National Land Use Act seeks to establish a coherent national policy framework and institutional mechanism to guide land classification and planning at national, regional, provincial, and local levels. The bill institutionalizes a comprehensive system of land use planning that harmonizes and integrates the sectoral plans of various government agencies and local governments. It mandates the formulation of a National Physical Framework Plan (NPFP), which will serve as the primary reference for all land-related decisions, ensuring consistency among agricultural, forest, urban, coastal, and protected areas. Also, a Regional Physical Framework Plans (RPFPs), Provincial Physical Framework and Development Plans (PPFDPs), and CLUPs, shall be prepared within their respective territories, consistent with the NPFP. The proposed Act also establishes a National Land Use Commission (NLUC) to oversee the formulation, implementation, and periodic updating of the National Land Use Plan. This agency shall coordinate with the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), Department of Agriculture (DA), Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR), and other concerned institutions to harmonize policies and resolve inter-sectoral land use conflicts. The bill further empowers local government units (LGUs) to align their comprehensive land use plans (CLUPs) with the national framework, while providing them with the necessary assistance to ensure effective implementation. By clearly defining land use categories—such as protection land, production land, settlements, and infrastructure areas—the measure ensures that development is both inclusive and sustainable. It seeks to protect agricultural lands to guarantee food security, preserve forest and watershed areas for ecological balance, and guide urban expansion to prevent congestion and hazards. This bill was already approved on Third Reading during the 19th Congress. With clear direction and strengthened coordination among agencies and LGUs, the Philippines can ensure that every parcel of land contributes to the nation’s prosperity, safety, and environmental well-being. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is eamestly sought. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution declares that all lands of the public domain, forests, watersheds, coastal zones, protected areas, agricultural lands, and other natural resources belong to the State. It further mandates that these resources be conserved, developed, and utilized under the principles of sustainability, social justice, and intergenerational equity. Despite these clear constitutional directives, the current system of land allocation and development remains fragmented, poorly coordinated, and vulnerable to abuse. Recent reports highlight continuing and escalating threats to the Philippines’ natural environment due to unregulated extractive activities, deforestation, and poor waste management. 1 In the country’s nickel belt, expanding nickel mining operations have been documented to seriously degrade ecosystems, harm the health and livelihoods of Indigenous Peoples and rural communities2, and threaten water quality and food security, with inadequate consultation and environmental safeguards drawing widespread criticism from rights and environmental groups.3 Forest loss remains a critical concern, particularly in key ecological zones such as the Sierra Madre, where illegal logging and mining contribute to significant annual forest destruction, undermining biodiversity and climate resilience while weakening natural protections against typhoons and landslides.4 Compounding these land-based impacts are failures in waste management: a catastrophic garbage landslide at the Binaliw landfill in Cebu City in January 2026 resulted in dozens of deaths and exposed systemic weaknesses in environmental oversight and solid waste governance. 1 https://www.philstar.com/headlines/climate-and-environment/2025/11/12/2486728/sierra-madre-losing-9000- hectares-forest-cover-each-year- haribon#:~:text=%22Based%20on%20what%20studies%20are,also%20added%20to%20the%20problem. 2 https://cri.org/reports/broken-promises/ 3 https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2025/01/philippines-nickel-mining-projects-approved-despite- inadequate-consultation-and-serious-risks-to-communities-health-and-environment In response, this proposed measure seeks to establish a National Land Use Act that provides an integrated, ridge-to-reef, ecosystem-based land use planning framework under national oversight. The bill mandates harmonized land use planning across national agencies and local government units, institutionalizes science- and data-driven decision-making, and ensures meaningful participation of stakeholders, including Indigenous Peoples. It aims to align existing laws and policies, safeguard watersheds, forests, coastal and marine areas, agricultural lands, and ancestral domains, and guide development toward outcomes that are environmentally sound, socially equitable, climate-resilient, and economically sustainable. The enactment of this measure is imperative to give full effect to the Constitution’s vision of responsible stewardship over land and natural resources. By instituting a rational and integrated land use policy, the State affirms its duty to protect the environment, reduce disaster risks, secure food systems, uphold the rights of present and future generations, and ensure that development serves the common good. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is respectfully sought. FRANZ S. By providing clear land use classifications, planning standards, and enforcement mechanisms, this bill seeks to ensure that land—being a finite and strategic national resource—is used efficiently, equitably, and sustainably in support of long-term national development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATINGS FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State is directly responsible for providing water security to all citizens and inhabitants of its territory. Water nurtures and sustains life. Civil societies worldwide can neither endure nor survive without properly managing their water resources for the effective and safe use of their people. The Philippines is a water-rich country. According to the World Bank (2015), the annual available water volume per capita in the country is twice that of Asia and six times the global scarcity threshold. Yet, many of our people are deprived of efficient access to affordable, safe, and reliable potable water and to proper sanitation services. This is because the governance and maintenance of our water resources remains fragmented and uncoordinated. To date, there are over 30 government agencies at both the national and local levels implementing separate and disharmonized policies, plans, and programs to develop and operate water facilities and related infrastructure for various uses, and to regulate water use, monitor water-related financial and technical parameters, and set water tariff. The bill proposes to create the Department of Water Resources to serve as the primary agency responsible for national policy-making, coordination, and management of all the water resources in the Philippines. All government agencies related to water shall be rationalized under this Department. Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) shall be adopted as the strategic framework for water management policy-making and planning in the country. IWRM promotes the coordinated development and management of water, land, and related resources in order to maximize economic and social welfare in an equitable manner without compromising the sustainability of vital ecosystems and the environment. The bill also proposes to create an independent Water Regulatory Commission to ensure the effective and adequate delivery of water and sanitation services throughout the country under a credible, transparent, and accountable regulatory tramework. This Commission shall always protect the consumer welfare and reject abusive practices in the water industry. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER, IRRIGATION, SEWAGE AND SANITATION RESOURCE MANAGEMENT, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to rationalize the water, irrigation, sewage, and sanitation resource management, including water rights, through the creation of the Department of Water, Irrigation, Sewage, and Sanitation Resource Management. The Philippines is rich in water sources like rivers, lakes, and groundwater reservoirs which assure its inhabitants adequate water supply for domestic, agricultural, and industrial purposes. However, at present, management of the said water source is lodged with different units or agencies of the government thereby resulting to poorly coordinated or even conflicts in the implementation of the national policies and plans on water, sewage, sanitation, and irrigation thereby resulting to backlog in the provision of water supply and sanitation services to the public. The present set-up for water, irrigation, sewage, and sanitation responsibilities of the government involves, among others, the following major government agencies: a) National Water Resources Board (NWRB), a government agency responsible for the enforcement of the Water Code of the Philippines which is under the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR); b) Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), a govemment-owned and controlled corporation (GOCC) attached to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWhH) and has regulatory powers over: 1) alllocal water districts (LWDs); and 2) rural waterworks and sanitation associations (RWSAs) nationwide; c) Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), aGOCC also attached to the DPWH, which is responsible for the water supply and sanitation in Metropolitan Manila and such contiguous areas as may be added to its area of jurisdiction, and; d) National Irrigation Administration (NIA), a government agency under the Office of the President primarily responsible for irrigation development and management. Upon the United Nations General Assembly's recognition of the human right to water and sanitation and acknowledgement that clean drinking water and sanitation are essential to the realization of all human rights, it is imperative upon the Philippine government to efficiently and effectively manage its water resources to attain ideal allocation of its water resources that will focus primarily on the people's right to safe and affordable drinking water and sanitation service that are indispensable to every citizen's basic health and economic prosperity. The Philippine government must consider the rapid population growth, common waterbome diseases like diarrhea, leptospirosis, and dengue, agricultural requirements for food production, water pollution, watershed degradation, climate change, and other related factors that need to be adequately addressed without delay. it must be stressed that the Philippine government's responsibility to safe, clean, accessible and affordable drinking water, sanitation, and irrigation service to the publicis of utmost importance and it is attainable through well-coordinated, effective, efficient and sustainable management of its water and sanitation resources. Hence, there is an immediate need to create the Department of Water, Irrigation, Sewage and Sanitation Resource Management which shall have the following primary functions: 1. Setthe policies for water supply and sewage and sanitation management; 2. Develop and manage the country's water resources to ensure optimal use, including but not limited to domestic usage, irrigation, power generation, industrial, agricultural and commercial use; 3. Build maintain and monitor water-related infrastructure water quality and accessibility; 4. Regulate the operation and management of water utilities such as MWSS, LWDs, RWSAs and other water and sanitation service providers; 5. Make available and/or provide financial assistance to non-viable LWDs for the improvement of water facilities or services through funds prior and future appropriations ofthe National Government for waterworks and sewerage systems; 6. Regulate and control the utilization, exploitation, development, conservation and protection of all water resources; 7. Administer and enforce the provisions of Water Code of the Philippines; 8. Plan, design, construct, and/or improve all types of irrigation projects and appurtenant structures; 9. Operate, maintain, and administer all national irrigation systems (NIS); 10. Supervise the operation, maintenance, and repair, or otherwise, administer temporarily all communal and pump irrigation systems constructed, improved, and/or repaired wholly or partially with government funds; 11. Delegate the partial or full management of NIS to duly organized cooperatives or associations; 12. Construct multiple-purpose water resources projects designed primarily for irrigation, and secondarily for hydraulic power development and/or other uses such as flood control, drainage, land reclamation, domestic water supply, roads and highway construction, and reforestation, among others, Provided, that the plans, designs, and the construction thereof, shall be undertaken in coordination with the agencies concemed; 13. Charge and collect from the beneficiaries of the water from all irrigation systems constructed by or under its administration. In view of the foregoing, approval of this measure is earnestly requested.
