explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 1 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution mandates that “The State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all.” In fulfillment of this constitutional mandate, Republic Act No. 6728, also known as the “Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education Act,” was enacted in 1989. This law was later expanded through Republic Act No. 8545 in 1998 under the “Expanded Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education Act.” These laws were designed to provide government assistance to students and teachers in private educational institutions as part of the government's broader effort to provide subsidies and incentives to both public and private learning institutions. However, despite the significant progress these laws have made in promoting access to education, the circumstances surrounding the educational landscape have evolved substantially over the past two decades. In recent years, there has been a notable decline in the enrollment figures for private basic education, and millions of students have been forced to either transfer to public schools or, worse, drop out altogether. Many of these students, specially those from disadvantaged backgrounds, are unable to continue their education due to financial constraints. The exodus of students from private to public schools and the decline in overall private school enrollment highlight a critical issue: the existing government support system is no longer sufficient to meet the needs of students in private elementary and lower secondary schools. This situation necessitates urgent legislative action. The current coverage of Republic Act No. 8545 is limited to students in private junior and senior high schools, leaving students in private elementary schools—many of whom are from the most disadvantaged sectors of society—without any form of financial assistance. In addition, teachers in private elementary schools have also been excluded from the Teacher’s Salary Subsidy Fund, despite facing similar financial pressures as their counterparts in higher education. This bill aims to address these gaps by expanding the scope of government support to include private basic education students at all levels—kindergarten, elementary, junior high, and senior high. Additionally, it will provide further assistance to the private institutions and teachers that are part of the government voucher program. The goal of this proposed legislation is not only to bridge the financial divide but also to ensure that every Filipino student, regardless of their chosen educational institution, has access to the resources and support they need to succeed. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. GISELLE MARY L. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 2022 Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) showed that the Philippines ranked 76th out of 81 countries in reading comprehension, mathematics, and science. This is a slight improvement from the country’s placing of being last among all 79 participating countries in 2018.1 However, this data showing lagging student competency remains a major concern, especially with the considerable delays in class openings due to extreme weather conditions affecting our students’ continuous learning. The Department of Education (DepEd) stated that 23.8 million students are enrolled from elementary to senior high school for School Year 2024-2025. Out of this number, 2.7 million are enrolled in private schools.2 Over the years, the private education sector played a crucial role in addressing the challenges haunting the education system of the country. It complements the efforts of the government in providing quality education to learners across all levels and expanding access to various learning opportunities for both learners and teachers. In recognition of the role of the private education institutions in providing quality education, Republic Act No. 8545, also known as the “Expanded Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education Act”, was enacted into law in 1998. This law sought to decongest our public schools and allowed the provision of financial aid to student and teachers in private schools, especially in geographically isolated areas. However, the fast- evolving concerns within the education system necessitate the more than two-decade old law to be updated. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Access to quality basic education remains a persistent challenge. Nearly one in three public schools continues to operate beyond ideal capacity, according to Department of Education (DepEd) 2024 data, hampering learning and widening achievement gaps. At the same time, many small and community-based private schools struggle with dwindling enrolment and limited resources, despite their crucial role in areas underserved by the public system. Republic Acts Nos. 6728 and 8545 laid the groundwork for Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education (GASTPE). However, narrow coverage, outdated subsidy levels, and inadequate institutional support have constrained their impact. Recognizing these gaps, Senator Paolo Benigno "Bam" Aquino IV filed a Senate bill proposing the Private Education Voucher Expansion (PEVE) Act. Guided by the spirit and substantive reforms of his measure, this counterpart House Bill seeks to modernize government support for private basic education, empower parental choice, and reinforce the complementary roles of public and private institutions. The bill expands voucher coverage from kindergarten through senior high school; creates the Bureau of Private Education (BPE) under DepEd to administer the program and oversee quality standards; establishes a Teachers’ Salary Subsidy Fund and an In-Service Training Fund; and streamlines program administration through the Basic Education Assistance Council (BEAC) and a dedicated Government Assistance and Subsidies Service. It provides an equitable, transparent framework to channel public funds where they generate the greatest learning gains while alleviating congestion in the public system. Prompt enactment of this measure will widen access, elevate teaching quality, and strengthen thousands of private schools that complement the State’s duty to provide basic education for all. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Education is a constitutionally guaranteed right and a cornerstone of national development. Under Article XIV, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution, the State is mandated to “protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all.” However, despite substantial government investment in public education, many Filipino learners, particularly those from poor, remote, or underserved communities, remain unable to access quality basic education due to overcrowded public schools, lack of nearby facilities, or limited capacity of the public school system. The Department of Education (DepEd) reported that over 23.8 million students were enrolled in basic education, of which 10.92% (2.6 million) were in private schools. Many of these private schools help fill gaps in access, especially in areas where public schools are congested or unavailable. Yet, despite their critical role, private schools have seen declining enrollment largely due to financial hardship among families and limited government support. To address these challenges and uphold the State's duty to provide equitable and quality education for all, this bill proposes the establishment of the Private Basic Education Voucher Program, as well as the creation of a dedicated Bureau of Private Education (BPE) under the Department of Education. This proposed measure aims to institutionalize a national voucher system that supports Filipino learners from underprivileged and middle-income families to enroll in qualified private schools for kindergarten, elementary, and secondary levels. The voucher amount will be determined based on need, congestion levels of nearby public schools, and geographic accessibility, giving priority to students who otherwise would have limited educational options. 1 Additionally, the proposed measure repeals selected provisions of Republic Acts No. 6728 and 8545 (GASTPE laws) to modernize and strengthen the legal framework of government assistance to students and teachers in private education. It also ensures that the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) can implement its own version of the program, while still coordinating with DepEd for technical assistance and national alignment. In a country where over 50% of public schools are considered overcrowded and where access to quality education remains highly unequal, this legislative measure will not only reduce the strain on public schools but will also protect educational choice for families, uphold teacher welfare, and revitalize the role of private institutions in nation-building. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The right to quality education is a cornerstone of national development and a fundamental guarantee under the 1987 Philippine Constitution. As provided in Article XIV, Section 1, the State is mandated to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and to take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all. While the government continues to strengthen the public education system, it also recognizes the indispensable role of private educational institutions in realizing this constitutional mandate. To this end, the State must adopt a more inclusive and equitable approach that empowers Filipino families with greater access to quality basic education, regardless of whether it is offered by public or private schools. Over the decades, this vision has been pursued through a dual system that recognizes the vital, complementary roles of both public and private educational institutions in delivering basic education. In many communities across the country, private schools have long filled the gaps left by limited public school capacity, especially in underserved or densely populated areas. Despite this, government support for private education remains constrained, fragmented, and in need of systemic reform. The current programs, while beneficial, are no longer fully aligned with the evolving needs of Filipino learners and the changing landscape of basic education. This proposed measure seeks to institutionalize a more effective, inclusive, and accountable mechanism for supporting private basic education in the Philippines. It aims to empower students and their families, particularly those in congested urban areas, low-income communities, and geographically disadvantaged regions—with real educational choices through a well-targeted voucher system. By providing financial assistance directly to learners, the government enables them to access private schools that meet minimum quality standards, helping to reduce class congestion in public schools while promoting equitable access to learning opportunities. Crucially, this bill affirms the principle of student-centered funding. Instead of relying solely on the expansion of infrastructure, the measure invests in learners themselves and strengthens the capacity of private institutions that commit to quality, transparency, and service to the Filipino public. It acknowledges the socioeconomic realities faced by many Filipino families and provides differentiated levels of support based on income brackets and school access. In doing so, the measure ensures that children from disadvantaged backgrounds are prioritized and empowered with genuine school choice. The measure also introduces governance reforms, including the creation of a dedicated bureau within the Department of Education to oversee private education policy, ensure quality assurance, and enforce standards. By streamlining administration and building institutional accountability, the State reinforces its responsibility to ensure that public funds are used effectively and that students’ rights to safe, inclusive, and high-quality education are upheld. In addition to student subsidies, the bill institutionalizes support for private school teachers through the creation of a Teachers' Salary Subsidy Fund and an In-Service Training (Inset) Fund. These funds are aimed at narrowing the resource and skills gap between public and private educators, especially those in schools located in remote or disadvantaged communities. Through targeted subsidies and professional development support, the bill seeks to uplift the teaching profession within the private education sector. Finally, this legislative proposal represents a long-overdue recalibration of the government’s education policy—one that is equitable, forward-looking, and rooted in the principles of inclusive development. By providing targeted financial assistance to deserving students and support to private educational institutions, this measure upholds the constitutional right to quality education and ensures that no Filipino child is denied the opportunity to learn simply because of where they live or how much their family earns. In view of the urgent need to strengthen the private education sector as a reliable partner in nation-building and to provide Filipino learners with greater access to educational choices, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 1 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution mandates that “The State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all.” Public and private educational institutions are partners in the delivery of basic education services. However, due to persistent issues in the public education system, including classroom shortages, overcrowding, and under-resourced facilities, many families turn to private schools, which often remain inaccessible to underprivileged students due to high costs. This proposed measure seeks to institutionalize a comprehensive and equitable Private Basic Education Voucher Program that will provide government subsidies to eligible students enrolling in recognized private basic education institutions. The measure addresses the need to create sustainable, transparent, and accountable funding mechanisms to assist deserving learners, especially those from middle- and low-income households, as well as those in underserved and geographically isolated areas. This bill builds upon the Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education (GASTPE) program, but also repeals several provisions under Republic Act Nos. 6728 and 8545 to modernize and restructure the delivery of assistance in a manner more responsive to current educational and socio-economic realities. This measure introduces differentiated voucher amounts based on vulnerability and need, empowers families with greater choice through access to a registry of participating schools, and mandates rigorous quality assurance and performance monitoring mechanisms. Furthermore, this bill affirms the equitable distribution of resources across all regions, including the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), with consideration for existing educational infrastructure and poverty incidence. It also provides mechanisms for transparency and accountability in the use of public funds by participating institutions. This proposed legislation ensures that the right to education is not determined by economic capacity or geographic location, but by a shared commitment to uplift the Filipino child through equitable support for both public and private education sectors. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. EMILIO BERNARDINO L. While the public school system remains the primary channel for delivering free basic education, persistent challenges such as classroom shortages, congestion in urban schools, and uneven teacher-student ratios continue to affect learning outcomes. These issues have been compounded by rapid population growth and the increasing demand for quality accessible education. To address these challenges, it is necessary to harness the capacities of both public and private education sectors in delivering basic education services. Republic 1|P age Act No. 6728, as amended by Republic Act No. 8545, otherwise known as the “Expanded Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education Act (E-GASTPE)” was enacted to provide financial support to students and teachers in private educational institutions. Private schools help fill gaps especially in areas where public schools are congested or unavailable. However, private schools have seen declining enrolment largely due to financial hardship among families and limited government support. The proposed Private Basic Education Voucher Program (PBEVP) seeks to institutionalize a national voucher system that will provide financial support to Filipino learners, especially the underprivileged, to enroll in qualified private basic education institutions for kindergarten, elementary, and high school when public schools are overcrowded or inaccessible. It shall establish clear eligibility criteria, accreditation standards for participating schools, and transparent mechanisms for voucher allocation. The Bureau of Private Education under the DepEd will also be established to oversee and regulate all matters related to private basic education, ensuring accountability and effective management of assistance programs. This measure likewise assists qualified teachers in private education institutions through the provision of in-service training fund, scholarships, and government-funded training and provides salary subsidies to teachers of private basic education. It mandates the DepEd to create a system that allows students and parents to select their preferred schools from a registry of participating schools. Through the PBEVP, the government can maximize existing educational infrastructure across sectors, alleviate pressure on the public school system, and provide Filipino learners with more choices for quality education. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE For the past years, the Department of Education (DepEd) has been concentrating mainly on the needs of public schools. Although problems in the public educational institution are enormous and deserving of much attention, the DepEd should not lose sight of the whole picture. Private Education also has its own problems, wants, and areas for improvement which have to be addressed and resolved as well. Yet, it cannot be denied that only limited time and efforts are given to private schools. To illustrate, DepEd assigns only one supervisor in charge of one division which houses many private schools. It is noteworthy that despite Metro Manila having close to 2,000 private schools, since there are only 16 divisions therein; accordingly, there are only 16 supervisors which oversee all these private schools. Clearly, there is a shortage of supervisors for private schools; and usually, the same supervisors are also tasked to attend to other assignments such as scouting, nutrition, teaching, and lastly, the organization and management of the private schools. Considering the dilemma faced by the private schools, it is about time that a bureau is created that will exclusively cater to the needs of private education specifically in the private elementary and high school levels. Through the creation of the Bureau of Private Schools, all matters concerning private education in private elementary and high schools shall all be directed to a centralized department. All concerns, problems, transactions, and activities relating to private schools will now be heard and catered to immediately by the said Bureau. By doing this, the DepEd's load of work will definitely be lessened and unclogged. On the other hand, meeting the concerns of the private elementary and high schools will be fast tracked. Clearly, the creation of the Bureau of Private Schools promises whether efficiency and output. Moreover, it also ensures that all problem coming from public or private schools, will be attended to extensively. This bill has been previously approved on Third Reading by the 19t Congress and recognizing the wisdom and noble intents of the colleagues in the last Congress, it is for this reason that the approval of this Bill is hereby being sought. ow CC. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 17, Article II of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall give priority to education, science and technology, arts, culture, and sports to foster patriotism and nationalism, accelerate social progress, and promote total human liberation and development. Further, Section 1, Article XIV provides that the State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all. Private educational institutions have been facing difficulties years. During the COVID-19 pandemic, enrollment dropped by 48%. Even thereafter, many students had already been transferring to public schools due to private school teachers moving 1 to the public sector due to better compensation and job security. This shift has not only strained private schools but has also placed immense pressure on the public school system, which must absorb the growing number of transferees, often without commensurate resources. Republic Act No. 6728, or the “Expanded Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education Act” (E-GASTPE) was enacted to provide financial support to students and teachers in private educational institutions. However, since its passage, the educational landscape has significantly evolved, rendering some of its provisions outdated and insufficient to address current challenges. Thus, there is a need to update and expand the scope of E-GASTPE — one that is responsive to the current realities, strengthens private education, and reinforces the complementary roles of public and private institutions in delivering accessible, quality basic education to all Filipino learners. This bill seeks to institutionalize and improve the voucher program and create the Bureau of Private Education – a specialized bureau under the Department of Education (DepEd) that will oversee and regulate all matters related to private basic education, ensuring accountability and effective management of assistance programs. This bill was filed by Representatives Roman T. Romulo, Ruth Mariano- Hernandez, Ron P. Salo, among others, during the Nineteenth Congress and was approved on Third Reading. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. YEDDA MARIE K. In the National Capital Region alone, there are 16 Schools Divisions with only 16 supervisors to oversee 516 public elementary and 456 public junior and senior high schools. In addition to that, there are also 1,982 private pre-schools, 2,122 private elementary schools, 965 private junior high schools and 721 private senior high schools serving more than 2.8 million children in the region which are also under their supervision. This bill seeks to establish a Bureau of Private Schools under the DepEd in full recognition of the vital role that the private education sector plays in the Philippine education system and to oversee and address the problems and concerns of private schools throughout the country. It is hoped that through this initiative, the private education in the country will be strengthened to become partners of the government in nation building through the promotion of accessible, affordable, and quality education for all the Filipino youth. In view thereof, early approval of this bill is earnestly sought. p< — Keith Micah “Atty. Mike” D.L. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Access to quality basic education remains a pressing issue in the Philippines. Many public schools continue to struggle with overcrowded classrooms, inadequate facilities, and limited resources—all of which negatively impact teaching quality and student learning. Data from the Department of Education show that nearly one in three public schools operate beyond their ideal capacity, making it difficult to deliver effective instruction. Meanwhile, numerous private schools—particularly small and community-based institutions—are facing declining enrollment and financial difficulties. These schools play an important role in serving areas that the public sector cannot fully reach. However, without adequate support, many of them cannot sustain operations or invest in improving education quality. Republic Act No. 6728, later amended by Republic Act No. 8545 or the Expanded Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education (E-GASTPE) Act, laid the groundwork for government support to private schools. Yet, its implementation has been limited due to narrow coverage, outdated systems, and insufficient institutional support for private schools and their teachers. To address these gaps, the proposed Private Education Voucher Expansion (PEVE) Act aims to modernize and strengthen government assistance for private basic education by repealing outdated provisions of RA 8545 and establishing a more inclusive, responsive, and accountable framework. The bill introduces the following reforms: ● Expanded Coverage: The voucher program will be extended to learners from kindergarten to senior high school, ensuring access to private education across all levels of basic education. ● Empowered Parental Choice: Eligible students and their families can select from a registry of DepEd-recognized private schools, depending on available slots. This learner-centered approach empowers parents to choose schools that best suit their children’s needs. ● Institutional Support for Private Schools: The measure provides additional government assistance, including in-service funds and a Teachers’ Salary Subsidy Fund, to improve teaching quality and attract competent educators. ● Creation of the Bureau of Private Education (BPE): A new bureau under DepEd will manage the voucher program, regulate private schools, enforce standards, and extend technical and developmental support to participating institutions. Through these reforms, the bill strengthens the government’s commitment to building a balanced and inclusive education system. It not only upholds the original intent of GASTPE but also responds to present-day challenges such as unequal access, the need for flexibility, and the demand for innovation. By reinforcing the complementary roles of public and private schools, the measure ensures that both sectors contribute effectively to national education goals. Ultimately, it seeks to expand opportunities for learners, reduce overcrowding in public schools, and support the sustainability and continuous improvement of private basic education. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The proposed amendment to the Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education Act which was passed on third reading by the 19th Congress, seeks to modernize and strengthen the framework for supporting students and teachers in private basic education in the Philippines. Recognizing education as a fundamental right, the measure aims to provide broader access to quality basic education for learners who choose to attend private institutions. The bill introduces a voucher-based system, empowering parents and students by allowing them to select their preferred schools from a registry of participating recognized private schools, enhancing equitable access to education. It also establishes the Bureau of Private Education under the Department of Education to oversee and regulate the program, ensuring participating schools meet quality standards, maintain accountability, and appropriately use allocated funds. The bill provides support not only for students but also for teachers in private basic education institutions, including salary subsidies, in-service training, scholarships for graduate studies, and institutional development assistance for schools. Participating schools are required to allocate at least 70% of any tuition increase to teaching and non-teaching personnel salaries and benefits, and at least 20% to modernization of facilities, with strict monitoring and reporting mechanisms in place. The program prioritizes equitable fund allocation across regions, including vulnerable and underprivileged learners, and enforces transparency, oversight, and accountability. Through these measures, the bill seeks to strengthen the capacity and quality of private basic education while promoting educational equity, accountability, and choice. It also addresses fiscal sustainability by gradually rolling out the voucher program in a phased manner and ensuring proper oversight of resources. By modernizing the assistance mechanism, establishing a dedicated regulatory bureau, and enhancing teacher and school support, the bill reinforces the complementary role of private schools in the Philippine education system. Ultimately, these reforms align with the State’s constitutional mandate to provide access to quality basic education for all learners, ensuring that both students and educators in private institutions are supported and empowered. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Philippine Constitution is very explicit in promoting the right of all Filipinos to quality education, to wit: "The State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such accessible to all" (Article XIV, Section 1). Article XIV, Section 1 provides: "The State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate actions to make such education accessible to all." Section 2 likewise provides that The State shall: 1. Establish, maintain, and support a complete, adequate, and integrated system of education relevant to the needs of the people and society; 2. Establish and maintain, a system of free public education in the elementary and high school levels. Without limiting the natural rights of parents to rear their children, elementary education is compulsory for all children of school age; 3. Establish and maintain a system of scholarship grants, student loan programs, subsidies, and other incentives which shall be available to deserving students in both public and private schools, especially to the under-privileged; 4. Encourage non-formal, informal, and indigenous learning systems, as well as self-learning, independent, and out-of-school study programs particularly those that respond to community needs; and 5. Provide adult citizens, the disabled, and out-of-school youth with training in civics, vocational efficiency, and other skills. Thus, it is the right of all students to keep their education, no matter what their social and economic status is. Republic Act No. 6728, as amended by RA 8545, otherwise known as the Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education Act, was enacted to provide a more cost-effective alternative to building more classrooms and hiring more teachers—which may take a while to complete compared with transferring public school students to private schools through the voucher program to immediately address school congestion. Through this bill, access to quality education especially to underprivileged students is within reach as a comprehensive voucher system aimed at helping poor students enroll in private basic educational institutions and alleviate congestion in public schools will be established. This measure also removes outdated provisions and integrates more flexible approaches to funding and regulation of private education through the voucher system. Further, a central government institution tasked with carrying out the objectives of this measure will be established. By redistributing the growing student population in public schools, this legislation not only enhances the student's access to quality education but also addresses the lingering issue of congestion in public schools nationwide. For these reasons, urgent passage of this bill is earnestly sought. These schools play a vital role in the education system, particularly in areas underserved by the public sector. Through these reforms, the bill strengthens the government's commitment to a balanced and inclusive education system. It builds on the original objectives of GASTPE but goes further by responding to the realities of today's education challenges, including inequality In access, and a need for greater flexibility and innovation. The measure reinforces the complementary roles of public and private educational institutions, ensuring that both sectors are equipped to contribute to national education goals. By promoting access, equity, and quality across the basic education system, the bill expands opportunities for learners, eases pressure on public schools, and supports the sustainability and continuous improvement of private basic education. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Education is the foundation of national progress. It empowers our youth, uplifts families, and builds a nation capable of competing in a globalized world. Under the 1987 Constitution, the State is mandated to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and ensure that such education is accessible to all.! It likewise recognizes the vital partnership between public and private institutions in fulfilling this constitutional promise.? In pursuit of this mandate, the government established the Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education (GASTPE) program. Piloted in the 1980s and later institutionalized under Republic Act (RA) No. 6728, as amended by Republic Act No. 8545 or the “Expanded Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education Act (E-GASTPE)’, the program aims to improve access and quality of education through shared responsibility between the public and private sectors. ' CONST., art. XIV, sec. 1. ° CONST., art. XIV, sec. 4 (1). Under E-GASTPE, the government provides financial assistance to students and teachers in private schools through key programs such as: (a) Educational Service Contracting (ESC) or financial assistance ranging from P8,500 to P13,000 to qualified elementary school graduates who wish to pursue Junior High School (JHS) in private schools; (b) Teacher’s Salary Subsidy of P1,500 per month for licensed teachers in ESC-participating JHS; and (c) a Voucher Program for Senior High School (SHS) in the form of around P14,000 to P22,500 in tuition subsidies to qualified Grade 10 completers to assist them in enrolling in SHS in private non-Department of Education public schools. While these programs have expanded opportunities for thousands of learners, challenges remain. Public schools continue to face overcrowding, and the selection and allocation process under the E-GASTPE does not guarantee that assistance reaches the most disadvantaged students. To address this pressing concern, this bill removes outdated provisions and integrates more dynamic, flexible approaches to funding and regulation of private education through vouchers; expands the government assistance to private basic education to include learners from Kindergarten to Grade 6, decongests overcrowded classrooms in public basic education schools through prioritization of learners belonging to low income households through targeted-beneficiary system, and supports teachers by providing in-service training funds, scholarships for advanced studies, and financial support for institutional enhancements in accredited private basic education schools. In view hereof, the urgent passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ‘ pant Ae MARK A. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Access to quality basic education remains uneven. Public schools continue to face overcrowding and resource constraints that impair learning outcomes, while many private basic education institutions, particularly small and community based schools, play a critical role in expanding access but are increasingly strained by declining enrollment and financial pressures. To address these challenges, the State has long pursued a policy of shared responsibility between the public and private sectors. Republic Act No. 6728, as amended by Republic Act No. 8545 or the Expanded Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education Act, established government support mechanisms for private education through financial assistance to learners and teachers. However, the existing framework has become fragmented and limited in scope. It does not adequately address public school congestion, ensure effective targeting of beneficiaries, or provide a coherent institutional structure for sustained engagement with private basic education. This measure seeks to modernize government support for private basic education by institutionalizing a Private Basic Education Voucher Program. It consolidates existing assistance mechanisms into a unified voucher based framework that expands coverage from kindergarten to senior high school, prioritizes learners from low income households, and supports the decongestion of overcrowded public schools. The bill further recognizes the complementary role of private schools by providing institutional support, including teacher development and targeted assistance to participating institutions. To ensure effective administration and quality assurance, it establishes a Bureau of Private Education under the Department of Education to oversee program implementation and regulatory compliance. By strengthening public private partnership in basic education, this bill promotes equitable access, more efficient use of public resources, and improved education outcomes. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is naturally endowed with rich coastal resources. It has a coastline of 36,289 kilometers. Its territorial waters including its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) total 2.2 million square kilometers, of which 266,000 are coastal while the rest are oceanic (Department of Agriculture-Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources, Philippine Fisheries Profile, 2011:15). The country's coral reef areas are amongst the most extensive in the world, second only to its neighbor Indonesia. It has large tracts of mangrove forests and sizable sea grass areas scattered around Its coasts. In fact, the country is considered to be the apex of the Coral Triangle, which is recognized as the world's center of marine biodiversity (National Plan of Action for the Coral Triangle Initiative on Coral Reefs, Fisheries and Food Security, 2009:1). A separate Department must be created to focus on fisheries and aquatic resources. Technically speaking, fisheries deal with the sustainable management of fisheries and other aquatic resources and ensuring an ecosystem-based approach to cover production, through capture and culture, processing and marketing of fish and other living species from the aquatic environment and the livelihoods and settlement of artisanal fisherfolk. On the other hand, agriculture refers to cultivation of land for crops and rearing animals to provide food. A separate department will institutionalize a workforce that is solely dedicated to the management of the country's fisheries and aquatic resources and untappIng the potentials of the blue economy. According to Philippine Agriculture 2020 of the National Academy of Science and Technology of the Department of Science and Technology (DOST), "Fisheries is too big of a problem to be handled by the DA which Is already beset with many problems and challenges like declining productivity and competitiveness." For an agency exercising supervision over fisheries and aquatic resources to be truly efficient, it must have necessary funding to undertake and implement comprehensive programs and policies. At present, BFAR has limited funding because it depends on the budgetary allocation of its mother agency, the DA. It covers the function meant for a department but only gets a limited budget meant for a line bureau. BFAR reported that It needs PHP 60 billion to properly implement fisheries law enforcement and management. But for Fiscal Year 2019, out of the DA budget of PHP 47,293,174,000, BFAR was only allocated PHP 5,758,003,000.10. Elevating the Bureau to a Department will likewise increase its budgetary allocations. The fisheries sector has a significant contribution to the country's economy hence it is only fitting that a government agency exercising authority over it will be equipped with financial muscle to perform its mandate. A Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources can provide Institutional support to maximize the potential of the Blue Economy and to Implement the Comprehensive National Fisheries Industry Development Plan and the Comprehensive Post Harvest, Marketing and Ancillary Industries Plan. The estimated total contribution of the maritime sector to the Philippine economy, including the fishing industry, was valued at Php210.39 billion in 2019. This accounts for 2.6% of the country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP). To reiterate the findings of the NAST study, potentially, the Net Annual Benefit from our marine ecosystem under the Blue Economy is conservatively estimated at Php 317.33 Billion. The Blue Economy has likewise produced employment to 1.53 million persons in 2019 and directly employs around 1.9 million registered fisherfolk. It still has great potential for growth if a strong institution will provide necessary staffing and funding. There is also a need for strong institutional support to implement the CNFIDP (2016- 2020) and the CPHMAIP (2018-2022). Over a 5-year period, given the funding of Php30.6 billion and the staffing, the CNFIDP targets a 1% annual growth in municipal capture fisheries, 5% annual growth in commercial capture fisheries and 10% reduction In post­ harvest losses. In aquaculture, the CNFIDP targets a 4% Increase in milkfish production, 25% increase in seaweeds production, 10% Increase in shellfish production, 5.4% increase in mangrove crab production, 10% increase in shrimp production and 6% increase in tilapia production. In terms of the CPHMAIP, total Investment requirement Is estimated at Php29 billion with projected accrued benefit at Php74 billion over a 5-year period. Moreover, under the developmental framework of the Blue Economy, DFAR will now have the necessary resources to capitalize the huge potential of our marine resources, thus restoring its condition, enhancing sustainability, and at the same time, providing Increased revenues to our country's coffers. « The passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is one of the countries often visited by strong typhoons. Around nineteen tropical storms enter the Philippine area of responsibility in a typical year and, of these, usually six or nine make landfall. Natural disasters of increasing magnitude and frequency, such as typhoon Haiyan, have continued to affect our country, which is now the second most vulnerable in the world to disasters and climate change. Nearly 74 percent of the population and 80 percent of the land area are identified as vulnerable to disasters, with the capital of Manila considered at "extreme risk." This "new normal” requires a more focused and in-depth attention in the way we understand, prepare, and respond to natural disasters. Notwithstanding all the disaster preparation and coordination plans, there were still significant losses of life, injury, and damage to property when Typhoon Yolanda (International Code Name: Hatyan), considered as the world's strongest typhoon ever recorded, struck Philippine territory. Despite the government's efforts and preparations, thousands of people perished. Damage to business, property, and agriculture were of such magnitude that economic activities were placed on standstill. A few days after Typhoon Yolanda ravaged the Visayas region, the national government was criticized by international media for the slow response and lack of support to the survivors in the affected areas. In light of this, it is high time that we create a truly empowered department that will focus on natural hazards and disasters, and characterized by unity of command, a science and ICT-based approach, and the capacity to take charge of three (3) key result areas: (a) disaster risk reduction; (b) disaster preparedness and response; and (c) recovery, rehabilitation and building forward better. As the country's primary disaster management agency, the Department of Disaster Resilience shall integrate and define what needs to be done, where it needs to be done, based on what standards, how it should be done, and how well it should be done. Some of the key elements and features of the proposed Department are as follows: a. Unity of command. The overall powers and functions to lead the country's disaster resilience efforts, both at the policy and execution stages will be placed under the Department. The Department shall be authorized to call upon relevant government agencies and facilitate the assistance of non- yEPRE SEN “KY ¢ & RECEIVED 3 paT pun 3 0 2022 bo res wi n wy Ss government and private organizations especially in emergency cases. The bill also defines the levels of responsibility for disaster preparedness and response between the national and local governments. b. Full-time focus on resilience to natural hazards. The Department is mandated to cover the disasters caused by or related to the above-stated natural hazards. The sheer volume and scale of these merit a single Department focused on preparing for and addressing these disasters. These would also require knowledge and skill set different from those needed to address human-induced disasters. c. Take-over capacity in times of disasters. Under extreme conditions, the Department shall have the authority to take the lead. in close collaboration with the local government units, in undertaking disaster preparedness and response in areas that are severely affected by natural disasters. The Department shall have the power to temporarily take-over or direct any private utility for urgent public purpose. d. Rationalized fund-use for disasters. The Department shall be mandated to manage and ensure the judicious and expeditious use of disaster-related funds. It shall streamline and rationalize the systems and procedures in accessing these funds to help ensure the timely provision of support where urgently and critically needed. e. Fast and responsive procutement. The Department shall institutionalize innovative and responsive procurement mechanisms, e.g. stand-by contracts, pre-arranged systems of procurement with a pre-approved list of contractors, pre-negotiated contracts, advanced procurement contracts, and framework contracts, among others, to ensure the country's resilience to natural hazards and disasters. f. Science- and ICT-based approach. The Department shall develop mechanisms to ensure the inter- operability of systems among relevant agencies to ensure real-time access to relevant information, including mulu-hazard mapping, risk assessment, early warning, exposure database, and emergency management systems, among others. g. Highly specialized functions and highly-skilled personnel requirements. The Department shall have the and authority to engage highly-skilled technical experts. e.g.. DRRM specialists, scientists, environmental and/or urban planners. Civil engineers, and public finance specialists. h. Institutional partnerships with LGUs. NGOs, and academia. Recognizing that disaster resilience is everybody's business, the Department shall adopt a whole-of-society approach to ensure our country's resilience to natural hazards. It shall be mandated to establish partnerships with stakeholders in order to attain the goals and objectives of the Department. A new Department of Disaster Resilience will effectively improve the institutional capacity of the government for disaster risk reduction and management, reduce the vulnerabilities surrounding the affected local population as well as build the resilience of local communities to both natural disasters and climate change. Given its exposure to disaster risk, the Philippines cannot continue to have a focal disaster organization that only has coordinative functions. Our personal experience during typhoon Hatyan has confirmed that the complexity of large-scale disasters undermines existing policies and structures. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF DISASTER RESILIENCE, DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE ON THE CREATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF DISASTER RESILIENCE (DDR): “TRUE STATE OF PHILIPPINE PREPAREDNESS TO AVOID OR REDUCE DISASTROUS IMPACTS OF CLIMATE CHANGE AND NATURAL HAZARDS” A. RATIONALE The Philippines is considered one of the most vulnerable countries in the world to the impacts of natural hazards, being in the circum Pacific ring of fire and the typhoon belt. With climate change, the nature of climate- influenced hazards, primarily typhoons, has changed. They have become more intense and unpredictable with increasing temperature and sea level rise. Geological hazards like earthquakes, threaten to manifest in their worst case forms, as with the “big one” for Metro Manila which is expected any time now. There is more predictability and clarity on this earthquake’s expected impact as its source, the West Valley Fault, is established and well studied. Climate-disaster related hazards, especially typhoons, on the other hand, are of increasing concern because of unpredictability and increasing magnitudes. Worst case climate-related hazard events have been observed to return with much more shortened timing (frequency) and ferocity, adding to their unpredictability. Reming (Luzon), Yolanda (Visayas) and the typhoons Sendong, Pablo, which devastated Mindanao, an island with relatively benign climate, are major manifestations of this uncertainty. The Inter-governmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the global observation expert on climate change, has documented these changes in its various reports, which have also become the basis of the global climate change negotiations. Page | 1 B. PREPAREDNESS OF THE PHILIPPINES TO DEAL WITH INTENSIFYING CLIMATE-DISASTER RELATED HAZARDS It is clear that climate change and disaster not only change our way of life. It is affecting everybody and everything on this planet, especially the most vulnerable countries like the Philippines. Therefore, the “business as usual” (BAU) way of doing things will not suffice to prevent potential catastrophes from happening. The fact that practically nothing changed in the way we plan, program and implement interventions to address natural hazard events despite the many disasters the Philippines experienced over recent years since climate change was discovered, is apparent in the reports of the national agencies. It must be noted that these accomplishment reports document “response and recovery” and “business as usual” actions which simply place affected Filipinos back where they were before the disasters happened. In many cases, the poor became poorer because of devastated livelihood and assets. The Philippine Government will never have enough resources to subsidize the recovery of all these losses. Improvement in the country’s development situation cannot be expected to happen under these circumstances where losses continue because of inability to adapt to rapidly changing climate hazards. The net result is negative, or painfully slow, national development. C. WHAT NEEDS TO CHANGE TO ENABLE THE PHILIPPINES TO COPE WITH DISASTER AND CLIMATE-RELATED THREATS At the global level, there is already a common understanding that to be able to adapt to a changing climate, we need to radically change the way we view climate-disaster related threats, including our responses to them. These changes, therefore, have to happen in the way we plan: (1) Analyze the problems confronting us in a new light. For example, we ask: How are the hazards changing? What potential impacts will they cause; (2) Use the results from this proposed new analysis to adjust planning, programming, implementation and regulatory processes so as to avoid and reduce potential negative losses, damages and disruption and devastating impacts, as well as, deal adequately with residual threats; and (3) Monitor the effects of these adjusted new plans, programs and projects on the quality of the lives of our people so that future adverse effects are averted and opportunities for development optimized. It is amazing how the simple use of a new analytical lens can lead to cost effective solutions that emphasize avoidance (prevention) of negative effects rather than reacting to and recovering from devastation. D. WHAT SPECIFICALLY NEEDS TO BE CHANGED IN THE ANALYTICAL PROCESSES OF THE COUNTRY (1) Treat disaster threats as “risks”, which are impacts that might probably happen in a particular way when vulnerable exposed elements like people and their socio-economic and natural support systems (ecosystems) interact or come Page | 2 in direct contact with natural hazards. The “probabilistic” nature of the threats also offer the opportunity to manipulate the exposed elements such that they are either moved out of harm’s way (preventing the negative impact from happening) or reinforced such that they are able to withstand the impact when it does occur from the interaction. (2) To enable this type of analysis, the one doing it cannot be “reactive”. It cannot use only data from events that already happened. A variety of data for “multiple scenarios” should be used to represent projections of probable results based on the various potential route(s) and assumed intensities of the hazard. What we have been using is only a “deterministic” or single scenario analysis corresponding to a particular hazard outcome already experienced in the past. Various other scenarios that may happen because of the uncertain and unpredictable behaviour of the hazard are ignored. The deterministic approach uses single scenario “multi-hazard” maps that have been drawn up based on the last known worst case events. These are what the “mandated” national government agencies are producing and disseminating to LGUs. For example, Leyte had these agencies’ maps when Yolanda happened, but the extent of the storm surge inundation was severely underestimated because a typhoon of its magnitude was not known to have happened before. This method needs to change. Modelling will need to be employed

title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF DISASTER RESILIENCE, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 10121 or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010 defined the powers of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council, which is composed of different members from different departments of the executive branch, with the Office of Civil Defense acting as its secretariat. As can be seen by its performance in recent disasters, the composition of the council slows down government preparation and response to these disasters. Thus, there is a need to create a separate department dedicated to disaster risk reduction and management. The Department of Disaster Resilience (the Department), once established by law, shall possess the necessary powers and functions, along with the technical expertise and government support to carry out its mandate. The Department shall initiate and integrate the crafting and implementation of comprehensive, continuous, and strategic plans, programs and projects aimed at reducing the risk of all types of 1 natural hazards and the harmful effects of climate change, with the primordial goal of ensuring the safety of our fellow Filipinos. The bill identifies three (3) key result areas to be focused upon by the Department upon its establishment: (1) Disaster Risk Reduction; (2) Disaster Preparedness and Response; and (3) Recovery and Building Forward Better. As such, the Department shall be armed with all the necessary powers by which it can effectively address these key result areas. The bill likewise authorizes the Department to exercise such emergency powers and remedial measures that will be necessary to provide for a timely response mechanism during, and in the aftermath of, a natural calamity or disaster. These powers and measures shall be granted to the Department primarily to help mitigate the unavoidable consequences of natural disasters, and to help alleviate any future harm that may be suffered by our fellow Filipinos. The bill also recognizes the importance of utilizing present, as well as future, developments in information technology as a means of achieving the Department’s primary functions. For instance, the bill requires the Department to establish an Integrated Disaster Resilience Information System (IDRIS), which shall serve as a national database of all relevant disaster risk reduction and climate change data. The bill also tasks the Department with the creation of an early warning system which shall make use of risk communication protocols to ensure effective and efficient measures to prepare for, respond to, and recover from present and potential risks and disasters. In terms of disaster relief and response operations, the bill seeks to streamline the process with the establishment of a Humanitarian Assistance Action Center (HAAC), which shall serve as a mechanism for the processing and release of of goods, articles, equipment and services, including international relief efforts. Furthermore, the bill also highlights the involvement of other government agencies and instrumentalities, such as the various Local Government Units (LGUS), 2 as well as civic society organizations and the communities that are in threat of being affected by natural calamities in addressing issues relating to disaster preparedness, prevention, reparation, and relief. As a final note, this bill strives to help ensure that the painful lessons learned from typhoons such as Ondoy and Yolanda, as well as natural disasters that befell our country in past, are translated into laws, systems, structures, and policies that are truly responsive, with the ultimate goal of protecting the present and future generations of Filipinos. In light of the foregoing, the immediate enactment of this proposed legislation is sought. MA. RENE ANN LOURDES G. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF DISASTER RESILIENCE, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE According to the 2021 Climate Risk Index, the Philippines is the 17th most vulnerable country to climate change. Our country has consistently ranked high in terms of climate vulnerability, experiencing an average of 20 storms per year. In less than nine years, the Philippines has suffered through two Category Five storms, Yolanda and Odette, the latter of which leveled our Province of Dinagat Islands along with other provinces from Western Visayas and Mindanao. For more than 12 years, RA 10121 or Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act has been the prevailing law on disaster response and resilience. Since 2010, RA 10121 has signified a shift towards a more proactive approach to preventing, mitigating, and reducing risk from natural disasters. While our established government institutions since then have done their very best to coordinate policies and programs in anticipation of and in response to disasters, the need and clamor for a high-level, independent government agency to take the lead in handling a comprehensive policy on disaster risk reduction and management, as well as in promoting resilience from the national to the local level. The need for mechanisms to offer a clear direction, chain of command, and accountability was experienced firsthand by the People of Dinagat Islands just last year. According to the Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction Management Office (PDRRMO) of Dinagat Islands, the Province recorded recorded twenty-two (22) dead and eight hundred three (803) injured persons; a staggering 1 billion-peso estimated partial damage to agriculture and fisheries and an additional 1 billion-peso approximate damage to some of the critical facilities in the Islands when Typhoon Odette made landfall on December 2021. Government buildings, public schools, healthcare centers, even the Provincial Capitol, were left totally destroyed by the Supertyphoon, making recovery and rehabilitation even more difficult than it should have been. All this, on top of an ongoing pandemic, engenders a climate of fear among those who have experienced firsthand the cost and the trauma of climate- related events. Typhoon Odette may not be the worst typhoon to devastate our Islands, but it surely will not be the last. With the worsening effects of climate change, we are set to experience more frequent and more extreme weather events. As our country faithfully performs its nationally-determined contributions to mitigating climate change, it is also incumbent upon us to mitigate the effects of climate-related weather events to our economy and society as a whole by promoting resilience and by engendering responsiveness and efficiency in the State’s response. As the state of the climate worsens, the state of our preparedness must conversely improve. The changing climate is a matter of survival for the Filipino people, and such a total order requires the dedication, expertise, resources, and full-time commitment of a National Agency dedicated to this end. During the Eighteenth Congress, | and my fellow Representatives from this Esteemed House pushed for the passage of this law, establishing a Department of Disaster Resilience, defining its powers, and appropriating funds therefor. Encapsulated herein are the fruits of deliberations, consultations, and learnings accumulated from that period. The Department of Disaster Resilience (DDR) is herein envisioned as the lead agency for implementing policies on reducing disaster risk and vulnerability, pursuing rehabilitation, recovery, and reconstruction, and assessing strides of progress towards greater resilience and disaster preparedness. It shall lead established offices, including PHILVOLCS, PAGASA, MGB, and the CCC, towards constructing a more comprehensive assessment of impending disasters and providing sufficient, pertinent, and urgent information on impending disasters. It sets forth a “whole-of- society, whole-of-government, and whole-of-nation approach” in disaster preparedness to increase collaboration, planning, and dialogue among all sectors of society in preparing for natural disasters and in improving their strategies and action plans for disaster risk reduction. Moreover, it provides measures for determining clear parameters for the responsibility of each office and actor, including penalties for those who will negligently or maliciously be in dereliction of their duties. The importance of the enactment of such a law cannot be understated. We must continue to be able to live and thrive even with the challenges of a worsening climate, without a climate of fear and mistrust. This can only be done through fostering a climate of preparedness and unity, a climate of accountability and integrity. Thus, the establishment of DDR is not only a matter of convenience, it is a matter of survival. As this Office has previously manifested to the plenary in the aftermath of Typhoon Odette: We owe it to the dead. We owe it to the survivors. We need to do better. And with this law, we will. In recognition of the urgent need for a more responsive, systematic, and comprehensive policy on climate change and disaster resilience that our Office is filing this Bill for its subsequent enactment as law. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The urgency of our country’s need for a fortified, resolute, committed, focused and organized strategy and process in facing the crises brought about by natural disasters cannot be overemphasized. We are approaching the 13-year anniversary of Typhoon Ketsana (Tropical Storm Ondoy) and the nine-year anniversary of Typhoon Haiyan (Super Typhoon Yolanda). There have been many, many disasters in between and beyond, including the eruption of Taal Volcano, several earthquakes, the on- going pandemic and the war in Marawi. As far as climate-related natural disasters are concerned, we are already certain that these will continue to pummel, damage and devastate our country and our people, unless we change the way we address disasters. I agree that we have gained ground in terms of improving our rate of immediate physical survival from storms, earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. We have certainly reduced the number of casualties in most recent disasters due to improved evacuation procedures, pre-disaster preparedness, and better rescue and disaster management. On the other hand, structural, economic and agricultural losses continue to be amplified. Reduction of casualties is definitely a win, but it is just not enough. During Super Typhoons Odette and Agaton, the casualties were not as pronounced as during Ondoy or Yolanda. However, the destruction of power, telecommunications and road infrastructure across provinces choked and paralyzed local economies that were already struggling due to the COVID-19 pandemic, for months after the actual natural disaster. 1 To dramatize our circumstances in relation to natural disasters—it is not enough to protect and save lives in a storm. We cannot stop there. We have to also protect and save our people’s houses and normal community operations; i.e., the resumption of power, telecoms and basic supplies. We have to protect and save jobs, agricultural production, and local economies. We have to pivot our attention and focus on Disaster Resilience. We have to go above and beyond disaster preparedness, disaster response and even disaster management. We have to begin thinking about solutions that will equip the entire nation, not just to survive natural disasters but create a line of defense that would shield us, as much as possible, from the powerful, destructive force that defines extreme weather, geological, war events and viral pandemics. These solutions require a holistic, expansive, and infrastructure-driven approach. We have to accept that an effort as huge and overarching as Disaster Resilience cannot happen in our current national and local government set up, This is simply because the solutions needed are not piece-meal in nature but all- encompassing instead. In pursuing the successes achieved in our current fragmented approach to disaster management, we have already exhausted the extent of its reach and capability. It is time to create a department that is solely tasked to address the main sources of most of our socio-economic problems. It is time to create a seat in the Cabinet, one that is responsible for protecting our entire nation against disasters. It is time to organize our national and local governments better to think beyond evacuation, search and rescue and disaster aid. I call on my fellow lawmakers to expedite the passing of this consolidated Disaster Resilience Act, which was passed in the 18th Congress. I acknowledge the authors of more than 30 bills that now compose this consolidated bill: REPS. JOEY SALCEDA , JOSE CHRISTOPHER BELMONTE, ESTRELLITA SUANSING, HORACIO SUANSING JR., XAVIER JESUS ROMUALDO, LRAY VILLAFUERTE, RODRIGO ABELLANOSA, FERDINAND MARTIN ROMUALDEZ, YEDDA MARIE ROMUALDEZ, LAWRENCE FORTUN, WILTER "SHARKY" II WEE PALMA, ERIC L. OLIVAREZ, BERNADETTE "BH" HERRERA-DY, CHERYL P. DELOSO-MONTALLA, LORD ALLAN JAY Q. VELASCO, JOHN MARVIN "YUL SERVO" C. NIETO,"KUYA" JOSE ANTONIO R. SY-ALVARADO, TYRONE D. AGABAS, DAVID "JAY-JAY" C. SUAREZ, ANNA MARIE VILLARAZA-SUAREZ, FERDINAND L. HERNANDEZ, SOL ARAGONES, JOY MYRA SALVADOR- TAMBUNTING, ALOY LIM, ERIC G. YAP, and MANUEL F. YAP ZUBIRI, under the leadership of former REP. LUCY TORRES-GOMEZ. More than a decade has passed since RA 10121 or the "Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010." A new approach to fighting 2 disasters is way overdue. Every few months or so, a disaster promptly reminds of the urgency of the creation of the Department of Disaster Resilience. We cannot afford even another year without taking actions in this direction. I enjoin this Congress for a swift proceeding on this bill. RICHARD I. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Philippines is one of the countries that experiences a number of calamities such as typhoons. In a typical year, around nineteen or more tropical storms enter the Philippine area of responsibility and of these, usually six or nine make landfall. Natural disasters of increasing magnitude and frequency, such as typhoon Haiyan, have continued to affect our country, which is now the second most vulnerable in the world to disasters and climate change. Nearly 74 percent of the population and 80 percent of the land area are identified as vulnerable to disasters, with the capital of Manila considered at "extreme risk." This "new normal" requires a more focused and in-depth attention in the way we understand, prepare and respond to natural disasters. Despite all the disaster preparation and coordination plans, there were still significant losses, injury, and damage to property when Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan), considered as the world's strongest typhoon ever recorded, struck Philippine territory. Notwithstanding the government's efforts and preparations, thousands of people perished during said Typhoon. Damage to business, properly and agriculture were of such magnitude that economic activities were placed on standstill. In line with this, it is high time that we create a truly empowered Department in the Government that will focus on natural hazards and disasters; and characterized by unity of command, a science-and ICT-based approach, and to take charge of three (3) key result areas: (a) disaster risk reduction; (b) disaster preparedness and response; and (c) recovery, rehabilitation and building forward better. As the country's primary disaster management agency, the Department of Disaster Resilience shall integrate and define what needs to be done. where it needs to be done, based on what standards, how it should be done and how well it should be done. This new department which will be called the Department of Disaster Resilience will effectively improve the institutional capacity of the government for disaster risk reduction and management, reduce the vulnerabilities surrounding the affected local population as well as build the resilience of local communities to both natural and man-made disasters and calamities. Given its exposure to disaster risk, the Philippines cannot continue to have a focal disaster organization that only has coordinative functions. Our personal experience during typhoon Haiyan has confirmed that the complexity of large-scale disasters undermines existing policies and structures. The current DRRM structure where authority is shared, responsibility is dispersed and resources are scattered, renders it difficult to operate an appropriate and immediate response, thus delaying critical disaster response and recovery. With the lives, safety and the welfare of our people at stake, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought BERNADETTE HERRERA-DY 1 Republic of the Philippines HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Quezon City NINETEENTH CONGRESS First Regular Session 1631 House Bill No._____ Introduced by Rep. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Due to its geographical location, the Philippines is exposed to high incidents of environmental hazards such as typhoons, floods, storm surges, tsunamis, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, landslides, and droughts. This leaves various communities throughout the country in highly vulnerable situations. Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda), one of the most powerful tropical cyclones ever recorded, was an example of how a natural disaster can devastate lives, properties, and entire communities. It left the country with more than 7,000 deaths (with thousands still unaccounted for) and 16 million affected people. The overall financial and economic impact of Typhoon Haiyan is estimated at $14 Billion. The Philippines ranked 17th in the world as the most affected country from extreme weather events in the Global Climate Risk Index (CRI) 2021 with a score of 26.67 using 2019 data.1 In 2018, we ranked third in the World Risk Index of most disaster- prone countries in the world published by the United Nations University Institute of Environment and Human Security (UNU-HES), with a risk index of 27.69%. The Philippines also ranks third on the WRI’s list of countries with the greatest exposure to natural disasters, with a score of 52.46%, just ahead of Japan (45.91%). Given our exposure to threats of natural disasters, Republic Act No. 10121, otherwise known as the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010” (PDDRM), was enacted on 27 May 2010. The Act shifted the policy environment and the way the country deals with disasters from mere response to preparedness. RA 10121 provides a comprehensive, all-hazard, multi-sectoral, inter-agency, and community-based approach to disaster risk management through the formulation of the National Disaster Risk Management Framework.2 Notwithstanding the efforts and resources to reduce the risks and vulnerabilities to natural disasters, challenges are abounding so much so that our government’s efforts 1 https://cpbrd.congress.gov.ph/images/PDF%20Attachments/Facts%20in%20Figures/FF2021- 09_Global_Climate_Risk.pdf 2 http://www.lse.ac.uk/GranthamInstitute/law/philippine-disaster-reduction-and-management-act-ra-10121/ to achieve the DRRM objectives are hampered. Some of the issues and challenges are: 1. Weak coordination and collaboration among stakeholders – national government agencies, LGUs, civil society organizations, volunteers, and the private sector; 2. Lack of capacity of line agencies and LGUs to perform DRRM functions; 3. Less priority given to DRRM activities; 4. Weak implementation of laws and policies; 5. The lack of and difficulty in accessing DRRM data/information; 6. Post-disaster focus of disaster funds; 7. Monitoring of disaster fund expenditures; 8. Slow disbursement of disaster funds; and 9. Difficulty in tracking foreign disaster assistance. 3 The need for greater coordination and synchronization of disaster risk management at all levels should be a top priority. Thus, this measure will create a single agency that has a distinct and separate mandate for disaster management. The Department of Disaster Management shall be the focal government agency for policy-making, coordination, integration, supervision, monitoring and evaluation for all disaster and rehabilitation management policies and programs in the country. 4 With strong institutions, we can reverse the current trends of rising disaster impact. Everyone of us must be empowered to make decisions which reduce risk – from government to citizens. In view of the foregoing, the immediate enactment and approval of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF DISASTER RESILIENCE, DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Natural calamities constantly beset the Philippines, be it super typhoons, earthquakes or volcanic eruptions, which have catastrophic consequences to the lives, properties and livelihood of the people in the affected areas. However, human might cannot control or even match, nature’s wrath. But with collective efforts and unified direction of all the stakeholders, we can mitigate its disastrous consequences with a timely and sound disaster preparedness and management programs and activities, and work on to build the resiliency of the people and the communities. Thus, there exists the urgency and the necessity to create a focal agency to be at the helm of the country’s disaster preparedness and management programs. This measure seeks to create a Department of Disaster Resilience with the following objectives: (1) To establish a primary government agency responsible for leading, organizing, and managing the national effort to reduce disaster risk, prepare for and respond to disasters, recover and rehabilitate, and build forward better after the occurrence of disasters. (2) To oversee and coordinate the preparation, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of disaster and climate resilience plans, programs, projects, and activities. (3) To provide leadership in the continuous development of strategic and systematic approaches to disaster prevention, mitigation preparedness response, recovery, and rehabilitation. (4) To provide a clear and comprehensive direction in the implementation of plans, programs, and projects to reduce the risk of natural hazards and the effects of climate change and manage the impact of disasters. 1 (5) To create a government agency to institutionalize the policies, structures, coordination mechanisms and programs on disaster risk reduction management and harmonize policies on climate change, sustainable development, and environmental management; (6) To enable the government to quickly respond, prepare, implement, monitor, and evaluate disaster and climate resilience plans, programs, projects and activities; and (7) To ensure that the government upholds the welfare of the people particularly the vulnerable sectors of the society specifically women, children, older persons, persons with disabilities, urban poor, and indigenous people by providing its citizens a safer, adaptive, resilient, and inclusive community. During the 18th Congress, 35 bills were consolidated into House Bill 5989, “An Act CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF DISASTER RESILIENCE, DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR”. Said measure was approved on 3rd Reading by the House but failed to hurdle the Senate’s scrutiny. The bill was thoroughly deliberated upon and studied for the purpose of establishing a Department consistent with the ideals of good governance, improved public service delivery and fiscal prudence. The same bill is being refiled this 19th Congress. Thus, the approval of this bill is earnestly requested. MARIO VITTORIO “MARVEY” A.
