title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF DISASTER RESILIENCE, DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill is the substitute bill of the same title, which consolidated 36 house bills in the 19th Congress, all with the intent to establish a Department of Disaster Resilience. The urgency of our country’s need for a fortified, resolute, committed, focused and organized strategy and process in facing the crises brought about by natural disasters cannot be overemphasized. It will be 16 years since Typhoon Ketsana (Tropical Storm Ondoy) and 12 years since Typhoon Haiyan (Super Typhoon Yolanda), and many, many disasters in between and beyond, including the eruption of Taal Volcano, and several earthquakes. As far as climate-related natural disasters are concerned, we are already certain that these will continue to pummel, damage and devastate our country and our people, unless we change the way we address disasters. We certainly have gained ground in terms of improving our rate of immediate physical survival from storms, earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. We have also reduced the number of casualties in most recent disasters due to improved evacuation procedures, pre-disaster preparedness, and better rescue and disaster management. On the other hand, structural, economic and agricultural losses continue to be amplified. Reduction of casualties is definitely a win, but it is just not enough. During Super Typhoons Odette and Agaton, the casualties were not as pronounced as during Ondoy or Yolanda. However, the destruction of power, telecommunications and road infrastructure across provinces choked and paralyzed local economies that were already struggling due to the COVID-19 pandemic, for months after the actual natural disaster. To dramatize our circumstances in relation to natural disasters—it is not enough to protect and save lives in a storm. We cannot stop there. We have to also protect and save our people’s houses and normal community operations; i.e., the resumption of power, telecoms and basic supplies. We have to protect and save jobs, agricultural production, and local economies. We have to pivot our attention and focus on Disaster Resilience. We have to go above and beyond disaster preparedness, disaster response and even disaster management. We have to begin thinking about solutions that will equip the entire nation, not just to survive natural disasters but create a line of defense that would shield us, as much as possible, from the powerful, destructive force that defines extreme weather, geological, war events and viral pandemics. These solutions require a holistic, expansive, and infrastructure-driven approach. It is time to create a department that is solely tasked to address the main sources of most of our socio-economic problems. It is time to create a seat in the Cabinet, one that is responsible for protecting our entire nation against disasters. It is time to organize our national and local governments better and think beyond evacuation, search and rescue and disaster aid. I call on my fellow lawmakers to expedite the passing of this consolidated Disaster Resilience Act. I acknowledge all the co-authors of this consolidated bill. More than a decade has passed since RA 10121 or the "Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010." A new approach to fighting disasters is way overdue. Every few months or so, a disaster promptly reminds of the urgency of the creation of the Department of Disaster Resilience. We cannot afford even another year without taking actions in this direction. I enjoin this Congress for swift proceeding on this bill. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF DISASTER RESILIENCE, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 10121 or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010 defined the powers of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council, which is composed of different members from different departments of the executive branch, with the Office of Civil Defense acting as its secretariat. As can be seen by its performance in recent disasters, the composition of the council slows down government preparation and response to these disasters. Thus, there is a need to create a separate department dedicated to disaster risk reduction and management. The Department of Disaster Resilience (the Department), once established by law, shall possess the necessary powers and functions, along with the technical expertise and government support to carry out its mandate. The Department shall initiate and integrate the crafting and implementation of comprehensive, continuous, and strategic plans, programs and projects aimed at reducing the risk of all types of natural hazards and the harmful effects of climate change, with the primordial goal of ensuring the safety of our fellow Filipinos. The bill identifies three (3) key result areas to be focused upon by the Department upon its establishment: (1) Disaster Risk Reduction; (2) Disaster Preparedness and Response; and (3) Recovery and Building Forward Better. As such, the Department shall be armed with all the necessary powers by which it can effectively address these key result areas. The bill likewise authorizes the Department to exercise such emergency powers and remedial measures that will be necessary to provide for a timely response mechanism during, and in the aftermath of, a natural calamity or disaster. These powers and measures shall be granted to the Department primarily to help mitigate the unavoidable consequences of natural disasters, and to help alleviate any future harm that may be suffered by our fellow Filipinos. The bill also recognizes the importance of utilizing present, as well as future, developments in information technology as a means of achieving the Department’s primary functions. For instance, the bill requires the Department to establish an Integrated Disaster Resilience Information System (IDRIS), which shall serve as a national database of all relevant disaster risk reduction and climate change data. The bill also tasks the Department with the creation of an early warning system which shall make use of risk communication protocols to ensure effective and efficient measures to prepare for, respond to, and recover from present and potential risks and disasters. In terms of disaster relief and response operations, the bill seeks to streamline the process with the establishment of a Humanitarian Assistance Action Center (HAAC), which shal] serve as a mechanism for the processing and release of goods, articles, equipment and services, including international relief efforts. Furthermore, the bill also highlights the involvement of other government agencies and instrumentalities, such as the various Local Government Units (LGUS), as well as civic society organizations and the communities that are in threat of being affected by natural calamities in addressing issues relating to disaster preparedness, prevention, reparation, and relief. As a final note, this bill strives to help ensure that the painful lessons learned from typhoons such as Ondoy and Yolanda, as well as natural disasters that befell our country in past, are translated into laws, systems, structures, and policies that are truly responsive, with the ultimate goal of protecting the present and future generations of Filipinos. The passage of the bill is earnestly sought. . fre HON. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines lies in the Pacific Ring of Fire. This is the region where a lot of volcanic and seismic activities are recorded. Moreover, the Philippines is also part of the Typhoon Belt, making the country prone to at least 20 storms a year. Out of the twenty typhoons each year, it is seen that at least five of these are expected to make landfall. It is for this reason that the Philippines is considered one of the world’s most disaster-prone countries. This bill aims to complement the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction Act signed into law in 2010 by then President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo. The bill mandated a framework to ensure swift, efficient, and orderly preparation for natural calamities. This also led to the institutionalization of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Plan. As a complement to the aforementioned law, this will ensure an institutionalized structure for natural calamities. The creation of the Department of Risk Reduction will ensure risk reduction, disaster preparedness, and response, and swift rehabilitation and recovery every time there is a natural calamity. It will also capacitate local government units, and other agencies, in ensuring that government response is harmonious with other simultaneous efforts. Moreover, the Department of Disaster Resilience would aid the government in disaster preparation, coordination, and immediate assistance, 1 especially in times of calamity where losses of life, injury, and destruction of property are seen and/or expected. This measure, initially envisioned by Rep. Yedda Romualdez in the 17th Congress, was subsequently refiled in the 18th Congress as a consolidation of several related bills passed by the House of Representatives. It has also been refiled during the 19th Congress. In view of the foregoing reasons, the approval of the bill is most earnestly sought. JC M. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF DISASTER RESILIENCE, DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, situated along the Pacific Ring of Fire and within the typhoon belt, is among the most disaster-prone countries in the world. Its geographical location makes it highly vulnerable to natural hazards such as typhoons, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, floods, and landslides - hazards that have only intensified due to the growing impacts of climate change. While Filipinos have long been admired for their resilience in the face of adversity, the reality remains that communities continue to suffer from the consequences of recurring disasters. Typhoons with wind speeds exceeding 300 km/h have devastated entire provinces, displacing families, destroying livelihoods, and exposing the persistent gaps in disaster response and preparedness systems. The toll on lives, property, and economic stability underscores the urgent need for a more robust institutional mechanism that ensures long-term, science-based, and coordinated disaster risk reduction and management. Despite a 5.7% improvement in the country's disaster preparedness over an eight-year period, this progress is neither sufficient nor sustainable given the magnitude and frequency of the threats we face. Preparedness must be institutionalized, not reactive or limited to isolated events. The current multi-agency framework, though well-intentioned, has often resulted in fragmented coordination and overlapping functions. This bill seeks to establish a Department of Disaster Resilience (DDR), a lead agency with a clear mandate to plan, manage, and coordinate disaster preparedness, risk reduction, response, and recovery efforts at the national and local levels. By centralizing responsibility under one permanent institution, the government will be able to strengthen anticipatory governance, improve accountability, and ensure efficient use of resources. The DDR shall serve as the primary government agency responsible for ensuring a proactive, integrated, and coherent approach to disaster risk reduction and resilience building. It shall work closely with local government units (LGUs), national agencies, civil society, and international partners to foster a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach. This proposed measure aligns with the country’s commitments under the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030 and complements the goals of the Climate Change Act, the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act, and the Universal Health Care Law. Ultimately, it affirms the State’s duty to protect its citizens and promote national resilience in the face of increasing natural and human-induced hazards. The enactment of this measure is not just timely - it is necessary. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Rep. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF DISASTER RESILIENCE, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The wisdom of our ancestors and the lessons of history have long taught us a fundamental truth: disasters are an inevitable part of life, and survival depends on our ability to adapt, prepare, and respond. Long before the advent of modern science and technology, early Filipinos already took proactive steps to safeguard their communities— building settlements away from flood plains, storing food in times of plenty, and relying on collective strength in the face of adversity. In the spirit of this inherited resilience, the Philippine government institutionalized disaster governance through the establishment of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) under Republic Act No. 10121. While this framework has guided disaster response efforts for more than a decade, recurring tragedies—from typhoons to earthquakes and pandemics—continue to expose its limitations. Lives are lost, livelihoods destroyed, and opportunities for growth are permanently erased. Public criticism has grown over the perceived inefficiency and fragmented approach of our disaster interventions. These realities compel us to act with urgency and clarity of purpose. This measure proposes the creation of a Department of Disaster Resilience—a dedicated executive department mandated to lead, coordinate, and operationalize national efforts in disaster preparedness, risk reduction, response, recovery, and rehabilitation. With a centralized structure and empowered mandate, the proposed Department will: 1. Leverage modern technology and data analytics to anticipate and mitigate the impacts of natural and man-made hazards; 2. Streamline disaster response operations through institutional coordination across national government agencies, local government units (LGUs), and other stakeholders; 3. Institutionalize a comprehensive, time-sensitive, and inclusive disaster management framework, involving the private sector, civil society, and local communities; 4. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines lies in a region where disasters happen, naturally. It is in the Pacific Ring of Fire where eighty percent (80%) of the volcanic eruptions and earthquakes occur. According to the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHILVOLCS), there are twenty-four (24) active volcanoes in the country, today. The country is also located along the “Typhoon Belt”, an area in the western Pacific Ocean where one-third of the world’s tropical cyclones originate. An average of twenty (20) typhoons visits the country every year, seven (7) of which taking landfall endangering lives and creating heavy damage to properties and infrastructures. These geographical location and environmental set up expose the country to climate conditions that increase in frequency and intensity, every year. According to the Global Risk Index 2021 published by Germanwatch, based on an annual average, from 2000 to 2019, the Philippines ranked fourth among countries most-affected by extreme weather events. This risk index measures and analyses impacts of extreme weather events in terms of fatalities and economic losses. Over the past two decades, our country had the highest extreme weather occurrence in the world experiencing 317 weather-related events. According to the same study, the average fatality per year over the same period was 859.36, ranking us seventh (7th) in the index. In terms of economic 1 losses, extreme weather events cost the Philippines an average of US$3.2 billion per year which ranked us at eighth (8th) in the world. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) in its 2020 published report put the damages at a total of Php463 billion from 2010 to 2019, with the agricultural sector taking most of the brunt at sixty-seven (62.7%). Our vulnerability to the impacts of climate change and natural hazards is exacerbated by the wanton destruction of our environment which causes floods, landslide, forest fires, heat waves, and droughts. It is even worsened by the growth of our population, increasing our consumption on energy which is dependent on fossil fuel. Population increase also means greater consumption of agricultural and marine resources, and an increasing pressure on the natural environment. The purpose of this measure is to create a department that will focus on our country’s effective response to the risks brought about by natural and human- induced calamities. It will be the mandate of this department to create policies to reduce disaster-risks, establish an enabling environment for local and national agencies to collaborate on climate change preparedness and create infrastructures to mitigate the impact of natural hazards. It will also harmonize all local and national plans and policies for short and long-term climate goals. Through the creation of this department, we are putting the climate agenda at the forefront of our policy decision-making. Our action on this matter, is extremely, urgent. The Climate Change Knowledge Portal even pegged the estimations that sixty percent (60%) of our land area and seventy-four (74%) percent of our population are exposed to natural hazards. We must keep in mind that of the 74% exposed population, most of them come from the marginalized and vulnerable sectors. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. LORDAN G. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE For three consecutive years (2022 to 2024), The Philippines consistently ranked as the highest on the World Risk Index among 193 countries. The World Risk Index is a tool used to assess and estimate the disaster risk of a country, using both external and internal hazard factors, including cyclones, floods, droughts, sea level rise and societal conditions. In fact, the Philippines risk rating even increased from 46.86 in 2023 to 46.91 in 2024, despite receiving financial aids and spending on projects and programs to mitigate the effects of hazard factors. Because of its precarious location in the world, the Philippines perennially experiences catastrophic disasters, such as strong earthquakes and destructive tropical cyclones which causes loss of lives, destruction of properties and displacement of people. In fact, based on the Global Report on Internal Displacement 2022, the Philippines recorded its highest figures of internally displaced people in five years at 5.7 million in 2021. Worldwide, weather-related hazards accounted for 94% of the total displacements, largely due to implementation of pre-emptive evacuations in face of cyclones and floods. In the Philippines this is magnified by the archipelagic configuration of the country and the propensity of Filipinos to reside in coastal communities for livelihood and subsistence. The enactment of Republic Act No. 10121, otherwise known as the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, aligned and harmonized the country’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) System by mainstreaming the same in all national and local development processes. It created an inter-agency council known as the NDRRMC, headed the Secretary of the Department of National Defense (DND) as the Chairperson, with the Secretary of the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) as Vice Chairperson for Disaster Preparedness, the Secretary of the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) as Vice Chairperson for Disaster Response, the Secretary of the Department of Science and Technology (DOST) as Vice Chairperson for Disaster Prevention and Mitigation, and the Director-General of the National Economic and Development Authority (NEDA; now DEPDev) as Vice Chairperson for Disaster Rehabilitation and Recovery. It also includes as members the Secretaries of other Departments and heads of other government agencies of various disciplines, all of which execute other functions not principally related to DRRM. The creation of a department with special focus and expertise on DRRM programs, projects and activities will minimize, if not prevent, loss of lives, destruction of properties and displacement of people, attributable to disasters. It will help stabilize social and economic order, especially in areas considered as disaster high risk. Also, RA No. 10121 identified the Office of Civil Defense as the lead agency for the implementation the law and tasked it with the primary mission of administering a comprehensive national civil defense and disaster risk reduction and management program by providing leadership in the continuous development of strategic and systematic approaches as well as measures to reduce vulnerabilities and risks to hazards and manage the consequences of disasters. Hence, projects, programs and activities identified at the grassroot level as essential in pre-empting or addressing the catastrophic effects of disasters are submitted to the OCD, which will then forward the request to the NDRRMC for recommendation to the President of the Republic of the Philippines for approval. Unfortunately, it appears that submission to the OCD of the proposed projects, programs and activities only add an additional layer of processing and delay the approval of the same. This runs counter intuitive to the essence of disaster risk response and management which must be swift and effective to minimize irreparable damages and consequences. Placing the National Disaster Resilience Fund (present NDRRM Fund) under the management and control of the proposed Department will align and harmonize the efforts of the national government in making the country more resilient to disaster and avoid piecemeal developments which are less effective. In view of the foregoing, immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. DALE B. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is the most exposed country in the world to tropical storms, with approximately 20 typhoons a year1. Storms frequently make landfall on the islands of Eastern Visayas, Bicol Region, and Northern Luzon, while the Southern Islands and region of Mindanao is often free of typhoons. In modern meteorological records, the deadliest storm was Typhoon Yolanda or internationally called as "Haiyan” which became the strongest landfalling tropical cyclone ever recorded as it crossed the Visayas in central Philippines on November 2013. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (DRRMC) was created through Republic Act No. 10121, otherwise known as the "Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010”. It was a response to Typhoon Ondoy which ruined 4.9 million families and led to the declaration of a state of calamity in 23 provinces and in Metro Manila. Despite the government’s efforts and preparations, 6,300 people perished. Damage to properties estimated at 100 billion pesos. Business, property, and agriculture were in such magnitude that economic activities were placed on standstill. A few days after typhoon Yolanda ravaged the Visayas region, the national government was criticized and blamed by 1 Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA). https://www.pagasa.dost.gov.ph/climate/tropical-cyclone-information international media for the slow response and lack of support to the victims in the affected areas. In 2022, a 7.0 magnitude earthquake in Northern Luzon, the country’s most populous island, killed five and injured more than a hundred. Across northern Luzon, infrastructures were heavily damaged, including 400 homes, dozens of schools, several hospitals and bridges, and the centuries-old Vigan Cathedral and Banta Bell Tower, according to the Office of Civil Defense.2 The damage from typhoons, earthquakes, and other disasters should never be this devastating. We must strengthen our disaster risk reduction strategies by institutionalizing a whole-of-society approach in implementing the Sendai Framework through a department focused on disaster risk reduction. This bill seeks to create a Department for Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council, Office of Civil Defense, and other Offices related thereto and shall be known as the Department of Disaster Resiliency and Alertness Management (DReAM). This new Department will drastically reduce, if not totally eliminate, the bureaucratic red tape which has caused many delays in the delivery of immediate assistance needed by calamity victims. More importantly, it will empower authorities to respond swiftly and effectively--- saving lives, protecting communities, and ensuring that no Filipino is left behind during disasters. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is urgently sought. REP. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF DISASTER RESILIENCE, DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This proposed bill, "An Act Creating the Department of Disaster Resilience," aims to establish a new executive department in the Philippines. This department would be dedicated to a more comprehensive and proactive approach to disaster risk reduction and management (DRRM). The bill seeks to unify the functions of various existing agencies, such as the Office of Civil Defense (OCD) and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC), into a single, cabinet-level department. This would consolidate authority and resources, streamlining the national response to natural disasters and other calamities. The primary rationale behind the DDR bill is to shift the country’s disaster management paradigm from a reactive to a proactive and anticipatory one. Instead of just responding after a disaster hits, the DDR would focus on all four pillars of DRRM: 1. Prevention and Mitigation: This involves long-term planning and investment in infrastructure to reduce the risks of disasters. Examples include building resilient structures, implementing early warning systems, and enforcing land-use policies. 2. Preparedness: This pillar focuses on ensuring that communities and government agencies are ready for an impending disaster. Activities include developing comprehensive emergency plans, conducting drills, and stockpiling relief goods. 3. Response: This is the immediate action taken during and after a disaster to save lives and provide humanitarian aid. The DDR would be the lead agency for search and rescue, evacuation, and the distribution of emergency supplies. 1 4. Rehabilitation and Recovery: This involves restoring affected communities to their pre-disaster state or better. The DDR would oversee efforts to rebuild homes, infrastructure, and livelihoods, ensuring the recovery process is built back better. The Department of Disaster Resilience would be a single, powerful entity with a clear chain of command, eliminating the current fragmented system where multiple agencies often have overlapping responsibilities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is hereby earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is globally recognized as one of the most disaster-prone countries, ranking first in the 2022 World Risk Index with an overail risk score of 46.8%, driven by high exposure to multiple natural hazards and vulnerabilities in socio-economic systems'. Situated along the Pacific Ring of Fire and in the path of the West Pacific typhoon belt, the country experiences an annual average of 20 tropical cyclones, several of which cause catastrophic flooding, landslides, storm surges, and extensive infrastructure damage. It is also subject to frequent earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, in addition to slow-onset hazards such as droughts and sea-level rise. These recurring disasters inflict enormous human and economic costs, with the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) recording damages amounting to billions of pesos annually, as well as long-term disruptions to livelihoods, education, and public services. The enactment of Republic Act No. 10121, the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, marked a paradigm shift from reactive emergency response to proactive disaster risk reduction and community-based resilience”. However, despite notable progress in local DRRM planning and early warning dissemination, significant institutional challenges persist, particularly the fragmentation of functions across various government bodies—such as the Office of Civil Defense (OCD), the NDRRMC Secretariat, sectoral agencies, and local government units— resulting in overlapping mandates, uneven capacities, and delayed decision-making during large- scale or cascading events. The intensifying effects of climate change further magnify these challenges, with scientific projections indicating stronger typhoons, more frequent extreme rainfall events, prolonged droughts, and rising sea levels threatening coastal communities. These compounding hazards underscore the urgent need for a centralized, science-based, and fully empowered institution to lead and coordinate national disaster resilience and climate adaptation efforts. The proposed creation of a Department of Disaster Resilience (DDR) responds to this imperative by elevating DRRM to the Cabinet level, consolidating key functions under a single authority, and ensuring a unified chain of command for preparedness, response, recovery, and rehabilitation. The DDR will formulate and 1 World Risk Report 2022 https://weltrisikobericht.de/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/WorldRiskReport- 2022_Online.pdf ? https://climate-laws.org/document/philippine-disaster-reduction-and-management-act-ra-10121_eda4?utm implement national resilience policies, integrate climate adaptation into development and infrastructure planning, and oversee the establishment of a National Integrated Disaster Resilience Information System (IDRIS) that harmonizes hazard maps, vulnerability assessments, loss and damage data, and resource inventories into an interoperable platform to support timely and risk- informed decision-making. It will also professionalize the disaster management workforce through standardized training, accreditation, and research programs, ensuring sustained technical capacity across all regions’. Moreover, the DDR will be tasked with managing nationwide early warning systems, pre- positioning strategic stockpiles of relief goods, mobilizing rapid-response teams, and leading post- disaster needs assessments to guide risk-sensitive rehabilitation and reconstruction. The Department will be empowered to coordinate closely with local government units, private sector actors, and civil society organizations to foster whole-of-society engagement in resilience building. It will also serve as the national focal point for accessing international climate and disaster financing, enabling the country to secure additional resources for adaptation and recovery projects. While initial appropriations will be required to establish the Department, the long-term economic benefits of reduced disaster losses, more efficient resource use, and faster recovery are expected to outweigh these start-up costs. By building upon and strengthening the principles enshrined in RA 10121, the DDR will address institutional fragmentation, enhance operational readiness, and mainstream disaster resilience in all levels of governance and development planning. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is among the most disaster-prone countries in the world, located within the Pacific Ring of Fire and along the typhoon belt. Every year, the country experiences a wide range of natural hazards— including powerful typhoons, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, floods, and landslides—which have collectively caused thousands of deaths, massive displacement, and billions in economic losses. These disasters continue to disrupt essential services, deepen existing social inequalities, and undermine national progress toward sustainable development. While the enactment of Republic Act No. 10121 or the “Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010” was a landmark policy reform, experience over the past decade has revealed significant gaps in the coordination, implementation, and sustainability of disaster- related programs. The current structure, where disaster management responsibilities are fragmented across various national and local government agencies, has resulted in overlapping functions, delayed response, and uneven institutional capacities, especially at the local level. In light of these enduring challenges and the increasing frequency and intensity of disasters exacerbated by climate change, there is a compelling need to institutionalize a more cohesive, empowered, and accountable disaster governance framework. This bill seeks to create the Department of Disaster Resilience (DDR)—a dedicated national agency solely focused on leading and coordinating the government’s efforts in building disaster and climate resilience. Page 1 The proposed DDR will centralize and harmonize policies and actions related to disaster risk reduction and management, climate change adaptation, environmental protection, and sustainable development. It will also provide direct support to local governments and communities before, during, and after disasters, with a strong emphasis on science-based planning, risk-informed governance, and inclusive, people-centered interventions. At its core, the creation of the DDR affirms the State’s duty under the Constitution to protect the life, health, and property of every Filipino, and to promote a balanced and healthful ecology. It also reinforces the Philippines’ commitments under international frameworks such as the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, the Paris Agreement on Climate Change, and the Sustainable Development Goals. This measure is not merely about institutional restructuring—it is about ensuring that no community is left behind in the face of crisis. It is about transforming the way we prepare, respond, and recover—by acting early, coordinating effectively, and building back stronger and safer. In view of the growing risks and urgent realities we face, the swift enactment of this measure is not only necessary, it is long overdue. MARLYN L. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) is a coordinating body under the Department of National Defense, which provides a comprehensive, all-hazard, multi-sectoral, and community-based approach to disaster risk reduction and management. However, considering the country’s location on the Pacific Ring of Fire and its recent ranking as the world’s most disaster-prone country for the 16th consecutive year, with an expected average of twenty-four (24) typhoons annually, the current structure of the NDRRMC has resulted in a fragmented disaster response. Hence, this bill seeks the immediate creation of the Department of Disaster Resilience (DDR) to serve as the primary government agency in preparing for, responding to, and building the nation's resilience against the constant threat of natural disasters and the effects of climate change. This also ensures a focused, full-time effort to protect our people and our future. The DRR will be empowered to: - Lead the implementation of programs, projects and activities to reduce the country’s vulnerabilities to natural hazards and climate change; - Oversee all aspects of the disaster cycle—from risk reduction, preparedness, and response to recovery and building communities; - Administer, mobilize and monitor the utilization of disaster-resilience related funds, including but not limited to, the National Disaster Resilience Fund, and the Supplemental Disaster Resilience Support Fund; - Inspect and examine the status of projects, programs, and activities undertaken by national government agencies and LGUs to support disaster resilience efforts; 1 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is frequently battered by powerful typhoons, with approximately nineteen tropical storms entering the Philippine area of responsibility each year, of which six to nine typically make landfall. In 2025, Typhoons Crising and Dante, along with frequent heavy rains brought by the habagat season, caused widespread flooding and devastation. These events reflect a broader global reality where climate change, an inevitable and pressing challenge faced by nearly every country, has intensified weather patterns, resulting in more frequent and severe storms and flooding worldwide. Nearly 74 percent of the Philippine population and 80 percent of its land area remain highly vulnerable to such natural disasters, with urban centers like Manila experiencing extreme risks. Given this “new normal,” it is crucial for the Philippines to establish a robust, science-based, and unified system to better prepare for, respond to, and recover from these calamities. Despite ongoing disaster preparedness efforts, recent typhoons and persistent heavy rains have exposed critical gaps in the current system which are characterized by fragmented authority, delayed response, and dispersed resources. To address these challenges, the creation of a dedicated Department of Disaster Resilience is necessary. This agency would serve as the country’s primary disaster management body, centralizing command over disaster risk reduction, preparedness, response, and recovery. It would ensure clear leadership, streamline coordination across national and local government units, and enable a swift and effective response during emergencies. The proposed department would have the authority to mobilize government agencies, non-government organizations, and the private sector, and, when necessary, temporarily take control of essential infrastructure to safeguard public welfare. It would also oversee the prudent management and timely deployment of disaster-related funds, while institutionalizing fast, innovative procurement methods to ensure the rapid delivery of critical resources. Leveraging science and information technology, the department would implement integrated systems for real-time hazard monitoring, risk assessment, early warning, and emergency management. The department will be composed of highly qualified professionals such as disaster risk specialists, scientists, engineers, and planners to ensure technical expertise. Additionally, understanding that disaster resilience requires collective effort, it will actively build strong collaborations with local governments, communities, academic institutions, and civil society organizations. While climate change is a global challenge that no country can address alone, it is imperative for the Philippines to build its own capable and empowered agency to mitigate disaster risks and respond promptly and effectively when calamities strike. By establishing the Department of Disaster Resilience, the country aims to strengthen institutional capacity, reduce vulnerabilities, and build resilient communities that can better withstand future disasters. The recurring devastation caused by Typhoons Crising and Dante, alongside the frequent heavy rains brought by the habagat season and the growing impacts of climate change, underscores the urgent need to move beyond fragmented disaster management toward a cohesive, science-driven, and responsive system that protects lives and livelihoods. 2 This bill has been approved on third reading in the 18 th Congress and was similarly filed during the 19 th Congress. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. Despite existing mechanisms under current laws and agencies, disaster management efforts remain fragmented, reactive, and constrained by coordination gaps, overlapping mandates, and limited institutional capacity. Furthermore, the measure provides for the establishment of integrated disaster resilience plans, dedicated funding mechanisms, streamlined procurement processes during emergencies, and improved systems for humanitarian assistance and resource mobilization. It strengthens accountability, transparency, and efficiency in disaster-related programs and ensures that government interventions are timely, coordinated, and responsive to the needs of affected communities. By consolidating functions and creating a dedicated department with clear authority and mandate, this bill seeks to address long-standing structural inefficiencies and elevate disaster resilience as a national priority essential to safeguarding lives, protecting property, and sustaining economic growth. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF DISASTER RESILIENCE, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every year, Filipino communities face the devastating impact of typhoons, floods, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and other natural hazards. These calamities not only threaten lives but also deprive families of their homes, livelihoods, and sources of income. Our Filipino workers, farmers, fisherfolks, and low-income communities are often the first and hardest hit whenever disasters strike. In 2025, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) recorded a total of 23 tropical cyclones that affected more than 20 million Filipinos nationwide.1 The challenges facing the country are expected to become even more complex in the years ahead. In a report released by the PAGASA on 9 June 2026, the agency warned of the possible persistence of El Niño conditions into early 2027, increasing the risk of drought, extreme heat, and disruptions to agriculture and water supply. These emerging threats, together with the country’s continuing exposure to other natural hazards, highlight the need for a more proactive and holistic approach to disaster resilience. Modern disasters can no longer be viewed solely as emergencies requiring immediate response. They require comprehensive year-round planning, risk reduction, rehabilitation, and coordinated recovery efforts across all levels of government. This demands sustained coordination among national agencies, local government units (LGUs), and affected communities to minimize risks and strengthen preparedness. This measure seeks to establish a Department of Disaster Resilience as the primary government agency in protecting communities before, during, and after disasters. It aims to strengthen coordination among national and local governments, improve disaster preparedness and emergency response, and ensure that efforts to save lives, protect livelihoods, and rebuild communities are carried out in a more efficient and coordinated manner. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Given its location just above the equator, facing the open western Pacific Ocean on the east, the Philippines is no stranger to natural disasters, with more or less 20 typhoons entering the Philippine Area of Responsibility every year. The country is also found along the Pacific Ring of Fire, an area in the basin of the Pacific Ocean where many earthquakes and volcanic eruptions occur. As a result, Filipinos have suffered numerous natural disasters over the years that have resulted to loss of lives, injuries, and damaged or destroyed houses and properties, with the cost of damage amounting to billions of dollars. The country has seen three of the top ten worst disasters in terms of casualties in recent years, with Typhoon Sendong (Wash!) killing 1,439 individuals in December 2011, Typhoon Pablo (Bopha) killing 1,901 individuals in December 2012, and Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan) killing 6,300 individuals in November 2013. Typhoon Yolanda, also referred to as Super Typhoon Yolanda, is considered to be the world's strongest typhoon to hit at the time and is also the deadliest typhoon, affecting mostly low-lying coastal islands where, according to World Bank estimates, more than 60 percent of the population lives. Considering the vulnerability of the Philippines to various natural disasters such as earthquakes, volcanic activities, tropical cyclones and other phenomena, it is about time that we create a department that would function as the lead agency in charge of, among others, disaster risk reduction, disaster preparedness and response, rehabilitation and recovery. This bill seeks to create a Department of Disaster Resilience, which shall take on the powers and functions of the Office of Civil Defense, Climate Change Office of the Climate Change Commission, Geo- Hazard Assessment and Engineering Geology Section of the Mines and Geosciences Bureau, Health Emergency Management Bureau of the Department of Health, Disaster Response Assistance and Management Bureau of the Department of Social Welfare and Development, Bureau of Fire Protection, and Program Management Office for Earthquake Resiliency of the Greater Metro Manila Area. The Department shall oversee and coordinate the preparation, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of disaster and climate resilience plans, programs, projects and activities to reduce the risk of natural hazards and effects of climate change, and manage the impact of disasters with the ultimate goal of saving lives and minimizing damage to property. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JUAN^MIGUEL F. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF DISASTER RESILIENCE, DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, located in the Pacific Ocean, is frequented by typhoons, causing immense damage to infrastructure and devastation to many villages. Situated in the Pacific Ring of Fire, the country is also prone to earthquakes and volcanic activities. Possessing one of the longest coastlines in the world, the country is also vulnerable to storm surges and severe flooding. Overall, the Philippines is considered as the country most at risk from climate crisis, and one of the most affected by extreme weather events in the past two decades. Considering the adverse impacts of natural disasters to the attainment of economic goals, it is imperative that the government institutes long-term strategies and effective mechanisms to mitigate and manage risks and reduce vulnerabilities of communities. The proposed Department of Disaster Resilience is envisioned as the principal government body with "sufficiently high level of authority to lead the coordination, monitoring, oversight, and implementation of disaster risk reduction and management efforts." It will also "be equipped with the necessary competency and resources to engage new actors, particularly in the field of risk transfer and insurance." Further, DDR will "provide a clear operational framework to address the fragmented institutional functions and actions among concerned agencies on climate change and disasters."1 This measure proposes the Department of Disaster Resilience to be the primary government agency responsible for leading, organizing, and managing the national effort to reduce disaster risk, prepare for and respond to disasters, recover and rehabilitate, and build forward better, after the occurrence of disasters. Its mandate shall cover all natural hazards, including biological hazards (epidemic and pandemic, insect infestation). Its functions shall include, among others: a) Conduct risk and vulnerability assessment at the local level; b) Undertake the construction of evacuation centers that conform to international standards; c) Implement programs relating to the construction of new settlements and relocation of settlements in safe areas; d) Lead and collaborate with various stakeholders in providing the minimum basic needs of people in affected areas before, during and/or after a disaster; and e) Organize and manage post-disaster assessment and recovery and rehabilitation programs. In view of upholding the sanctity of human life and proactively addressing humanitarian emergencies, the immediate passage of this legislation is earnestly sought. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 5 of the 1987 Constitution provides that 'the State shall maintain peace and order and protect life and property. The State recognizes its duty to ensure immediate and continuing means of assistance by the National Government to local government units on their responsibility in reducing the loss of life and property and protect the nation from all hazards." The Philippines consistently ranks as one of the world's countries most exposed to all types of hazards - storms, volcanoes, epidemics, industrial accidents, etc. The country is even described as one of the most "typhoon-ravaged countries in the world." The Philippines experiences an average of 20 typhoons per year, with its urban residents facing risks from rising sea levels and increasing frequency of extreme weather events which cause economic losses that are increasing over time. Scientists believe this occurred because of climate change, in addition to the country's significant geographic location with over 7,641 islands. Apart from natural calamities, armed conflict and other man-made hazards further threaten the lives of Filipino communities. The country is said to be a "haven for terrorists" and was reported as one of the countries with the greatest number of terrorist organizations over the last decade. The current practice in disaster risk reduction, however, requires going through different government agencies delaying the mobilization of resources in times of disaster. During these events, lives are put in danger, basic needs like food, shelter water, and utilities are compromised and public infrastructures destroyed. The measure seeks to create an Authority rather than a Department because the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) itself prefer to be under the Office of the President since their response and rescue capabilities require the cooperation of other departments and agencies. Moreover, the additional creation of a department would be in contrast to the administration's effort and direction in rightsizing the government. Thus, it is imperative that an Authority be created under the Office of the President which will have the capacity to exercise command and control over concerned departments, agencies, government-owned and controlled corporations, and local government units, including the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and the Philippine National Police (PNP), on their respective functions, and be able to provide immediate response in times of disaster and other hazards. In light of this, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MARCOSr of !o. ■ . explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE For more than Thirty -Two (32) years ago, last January 24, 1990, Congress enacted Republic Act No. 6847, otherwise known as the “Philippine Sports Commission Act” which created the Philippine Sports Commission (PSC). Unfortunately, the PSC seems to fail in living up to its mandate of providing leadership, formulating the policies and setting the priorities and direction of all national amateur sports promotion and development, particularly giving the emphasis on_ grass-roots participation; encouraging wide participation of all sectors, government and private, in amateur sports promotion and development; and supplement government appropriations for sports promotion and development. Considering the dull state of Philippine sports, there is much to be desired for the betterment of the sports for the benefit of our athletes and coaches. The seeming deterioration of Philippine sports should be addressed. There was a time when our athletes are considered serious contenders in any sporting event we participate, unfortunately, those times has passed. Since Mansueto Velasco won a silver medal in boxing during the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, the Philippines has not won a single medal in the succeeding editions of the Summer Olympics. When the Philippines won its first ever overall championship in the Southeast Asian Games during the 2005 edition held in Manila, Philippine sports seemed to have reached its threshold. Unfortunately, the experiences and the lessons learned in earning that victory were not sustained. The Philippines is rich in talent as can be proven by the many sports heroes that the country has produced in various sports disciplines. The success of the Honorable Senator Emmanuel D. Pacquiao in boxing, Gilas O Pilipinas in Basketball and Azkals in football have brought pride to the country. The Philippines have always impressed international and foreign sports personalities with our remarkable achievements. With our rich talent pool for any sporting event, we can be a perennial face in any sports competition we join. This measure will address the various challenges that confront Philippine sports. This bill proposes the creation of a Department of Sports, a cabinet-level agency that will provide leadership in the promotion and development of sports in the country and set the parameters to address the needs of our athletes, coaches, trainers and sports officials, The Department of Sports will be responsible for promulgating policies that will help the country improve its performance in _ international competitions. Equally important is the role in finding solutions to the problems besetting Philippine sports including the lack of a comprehensive national sports program, the need to enhance the partnership with various sectors involved in sports, obsolete training methods, lack of modern and high quality training facilities, equipment, and sport venues. It is now high time for the government to prioritize sports in the national agenda, and consider sports as an integral factor in nation building. This House Bill seeks to create the Department of Sports, the government entity that shall lead the implementation of policies on the promotion and development of sports and health fitness programs in the country. Thus, the early passage of this bill is earnestly requested. MIC LL. title: AN ACT DECLARING A NATIONAL POLICY FOR SPORTS AS AN ENGINE FOR NATION-BUILDING, SOCIAL PROGRESS, AND PROMOTION OF TOTAL HUMAN DEVELOPMENT, AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF SPORTS, DEFINING ITS POWER AND FUNCTIONS AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Great physical and mental health, self-discipline, competitiveness, development of strong social bonds, and holistic character development are a few of the various benefits one may receive when engaging in sports. Aside from these benefits that individuals may attain, taking part in sports also has the ability to leave a lasting and advantageous impact on society. For instance, from an economic standpoint, the sports industry is capable of pooling funds around the local economy, as well as providing jobs for coaches, referees, gym employees, stadium vendors, and many more. Another way sports can affect the community is through the unity, patriotism, and nationalism that it can bring through its athletes. When Manny Pacquiao, one of the most successful Filipino athletes, made his professional debut as a boxer in 1995, the entire country would come together with their friends and families to watch his match and cheer for him. The same spirit was shown during the 2020 Olympics —the year of the most medals won by the Philippines— when the country garnered four (4) medals, one of them from Hidylin Diaz, the country's first Olympic Gold medalist, who clinched a victory that would later go down in history. Numerous Filipinos, as well as public and private institutions, showed their support to the athletes by posting promotions as well as their congratulations. To say the least, the sense of pride one may feel to see someone from their home country participating in an international competition, let alone winning, is a feeling like no other. This feeling of victory not only uplifts people, but also inspires them to work hard and aim high - a kind of attitude that is important in society. While joining an international competition is the ultimate goal of most athletes, it must be remembered that the benefits sports may bring to society can still be attained through lower divisions such as amateur, local, and national sports. The National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) and The University Athletic Association of the Philippines (UAAP) have been grooming skillful athletes for decades, and every year, their sporting events are highly anticipated by many fans around the country as it provides a sense of excitement and passion for the athletes that they support. The Philippines Sports Commission (PSC) which was established in 1990 was made with the purpose of encouraging and promoting sports in all sectors. However, it seems that after about three (3) decades, the government agency became unsustainable and is no longer able to live up to its mandate. Given this, this Bill seeks to establish a Department of Sports in order to fully focus, implement, promote, and better execute all aspects related to the development of sports and athletes in the country. The cabinet-level agency aims to provide leadership in the advancement of sports in the country, as well as aspires to address the various challenges of the sports industry such as the lack of adequate facilities and equipment, the improvement of training programs, and the absence of a comprehensive nationwide sports program. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this Bill is earnestly sought. EDWIN L. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution states that the State shall promote physical education and encourage sports programs, league competitions, and amateur sports, including training for international competitions, to foster self-discipline, teamwork, and excellence for the development of a healthy and alert citizenry. During the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, Hidilyn Diaz created history by bagging the first- ever gold medal of the country. Recently, during the Paris Olympics, Carlos Edriel Yulo bagged two gold medals, which created another milestone for the country. Despite these remarkable achievements, there is still a need for a more centralized, cohesive, and well-funded approach to sports development in the country. This measure seeks to address the gaps in sports management and development in the Philippines through the creation of the Department of Sports which shall streamline the government’s efforts and allocate the necessary resources to support the country’s current and budding athletes. By institutionalizing this Department, the government can also ensure the continuity of programs, policies, and support to athletes and sports development in the country. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this measure is earnestly sought. CRISPIN DIEGO “PING” D. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF SPORTS, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE “We, the sovereign Filipino people, imploring the aid of Almighty God, in order to build a just and humane society and establish a Government that shall embody our ideals and aspirations, promote the common good, conserve and develop our patrimony, and secure to ourselves and our posterity the blessings of independence and democracy under the rule of law and a regime of truth, justice, freedom, love, equality, and peace, do ordain and promulgate this Constitution.” The national vision embodied in the 1987 Constitution, through its Preamble, requires a citizenry with a strong foundation of discipline, teamwork, commitment, and resilience. Sports is a powerful, primary instrument for the formation of these values. It teaches us to strive, to collaborate, and to maintain not just physical fitness, but total mental, emotional, and even spiritual formation and health. Beyond character formation, which is invaluable, sports and sports tourism represent a huge opportunity for the Philippines. Globally, sports tourism is emerging as one of the fastest-growing sectors in the tourism industry. The global sports tourism market is projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 16.43% between 2024 and 2032, from USD 544.38 billion in 2023 to USD 2,089.58 billion by 2032.1 Our own experience confirms this potential. The 2019 30th Southeast Asian (SEA) Games generated over Php 500 million in revenue.2 On a larger scale, co-hosting the 2023 FIBA Basketball World Cup created an economic impact of Php 17.8 billion.3 Projections for hosting a single future event like the Volleyball World Championship estimate a total economic impact of over USD 40 million and an alignment with a destination tourism market valued at USD 5.4 billion.4 1 World Tourism Forum Institute (2025). The Explosive Growth of the Sports Tourism Market: A $2 Trillion Opportunity by 2032. https://live.worldtourismforum.net/news/Catch-up-the-latest-news-in-tourism-industry/The-Explosive-Growth-of-the-Sports-Tourism- Market-A-2-Trillion-Opportunity-by-2032 2 Partlow, M. Philippine News Agency (2019). Sports tourism boosts tourist arrivals in Dumaguete. https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1088794 3 Henson, J. The Philippine Star (2024). P17.8 billion impact from FIBA World Cup. https://www.philstar.com/sports/2024/02/03/2330530/p178-billion-impact-fiba-world-cup 4 Projections from Volleyball World Championship 1 Yet, despite our proven capability to host world-class events and earning praise for our people’s renowned hospitality, we fail to consistently translate this potential into lasting national success. For too many Filipinos, sports remains a dream rather than a viable and honored profession. It is a calling we deny to our own people because we lack the right systems, support, and structures. This systemic weakness is most evident in the Olympics. The long wait between the 1996 boxing silver medal by Mansueto Velasco and Hidilyn Diaz's historic gold in weightlifting in 2020 highlights the challenges faced by Filipino athletes in reaching their full potential on the world’s biggest sporting stage. The Philippine Sports Commission (PSC), established in 1990 through Republic Act No. 6847, is mandated to, among others, “provide the leadership, formulate the policies and set the priorities and direction of all national amateur sports promotion and development, particularly giving emphasis on grassroots participation.” However, its focus on grassroots participation may not fully address the needs of elite athletes to compete at the highest levels of sports competitions. In 2001, Republic Act No. 9155 or the “Governance of Basic Education Act of 2001” abolished the Bureau of Physical Education and School Sports (BPESS) and transferred “[a]ll functions, programs and activities of the Department of Education related to sports competition” to the Philippine Sports Commission (PSC). While physical education remains in the curriculum, this shift has weakened overall sports development. This measure will address the perennial challenges that hinder the growth of Philippine sports. This bill proposes the creation of a Department of Sports, a cabinet-level agency that will provide focused leadership for national sports promotion and development, and address the needs of athletes, coaches, trainers, and sports officials across all levels. With a dedicated department, we can find comprehensive solutions to the problems besetting Philippine sports, particularly the lack of a coherent national sports program, the need to enhance the partnership with various sectors involved in sports, obsolete training methods, lack of modern and high-quality training facilities, equipment, and sports venues. In line with the policy adopted by its original proponent Senator Alan Peter “Compañero” S. Cayetano, this bill therefore serves as a counterpart measure. It is for the reason stated above that the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. RICARDO S. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine Constitution mandates the State to promote physical education and support sports programs that build discipline, resilience, and excellence. Yet decades later, Filipino athletes continue to train under fragmented systems, with limited support and inconsistent long-term planning. In 2021, the world watched as Hidilyn Diaz lifted not only a barbell but an entire nation, bringing home the Philippines’ first Olympic gold medal. In 2024, Carlos Yulo soared to double gold at the Paris Olympics. These victories are historic. But they were achieved despite systemic limitations, not because of institutional strength. The reality is clear: our athletes have the talent. What they need is a nation that fully supports them. This bill seeks to create a Department of Sports that will lead the development of grassroots programs, unify national and local initiatives, and provide sustained support to both amateur and elite athletes. By elevating sports to a full department, the government can ensure consistent funding, strategic planning, and long-term vision. It will allow athletes to focus on their training, knowing their country stands firmly behind them. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this measure is earnestly sought. CRISPIN DIEGO “PING” D. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE “Similarly, anyone who competes as an athlete does not receive the victor’s crown except by competing according to the rules.” 2 Timothy 2:5 Sports is a cross-cutting vehicle that will contribute to achieving national development and a healthy society. It is essential for the development of our youth and future generations. Sports brings together quality interactions among people, and serves as a healthy outlet to release tension and stress. It is also an important avenue for academic advancement and an opportunity for social mobility. The strategic role of sports in the achievement of sports development goals and national growth cannot be overstated. Thus, a dedicated agency must be proactive in exhausting every opportunity to diversify and develop the economy while strengthening the communities. The growth and future development of sports requires innovative and creative thinking. It requires bold and fearless leadership and a willingness to go beyond the status quo. The opportunities and potentials seem limitless. Hence, there is a need for people with strong spirit and great love for sports who could provide the greatest natural assets to direct relevant and applicable sports evolution. Through the years, sports has evolved into a pathway for a better quality of life, a source of honor and national pride, an inspiration to face up to the challenges of the modern world and a popular form of entertainment. It is not merely a spectator’s pastime, it becomes a primary influencer in society as a driver for physical fitness and a healthy lifestyle. There is a reason why Article XIV, Section 19 of the 1987 Constitution provides that “the State shall promote physical education and encourage sports programs, league competitions and amateur sports, including training for international competitions, to foster self-discipline, teamwork and excellence for the development of a healthy and alert citizenry.” At present, the Philippine Sports Commission (PSC), established in 1990 through Republic Act No. 6847, is the sole policy-making and coordinating body of all amateur sports development programs and institutions in the Philippines. It is mandated to, among others, “provide the leadership, formulate the policies and set the priorities and direction of all national amateur sports promotion and development, particularly giving emphasis on grassroots participation.” However, its focus on grassroots participation may not fully address the needs of elite athletes to compete at the highest levels of sports competitions. Sports development, however, is an intricate process that begins with early talent education through grassroots programs on a nationwide basis, harnessing the resources of the Department of Education (DepEd) and Department of the Interior and Local Government. Then, athletes are brought to a stage to display their potential through Batang Pinoy for 15 years old and below, Palarong Pambansa for high school students and the Philippine National Games to ferret out elite performers. In Taguig City, we value and enrich every Taguigeños’ sports inclinations by conducting tournaments and sports camps for basketball, volleyball, football, baseball, badminton, among others. Concretely, the Taguig Sports Training and Enhancement Program is crafted based on the Special Program for Sports (SPS) in the Philippines, a DepEd initiative designed to foster a career path for learners with interest and talent in sports. This program provides structured training and support to develop athletes and sports professionals. And through this measure, we wish to replicate our humble beginnings by espousing for a sports-focused department. This measure will address the perennial challenges that hinder the growth of Philippine sports through the creation of a Department of Sports, a cabinet-level agency that will provide focused leadership for national sports promotion and development, and address the needs of athletes, coaches, trainers, and sports officials across all levels. The proposed department will spearhead the formulation and implementation of the “National Sports Development Agenda” focusing on grassroots and elite sports, sports science and education, sports infrastructure, coaching and human resource development, public-private sector partnership and sports for all. Further, the bill seeks to provide incentives to the private sector, particularly exempting them from payment of customs duties, taxes, and tariffs for their donations, contributions, bequests, and grants of any imported sports equipment, instruments and capital equipment that are not locally available. Hence, the approval of this Bill is earnestly requested. JORGE DANIEL S. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF SPORTS, CULTURE AND THE ARTS DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution declares that the State shall “promote physical education and encourage sports programs, league competitions, and amateur sports, including training for international competitions” as well as “foster the preservation, enrichment, and dynamic evolution of a Filipino national culture based on the principle of unity in diversity.” Yet despite these constitutional mandates, the present structure of government has fragmented the promotion, development, and administration of sports, culture, and the arts into multiple agencies with overlapping mandates and limited coordination. This has resulted in bureaucratic inefficiencies, underinvestment in grassroots talent, and gaps in long-term national planning. Filipino athletes continue to rely heavily on individual initiative and private sponsorship to excel in international competitions, while Filipino artists and cultural workers face unstable funding and inadequate institutional support. Meanwhile, world-class sports and cultural facilities remain unevenly distributed and underutilized across the country. This bill seeks to create a Department of Sports, Culture, and the Arts to unify governance, strengthen support systems, and ensure that Filipino talents, whether on the global sports stage or in cultural and artistic arenas, receive the recognition, development, and social protection they deserve. By integrating national policy direction, facilities management, grassroots development, and international relations under one department, this measure aims to address longstanding structural barriers and build a sustainable ecosystem for national excellence. It likewise establishes mechanisms for incentives, quality infrastructure, and comprehensive cultural and sports development planning that align with the nation’s long-term socio-economic goals and global competitiveness. epi In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. label: HB 7610
title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF SPORTS, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Sports in all levels is more than competition, it is a pathway to building strong communities, improving health, and honing personal development. Organized sports programs provide structure, positive role models, and constructive outlets to the youth, adults, and communities vulnerable to poverty, crime, and social exclusion alike. In recent years we have seen the positive effects of success from athletes like Hidilyn Diaz and Carlos Yulo on Filipino morale and pride. The Filipino sporting talent is evident and strong, but it lacks the appropriate institutional support and guidance to help it truly flourish and reach its potential. Despite its importance, sports development in the Philippines remains fragmented, underfunded, and institutionally lacking. While the PSC is mandated to formulate policy and coordinate amateur sports development, it does not possess the institutional authority, budgetary scale, or structural reach required to lead a comprehensive and sustained national sports program. Sports-related functions and policy are dispersed across multiple agencies, including the Department of Education, the National Academy of Sports, local government units, and private and national sports associations. This horizontal and decentralized arrangement has resulted in inefficient coordination, overlapping responsibilities, inconsistent standards, and the absence of a unified national strategy. As a result, athlete development pathways, from grassroots and school sports to elite and international competition are often disjointed and under resourced. The consequences of this fragmentation are borne most heavily by Filipino athletes. Many athletes train and compete with limited financial support, inadequate access to modern facilities and equipment, outdated training methods, and insufficient sports science, medical, and career-transition assistance. Despite representing the country on the international stage and bringing honor to the nation, athletes remain underappreciated and underfunded, often relying on personal resources, private donations, or short-term incentives rather than stable institutional support. Sports for many Filipinos is treated as a hobby rather than a legitimate and dignified profession. In contrast to our South East Asian neighbor, Thailand offers a compelling regional model of centralized sports governance. Sports policy in Thailand is led by the Ministry of Tourism and Sports, a cabinet-level department with direct authority over national sports development. Under this Ministry operates the Sports Authority of Thailand, a corporatized implementing body responsible for athlete development, training systems, infrastructure, and funding. Grassroots, school sports, elite training, and international competition are aligned under a vertical and centralized structure, allowing for clear accountability, coherent planning, and efficient execution. This system has enabled Thailand to achieve consistent success across regional and continental competitions, supported by strong state backing and institutional continuity. Having a dedicated Department of Sports would allow the country to integrate athlete development, event hosting, infrastructure planning, tourism promotion, and private sector partnerships into a single, coherent framework. This would enable the Philippines to position itself as a regional hub for international competitions, training camps, and sports-related investments—creating jobs, stimulating local economies, and strengthening national branding. This measure proposes the creation of a Department of Sports, a cabinet-level agency that will provide focused leadership, clear responsibilities, and sustained institutional support to address the needs of athletes, coaches, trainers and sports officials across all levels. Elevating sports governance to the cabinet level helps ensure that Philippine sports policy is no longer secondary, unpredictable or dependent on short-term initiatives, but is treated as a core pillar of national development. Ultimately, a Department of Sports creates a system where success is planned, supported, and sustainable, allowing Filipino athletes to reach their full potential while strengthening national pride and international competitiveness. By focusing on sports governance, the State affirms its commitment to the youth, honors the sacrifices of Filipino athletes, strengthens national pride, and harnesses sports as a driver of social, cultural, and economic progress. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this Bill creating a centralized Department of Sports is earnestly sought. REP. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE “We, the sovereign Filipino people, imploring the aid of Almighty God, in order to build a just and humane society and establish a Government that shall embody our ideals and aspirations, promote the common good, conserve and develop our patrimony, and secure to ourselves and our posterity the blessings of independence and democracy under the rule of law and a regime of truth, justice, freedom, love, equality, and peace, do ordain and promulgate this Constitution.” The national vision embodied in the 1987 Constitution, through its Preamble, requires a citizenry with a strong foundation of discipline, teamwork, commitment, and resilience. Sports is a powerful, primary instrument for the formation of these values. It teaches us to strive, to collaborate, and to maintain not just physical fitness, but total mental, emotional, and even spiritual formation and health. Beyond character formation, which is invaluable, sports and sports tourism represent a huge opportunity for the Philippines. Globally, sports tourism is emerging as one of the fastest-growing sectors in the tourism industry. The global sports tourism market is projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 16.43% between 2024 and 2032, from USD 544.38 billion in 2023 to USD 2,089.58 billion by 2032.1 Our own experience confirms this potential. The 2019 30th Southeast Asian (SEA) Games generated over Php 500 million in revenue.2 On a larger scale, co- World Tourism Forum Institute (2025).
