Philippine News Agency (2019). Sports tourism boosts tourist arrivals in Dumaguete. https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1088794 hosting the 2023 FIBA Basketball World Cup created an economic impact of Php 17.8 billion.3 Projections for hosting a single future event like the Volleyball World Championship estimate a total economic impact of over USD 40 million and an alignment with a destination tourism market valued at USD 5.4 billion.4 Yet, despite our proven capability to host world-class events and earning praise for our people’s renowned hospitality, we fail to consistently translate this potential into lasting national success. For too many Filipinos, sports remains a dream rather than a viable and honored profession. It is a calling we deny to our own people because we lack the right systems, support, and structures. This systemic weakness is most evident in the Olympics. The long wait between the 1996 boxing silver medal by Mansueto Velasco and Hidilyn Diaz's historic gold in weightlifting in 2020 highlights the challenges faced by Filipino athletes in reaching their full potential on the world’s biggest sporting stage. The Philippine Sports Commission (PSC), established in 1990 through Republic Act No. 6847, is mandated to, among others, “provide the leadership, formulate the policies and set the priorities and direction of all national amateur sports promotion and development, particularly giving emphasis on grassroots participation.” However, its focus on grassroots participation may not fully address the needs of elite athletes to compete at the highest levels of sports competitions. In 2001, Republic Act No. 9155 or the “Governance of Basic Education Act of 2001” abolished the Bureau of Physical Education and School Sports (BPESS) and transferred “[a]ll functions, programs and activities of the Department of Education related to sports competition” to the Philippine Sports Commission (PSC). While physical education remains in the curriculum, this shift has weakened overall sports development. This measure will address the perennial challenges that hinder the growth of Philippine sports. This bill proposes the creation of a Department of Sports, a cabinet-level agency that will provide focused leadership for national sports promotion and development, and address the needs of athletes, coaches, trainers, and sports officials across all levels. With a dedicated department, we can find comprehensive solutions to the problems besetting Philippine sports, particularly the lack of a coherent national sports program, the need to enhance the partnership with various sectors involved in sports, obsolete training methods, lack of modern and high-quality training facilities, equipment, and sports venues. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE As the agency responsible for training and capacitating the country's workers, the Technical Education and Skills Education (TESDA) was established to encourage the full participation of and for the mobilization of the industry, labor, local government units and technical-vocational institutions in the skills development of the country's human resources. The COVID-19 pandemic brought the world to an unprecedented level of societal disruption. Many industries were immediately impacted by this: with the loss of markets came the loss of jobs. Prior to the pandemic, Asia Pacific had some of the highest economic growth rates in the world; but still afflicted with high levels of worker hardship, with 300 million workers living with their families in poverty and some 58 million in extreme poverty in 2019.1 Through the Employment Recovery Agenda of the National Employment Recovery Strategy (NERS) 2021-2022 Task Force, TESDA took part and facilitated trainings and introduced approaches to restart economic activities, restore business 1 https://www. iio.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/—dgrcports/—dcomm/— publ/documents/publication/wcms_795453.pdf and consumer confidence, upgrade and retool the workforce, and facilitate labor market access. It has assisted 2.08 million individuals and benefitted 129,000 establishments, with 780,119 jobs generated.2 In order to comply with the growing demand of labor resources, TESDA is developing strategies on Technical Vocational Education and Training (TVET) for global competitiveness and social equity. However, these strategies may not be attained if TESDA's organizational structure, its own manpower and ability to produce higher quality of learning and training materials are still among the primary hindrances that prevent the progress of TESDA. This bill seeks to create a Department of Technical Education Training and Certification, which will take the place and absorb the current TESDA. It is high time to empo wer TESDA and enable the agency to fulfill its mandate as the leading partner in the development of the Filipino workforce. ■ In lieu of the foregoing, immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought NLEGARDA ■■ t-t. i. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF TECHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS DEVELOPMENT, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, REPEALING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7796, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE TESDA ACT OF 1994 AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The creation of the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) paved the way in providing millions of Filipnos with relevant, accessible, high quality and efficient technical education and skills development in support of the development of high quality Filipino middle-level manpower responsive to the country’s development goals and priorities. In 2018 alone, there are more than 2 million who benefitted in the agency’s various Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) program. For twenty-five (25) years, after the passage of Republic Act No. 7796 or the TESDA Act which was enacted on August 25, 1994, continues to be in the forefront in ensuring that Filipinos have access to technical education and skills development (TESD) that is not only relevant and efficient, but also accessible and of high quality. Despite much progress and lives changed, the agency is facing various and enormous challenges in order to adapt to the ever- changing local and global environment that the organization needs to focus on. In order to meet world standards, TESDA must address the need for modern facilities and equipment to level with the requirements in addressing the challenges created by the 4IR (Fourth Industrial Revolution) and other advancements that may happen in the future. It must also be bestowed with the police powers to impose sanctions and penalties to erring TESD implementers. These are among the limitations to what TESDA can do which can be ultimately addressed if the agency will be elevated into a line Department of the government. This proposed Bill seeks to repeal R.A. 7796 or the TESDA Act of 1994 and to reinforce the powers and organizational function of TESDA by turning it into a Department. The proposed Department shall become the primary policy formulation, planning, coordinating, implementing, regulating and administrative entity of the government for technical education and training and certification policies, plans and programs. It shall be headed by a Secretary, four (4) Undersecretaries and four (4) Assistant Secretaries. Page | 1 With the proposed legislative measure, TESDA will be strengthened as an implementing and regulatory institution of the Technical and Vocational Sector of the country’s trifocal education system. This measure is made in the interest of the Filipinos who wants to regain new skills and improve their well-being, and will be achieved in greater capacity vision as the transformational leader in the technical education and skills development of the Filipino workforce. The immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. TESDA's mandate is relevant since skills and training are essential to the workforce. To properly support such relevant activities, there is a need to revamp the system. By elevating the authority into a department, adequate budgetary support, personnel, and resources will be provided to fUrther develop the projects and programs of TESDA.

explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 7796 or the TESDA Act of 1994 was approved on August 25, 1994 which paved the way for the creation of the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA). Sec. 2 of the law specifically mandated TESDA to carry out the government efforts in providing relevant, accessible, high quality and efficient technical education and skills development in support of the development of high quality Filipino middle-level manpower responsive to the country’s development goals and priorities. By virtue of this law, the former National Manpower and Youth Council (NMYC), the Bureau of Technical Vocational Education of the then Department of Education, Culture and Sports (BTVE-DECS) and the Apprenticeship program of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) were integrated into TESDA. The merger of these entities was based on the recommendation of the Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM) that had undergone a nationwide review of the state of the Philippine education and training system in 1991. Twenty-five (25) years hence, TESDA has been the leading authority in ensuring that technical education and skills development (TESD) is relevant, efficient, accessible, and of high quality. However, the agency has been facing enormous challenges due to changes in the local and global environment that the organization needs to focus on. There are limitations to what TESDA can do which can be addressed if it will be elevated into a line Department of the government. TESDA must address the need for modern facilities and equipment in order to be at par with the requirements of the challenge posed by the Fourth Industrial Revolution and other advancements that may happen in the future. The bill seeks to repeal R.A. 7796 or the TESDA Act of 1994 and to strengthen the powers and the organizational function of TESDA by elevating it into a Department. The proposed Department shall be the primary policy formulation, planning, coordinating, implementing, regulating and administrative entity of the government for technical education and training and certification policies, plans and programs. It shall be headed by a Secretary, four (4) Undersecretaries and four (4) Assistant Secretaries. Carrying out the functions of the new Department shall be done by the various bureaus, service offices and Regional/ Provincial/ District Offices. Implementation of direct training programs will be done by the technology institutions. With the proposed legislative measure, TESDA will be strengthened as an implementing and regulatory institution of the Technical and Vocational Sector of the country’s trifocal education system. The agency will have a better capacity to fulfill its vision as the transformational leader in the technical education and skills development of the Filipino workforce. The immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MARK O. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) was established through the enactment of Republic Act No. 7796 otherwise known as the "Technical Education and Skills Development Act of 1994" with the aim to encourage the full participation of and mobilize the industry, labor, local government units and technical vocational institutions in the skills development of the country's human resources. The said Act integrated the functions of the former National Manpower and Youth Council (NMYC), the Bureau of Technical-Vocational Education of the Department of Education, Culture and Sports (BTVE-DECS) and the Office of Apprenticeship of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) as a result of a national review of the state of Philippine education and manpower development which was undertaken by the Congressional Commission on Education back in 1991. TESDA has been the leading authority managing technical skills education in the Philippines. Its major thrust is the formulation of a comprehensive development plan for middle-level manpower based on the National Technical Education and Skills Development Plan that includes apprenticeship, dual training system and other similar schemes. TESDA is also improving its language course offerings in partnership with foreign embassies and international organizations consistent with the strategy to reposition technical vocational education and training (TVET) for global competitiveness. The language-related courses —Arabic, Mandarin, Korean, Italian and French —will be added to the existing courses under its National Skills Language Center (NLSC). President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said in his inaugural address on June 30 that “sharpening the language skills” of Filipino workers, including Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs), is important to give them the advantage to survive and thrive in foreign countries. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF TECHNICAL EDUCATION TRAINING AND CERTIFICATION, PROVIDING FOR ITS POWERS, STRUCTURE AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 7796 or the Technical Education and Skills Education Act (TESDA) was passed into law in 1994. It was created to provide relevant, accessible, high quality and efficient technical education and skills development of the country’s human resources. Over the years, TESDA has established itself as the nation's leading source of labor in highly technical disciplines. The agency’s purpose was all the more highlighted during the pandemic when TESDA launched its TESDA Online Program (TOP) and “TESDA Abot Lahat ang OFWs” program which aims to upskill and retool workers in order to recoup job losses.1 Nonetheless, the current system leaves much to be desired and it is evident that changes must be had in order to make technical and vocational education in our country more efficient. Thus, this bill seeks to create a Department of Technical Education Training and Certification, which will take the place and absorb the current TESDA with the end goal of providing more quality and accessible technical and vocational education for all. In line with the policy adopted by its original proponent Senator Loren Legarda, this bill therefore likewise serves as a counter-part House Bill. It is for the reasons stated above that the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTONIO B. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The creation of the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) on August 25, 1994, through the merger of the former National Manpower and Youth Council (NMYC), the Bureau of Technical Vocational Education of the then Department of Education, Culture and Sports (BTVE-DECS) and the Apprenticeship program of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE), was an offshoot of the trifocalization of education recommended by the 1991 Congresssional Education Commission or EDCOM. By virtue of Republic Act No. 7796 (TESDA Act of 1994), the TESDA is mandated to ensure the delivery of relevant, accessible, high quality and efficient technical education and skills development and to develop high quality middle-level manpower responsive to the country’s development goals and priorities. However, after more than two decades of delivering relevant, accessible, and efficient technical education and skills development thoughout ther country, TESDA has been encountering many challenges and limitations that affect the performance of its functions, delivery of technical-vocational education and training (TVET) programs, and fulfillment of its vision. One of these is the need to sstrengthen its organizational structure and functions to keep pace with the advent of technology and the demands of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR). The frequent transfer of the TESDA from one office to another has also affected its functions, programs and projects, and delivery of educational services. From an attached agency of the Department of Labor and Employment, TESDA was transferred to the Office of the President and now, to the Department of Trade and Industry through executive order signed by President Duterte. Moreover, under the TESDA Charter, the TESDA Director-General shall enjoy the benefits, privileges ad emoluments equivalent to the rank of Undersecretary. However, the current and past two Presidents of the Philippines appointed the TESDA Director General with a Cabinet rank position or equivalent to a Secretary. By elevating the TESDA into a department, it shall be headed by a Secretary, four (4) Undersecretaries and four (4) Assistant Secretaries and attain self-determination to ensure permanence and continuity of mandated programs. This will also strengthen the implementing, regulatory, and policy-making functions of the agency, as well as make it more responsive and agile in the era of the 4IR and digital economy. The proposed Department of Technical Education and Skills Development (DTESD) will not only improve the resource/budget allocation for TVET programs, but will also ably represent the TVET sector as a whole, changing its “second class” perception. More importantly, the proposed DTESD will have a better capacity to fulfill its vision as the transformational leader in TVET in the country. The immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF THCHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS DEVELOPMENT, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSH REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7796, OTHERVISE KNOWN AS THE TECHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS I)EVELOPMENT AUTHORITY OR TESDA ACT OF 1994, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution of the Philippines Article XII, Section 14 provides that "The sustained development of a reservoir of national talents consisting of Filipino scientists, entrepreneurs, professionals, managers, high-level technical manpower and skilled workers and craftsmen in all fields shall be promoted by the State." The Constitution likewise asserts in Article XIV, Section 1 that "The State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all." Also, Article XIV, Section 2 emphasizes the govemment's duty to ensure a complete and suitable education system that meets the needs of the people in an ever-changing environment. It also calls for support for students through scholarships and other aid, especially for those from underprivileged backgrounds. Additionally, it promotes alternative leaming approaches, including informal and community-based programs. Critical to the promotion of sustained development of a highly skilled work force, the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) was established through Republic Act No. 7796 (TESDA Act of 1994) on August 25,1994. Through the merging of National Manpower and Youth Council (NMYC), Bureau of Technical and Vocational Education (BTVE), and the Apprenticeship Program of the Bureau of Local Employment a3LE), TESDA is mandated to oversee skills development, set standards, accredit institutions, fund projects, and support trainer programs for the development of a top-quality middle-level manpower capable of adapting towards emerging issues and necessities of the Fourth Industrial Revolution. TESDA has aimed to set the direction, promulgate relevant standards, and implement programs geared towards a quality-assured and inclusive technical education and skills development and certification system for the country's technical-vocational education and training (TVET) system. The frequent transfer between various administrative entities has been driven by different factors, including changes in government priorities, administrative restructuring, and attempts to enhance coordination between TESDA and other government agencies. However, these transfers have often resulted in disruptions to TESDA's operations, delays in the implementation of programs, and challenges in maintaining continuity and coherence in policy and programmatic efforts. Recognizing the need for stability, coherence, and focused leadership in the promotion of technical education and skills development, this bill proposes the establishment of the Department of Technical Education and Skills Development (DTESD) as a permanent and dedicated government agency. By elevating TESDA into a department, the bill aims to provide TESDA with the necessary institutional franiework, authority, and resources to effectively cany out its mandate in a sustained and coherent manner. The creation of the DTESD is envisioned to address the ever-changing labor landscape and its frequent transfers between different government offices. By consolidating efforts in TVET development under a single department, the bill seeks to streamline governance, enhance coordination, and ensure the continuity and effectiveness of policies and programs aimed at developing a skilled and globally competitive workforce in the Philippines. Approval of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution provides that: the State shall promote a just and dynamic social order that will ensure the prosperity and independence of the nation and free the people from poverty through policies that provide adequate social services, promote full employment, a rising standard of living, and improved quality of life for all (Sec. 9, Art. II); the State shall promote social justice in all phases of national development (Sec. 10, Art. II); the State shall give priority to education, science and technology, arts, culture, and sports to foster patriotism and nationalism, accelerate social progress, and promote total human liberation and development (Sec. 17, Art. II); the Congress shall give highest priority to the enactment of measures that reduce social, economic, and political inequalities (Sec.1, Art. XIII); the State shall encourage non-formal, informal, and indigenous learning systems, as well as self- learning, independent, and out-of-school study programs particularly those that respond to community needs (Sec 2[4], Art. XIV); and Science and technology are essential for national development and progress. The State shall give priority to research and development, invention, innovation, and their utilization; and to science and technology education, training, and services. It shall support indigenous, appropriate, and self-reliant scientific and technological capabilities, and their application to the country’s productive systems and national life (Sec. 10, Art. XIV). In this regard, the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) which was created by virtue of Republic Act 7796, otherwise known as the “Technical Education and Skills Development Act of 1994” is the government agency tasked to manage and supervise technical education and skills development in the Philippines. TESDA’s vision is a transformational leader in the technical education and skills development of the Filipino workforce, with a mission of setting directions, promulgating relevant standards, and implementing programs geared towards a quality-assured and inclusive technical education and skills development and certification system. Under the bill, the proposed Department of Technical Education and Skills Development (DTESD) shall be the primary policy formulation, planning, coordinating, implementing, regulatory, and administrative entity of the government for technical education and training programs. With its gargantuan task, it is believed that by converting Page 1 of 15 it into a Department, TESDA will be strengthened as an implementing and regulatory institution of the technical and vocational sector. It will make this Agency in a better position to fulfill its vision and mission, believing in demonstrated competence, institutional integrity, personal commitment, culture of innovativeness, and a deep sense of nationalism. The early passage of this Bill, therefore, is earnestly requested. BIENVENIDO M. ABANTE, JR. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) was established on August 25, 1994, by virtue of Republic Act No. 7796, otherwise known as the “Technical Education and Skills Development Act of 1994.” Since its creation, TESDA has remained an essential contributor to the National Government’s mission of providing Filipinos with quality-assured technical education and skills development programs, and mobilizing technical-vocational institutions across the country. Over three decades after its establishment, TESDA continues to serve as the leading government agency responsible for setting the direction of, and ensuring the efficient delivery of, technical education and skills development programs across various sectors nationwide. However, TESDA has also faced challenges and limitations, particularly in today’s ever-changing local and global environment. To address pressing concerns such as strengthening TESDA’s organizational structure and modernizing skills training facilities, the overall system of the Authority must be enhanced through an increased budget, as well as sufficient personnel and resources. Hence, this proposed measure seeks to repeal Republic Act No. 7796, or the “Technical Education and Skills Development Act of 1994,” and strengthen the powers and organizational functions of TESDA by transforming it into a full-fledged Department. The Department shall serve as the primary policy- making, planning, coordinating, implementing, regulating, and administrative entity of the government for technical education, training, and certification programs. It shall be headed by a Secretary, supported by four (4) Undersecretaries and four (4) Assistant Secretaries. Such a reform is necessary to address challenges and implement policies consistent with the demands of the Fourth Industrial Revolution and other global advancements. Through this proposed legislative measure, TESDA will be further strengthened as the implementing and regulatory institution for the Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) sector within the country’s trifocal education system. Most importantly, this measure is being filed to promote the interests and meet the needs of the hardworking and highly skilled Filipino workforce. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. JONATHA) T. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The creation of the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) on August 25, 1994, through the merger of the former National Manpower and Youth Council (NMYC), the Bureau of Technical Vocational Education of the then Department of Education, Culture and Sports (BTVE-DECS) and the Apprenticeship program of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE), was an offshoot of the trifocalization of education recommended by the 1991 Congresssional Education Commission or EDCOM. By virtue of Republic Act No. 7796 (TESDA Act of 1994), the TESDA is mandated to ensure the delivery of relevant, accessible, high quality and efficient technical education and skills development and to develop high quality middle-level manpower responsive to the country’s development goals and priorities. However, after more than two decades of delivering relevant, accessible, and efficient technical education and skills development thoughout ther country, TESDA has been encountering many challenges and limitations that affect the performance of its functions, delivery of technical-vocational education and training (TVET) programs, and fulfillment of its vision. One of these is the need to sstrengthen its organizational structure and functions to keep pace with the advent of technology and the demands of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR). The frequent transfer of the TESDA from one office to another has also affected its functions, programs and projects, and delivery of educational services. From an attached agency of the Department of Labor and Employment, TESDA was transferred to the Office of the President and now, to the Department of Trade and Industry through executive order signed by President Duterte. Moreover, under the TESDA Charter, the TESDA Director-General shall enjoy the benefits, privileges ad emoluments equivalent to the rank of Undersecretary. However, the current and past two Presidents of the Philippines appointed the TESDA Director General with a Cabinet rank position or equivalent to a Secretary. By elevating the TESDA into a department, it shall be headed by a Secretary, four (4) Undersecretaries and four (4) Assistant Secretaries and attain self-determination to ensure permanence and continuity of mandated programs. This will also strengthen the implementing, regulatory, and policy-making functions of the agency, as well as make it more responsive and agile in the era of the 4IR and digital economy. The proposed Department of Technical Education and Skills Development (DTESD) will not only improve the resource/budget allocation for TVET programs, but will also ably represent the TVET sector as a whole, changing its “second class” perception. More importantly, the proposed DTESD will have a better capacity to fulfill its vision as the transformational leader in TVET in the country. The immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF TECHNICAL EDUCATION, TRAINING AND CERTIFICATION, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7796, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “TESDA ACT OF 1994”, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, with its growing economy, faces a significant challenge in bridging the skills gap in its workforce. Technical-vocational education and training (TVET) play a crucial role in developing a skilled labor force capable of meeting the demands of modern industries. However, the country has long faced inefficiencies in the management and delivery of TVET programs. These challenges stem from fragmented governance, outdated curricula, underfunding, and mismatched industry needs, among others. The Philippine technical education system is divided among various government agencies, which results in inconsistent policies, misallocation of resources, and lack of coordination. TESDA oversees skills development, while DepEd handles secondary-level vocational programs. Higher education institutions (HEIs) also offer technical courses under the Commission on Higher Education (CHED). This fragmented structure complicates the implementation of nationwide reforms and makes it difficult to monitor and evaluate the quality of training programs. Likewise, the skills taught in many TVET programs do not always meet the evolving demands of industries. While TESDA has attempted to bridge this gap, there is still a lag in updating curricula and aligning programs with technological advancements and market needs. Many TVET institutions lack modern equipment, and instructors often receive inadequate training. These deficiencies hinder the development of a skilled workforce capable of competing in global markets. There are geographic and socioeconomic barriers that limit access to quality technical education. Many regions, particularly in rural areas, lack sufficient training centers and resources to support the growing demand for skilled workers. The establishment of a Department of Technical Education and Training (DTET) will centralize the management of technical education and training across various levels. This new department will be tasked with the integration of TVET programs under one cohesive strategy, improving coordination among government agencies, educational institutions, and industries. The DTET will streamline decision-making processes, ensuring that policies and programs are coordinated and aligned with national economic priorities. This unified governance will help resolve issues of duplication and inefficiency, leading to a more coherent and effective TVET system. The DTET will be empowered to work closely with industries and employers to identify current and future skill requirements. By fostering partnerships with private sector organizations, the DTET can ensure that TVET curricula are continuously updated to meet the demands of emerging industries such as digital technologies, renewable energy, and healthcare. Studies, such as those by the Asian Development Bank (ADB), have stressed the need for curricula reforms that align education with labor market needs to reduce the skills mismatch. The creation of a dedicated department will allow for better prioritization and allocation of resources toward upgrading infrastructure, purchasing modern equipment, and improving the professional development of trainers and instructors. This will ensure that TVET institutions are equipped to deliver high-quality education. Additionally, the DTET can advocate for more sustainable and long-term funding for technical education programs, ensuring their continuity and expansion. With a single department overseeing all aspects of TVET, the DTET will be able to implement nationwide strategies to expand access to training, especially in underserved regions. Through initiatives like mobile training units, partnerships with local government units (LGUs), and the expansion of online and blended learning, the DTET can ensure that technical education opportunities are available to all Filipinos, regardless of their geographic or socioeconomic background. The creation of the Department of Technical Education and Training in the Philippines is a vital step toward improving the country’s technical education system. By centralizing governance, aligning curricula with industry needs, improving resource allocation, and expanding access, the DTET will help produce a highly skilled and employable workforce capable of driving economic growth and meeting the demands of an evolving labor market. Through this proposed legislation, the Philippines can build a robust technical education system that supports both individual and national development. In view of the foregoing, immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. DALE B. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF TECHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS DEVELOPMENT, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7796, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE TESDA ACT OF 1994 AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In an increasingly competitive and rapidly evolving global economy, the country must ensure that its workforce possesses relevant, high-quality, and industry-responsive skills. While existing systems under the Republic Act No. 7796 created the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA), there is a growing need to elevate and strengthen this mandate into a full-fledged department to better address persistent issues such as job mismatch, unemployment, underemployment, and unequal access to skills training. Thus, this bill measure seeks to establish the Department of Technical Education and Skills Development (DTESD) as the primary government body responsible for the formulation, coordination, implementation, and regulation of policies and programs on technical education and skills development (TESD) in the Philippines. 1 The DTESD will be mandated to formulate a National Technical Education and Skills Development Plan (NTESDP) to guide the country’s manpower development strategy and ensure alignment with national development goals. Further, it will prioritize access to technical education for marginalized and disadvantaged sectors, including beneficiaries of the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps) under Republic Act No. 11310, to support poverty reduction and inclusive growth. By transforming TESDA into a full department, we can expect improvement in the quality and global competitiveness of Filipino workers, reduction in job-skills mismatch, expansion of employment and livelihood opportunities, strengthening of industry participation in workforce development and enhancement of social mobility. Finally, we recognize Rep. Mark O. Go of the Lone District of Baguio for filing a similar bill in the Nineteenth Congresses. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE DEPARTMENT OF CULTURE, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The culture and the arts are not just mere forms of expression and entertainment, more importantly, they are essential tools for nation-building. Arts and Culture are integral to a nation’s struggle for national identity as they can evoke dialogue, induce reflection, and charter new relationships and ideas—all of which are essential to a healthy society. This is exemplified through the works of renowned Filipino artists during the Spanish and American Colonial Period, which have helped shape a sense of national identity among Filipinos. It is the policy of the State under Section 17, Article II of the Constitution to give priority to arts and culture so as to “foster patriotism nationalism, accelerate social progress, and promote total human liberation and development.” However, with the transfer of the administration of cultural agencies to the National Commission on Culture Arts from the then Department of Education, Culture and Sports, effective promotion of the culture and arts took the sidelines due to the limited powers and resources of the NCCA and attached agencies. To this end, this proposed measure seeks to reorganize the National Commission on Culture and Arts into an independent Department of Culture or Kagawaran ng Kultura which shall be the primary policy- formulating, planning, coordinating, implementing, and administrative entity of the executive branch of the National Government that will develop, manage and implement the pertinent provisions of the Constitution regarding culture and arts. With more powers and better resources, the creation of the Department of Culture would be better equipped for the enormous task of preservation of the Filipino heritage and the promotion and advancement of cultural education among Filipinos. On behalf of the people of Parañaque City’s Second District, and for the common good of the Filipino people, the approval of the said measure is earnestly sought. REP. GUSTAVO S. At its core, the concepts of "pakikipagkapzm tao/' the celebration of life, and oneness with nature have shaped our way of life for centuries. label: SB 817
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE DEPARTMENT OF CULTURE, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Culture is a key driver of inclusive development, soft power, innovation, and national identity. Deeply rooted in history and tradition, it shapes who we are as a people and unites Filipinos across regions and generations. The 1987 Constitution affirms this by mandating the State to prioritize arts and culture to foster patriotism and nationalism, accelerate social progress, and promote total human liberation and development. Culture empowers local and Indigenous communities, fosters participation and solidarity, and contributes to human development, community cohesion, and socio­ economic transformation. It also offers sustainable pathways for development through the conservation of heritage structures, the promotion of cultural tourism, and the revitalization of local economies. Yet despite this vast potential, the Philippines has yet to establish a dedicated Department of Culture, unlike many of its neighbors in Southeast and East Asia. This institutional gap has led to fragmented policy direction, chronic underinvestment, and missed opportunities to fully harness our rich cultural assets. While the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) serves as the primary coordinating and policy-making body, it is not a line agency and lacks direct authority over many of the cultural institutions responsible for implementation. As a result, the cultural sector remains underprioritized in national development planning and falls short of its potential as a strategic pillar of growth and national unity. According to UNESCO, cultural and creative industries generate nearly US$2.3 trillion in annual global revenues, equivalent to 3.1 percent of the world's gross domestic product (GDP). Their contribution to national value added varies among G20 economies, ranging from 0.7 percent in Mexico to 3 percent in the United States. These industries also provide employment for approximately 6.2 percent of the global workforce.1 In the Asia-Pacific region, countries like Japan and South Korea have successfully institutionalized cultural governance, generating massive returns. In 2023, Japan's anime industry (including television and film productions, streaming distribution, merchandising, music, events, and overseas licensing), supported by Agency for Cultural Affairs (Bunkachd) under the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT), reached an all-time high of ¥3.3465 trillion (approximately US$22.3 billion). Of the total revenue, ¥1.6243 trillion (around US$10.8 billion) came from domestic sources, while ¥1.7222 trillion (about US$11.5 billion) was generated from international markets.2 South Korea's cultural content industry (Korean Wave or Hallyu), supported by its Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, has steadily grown into a high value-added sector marked by robust domestic sales and expanding exports. South Korea's cultural content industry grew steadily from 2021 to 2023, with total sales rising from W137.5 trillion (US$105.8 billion)3 to W154.2 trillion (US$110.5 billion),4 and exports increasing from US$12.45 billion to US$13.3 billion during the same period. 1 UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD). Retrieved July 31,2025, from https://japantoday.com/category/features/lifestyle/anime-industry-report-shows-overseas-anime- market-is-bigger-than-japanese-one-but-is-this-a-cultural-tipping-point-2 3 Invest KOREA, (n.d.). Cultural Content Invest KOREA. Retrieved August 1,2025, from https://www.investkorea.org/ik-en/cntnts/i-326/web.do 4 Son, J.-h. (2025, April 18). Policy Watch: Lee Jae-myung to double Korean culture industry revenue, exports in 7 years. The Korea Herald. Retrieved August 1,2025, from https://www.koreaherald.com/article/10468573 In contrast, the Philippines' creative economy reached PhPl.94 trillion (USD 34,64 billion) in 2024. This marked an 8.7 percent increase from the PhPl.78 trillion (USD 31.95 billion) recorded in 2023, reflecting continued expansion across key creative sectors such as digital media, advertising, symbolic content, and traditional cultural expressions,5 These data points underscore a vital truth: countries that invest in strong cultural governance and infrastructure reap significant returns, not only in terms of economic growth, employment, and exports, but also in global influence, innovation, and national unity. In contrast, the Philippines continues to operate without a dedicated Department of Culture, limiting its ability to fully harness the value of its diverse cultural assets. With the Philippines'creative economy already contributing 7.3 percent to Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and growing, the absence of a dedicated department risks leaving our rich cultural capital under-leveraged and fragmented. This bill seeks to address that institutional gap. By establishing the Department of Culture, it provides the policy leadership, operational mandate, and organizational structure necessary to protect, develop, and promote Philippine culture, both as a heritage to be preserved and as a resource to be activated for inclusive growth. Among its key features are the following: 1. Centralized cultural governance through the integration of policy, regulatory, and programmatic functions currently dispersed across multiple agencies; 2. Nationwide and international reach via regional offices and Sentro /?/za/centers to bring cultural development closer to communities and diaspora networks; 3. Capacity-building and education through national institutes dedicated to living traditions, heritage

label: HB 11339
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A MAGINHAWANG BUHAY SUPPORT FRAMEWORK FOR LOW- INCOME AND MIDDLE-CLASS HOUSEHOLDS, PROVIDING A TWENTY PERCENT (20%) DISCOUNT ON ESSENTIAL NEEDS INCLUDING BASIC UTILITIES, HEALTHCARE, EDUCATION, AND HOUSING, ESTABLISHING AN INFLATION-RESPONSIVE AND INTEGRATED DELIVERY MECHANISM, PROVIDING FOR BENEFIT CEILINGS, TARGETING, FISCAL SAFEGUARDS, INTER-AGENCY COORDINATION, TRANSPARENCY, ACCOUNTABILITY, AND CONGRESSIONAL OVERSIGHT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In every economy, there is a quiet line that separates stability from vulnerability. It is the line where income, though earned honestly and steadily, is no longer enough to keep pace with the cost of living. For millions of Filipino families, particularly those in the low-income and middle-class sectors, that line has been crossed not because of idleness or failure, but because prices have risen faster than wages, and essential needs have become increasingly unaffordable. Electricity, water, healthcare, education, and housing are not discretionary expenses. They are the fixed costs of dignity. When these become too expensive, households are forced into painful trade-offs—between food and medicine, tuition and rent, work and care. Over time, these trade-offs accumulate into deeper inequality, poorer health outcomes, educational attrition, and economic fragility. This proposed measure seeks to correct that imbalance by institutionalizing a Maginhawang Buhay Support Framework, grounded on the principle that every Filipino household is entitled to a basic social floor of economic security, regardless of income level, so long as they remain within the broad low-income and middle- class spectrum. In this sense, the measure draws from a universal income perspective—not by distributing cash, but by protecting real income at the point where it matters most: the price of essentials. Persistent inflation in recent years has eroded household purchasing power, disproportionately affecting families whose incomes are fixed or slow-moving. While emergency subsidies and conditional assistance programs have provided temporary relief, these measures are often reactive, fragmented, and dependent on discretionary political action. Moreover, existing social protection mechanisms are largely targeted at the poorest households, leaving a growing segment of the middle class exposed—too “rich” to qualify for aid, yet too financially constrained to absorb rising costs. This condition has created a silent crisis. Middle-income households increasingly rely on debt, reduce preventive healthcare, delay education, or accept substandard housing conditions. The long-term cost of these decisions is borne not only by families, but by the State itself, through higher healthcare expenditures, lower educational attainment, reduced productivity, and social instability. 2 There is therefore a clear need for a permanent, automatic, and inflation- responsive mechanism that stabilizes household welfare before economic stress turns into economic damage. This bill establishes a Maginhawang Buhay Support Framework that grants qualified low-income and middle-class households a twenty percent (20%) discount on essential needs, specifically basic utilities, healthcare, education, and housing expenses. The discount is designed as a baseline social protection measure that operates continuously, rather than episodically. The measure is carefully integrated with existing lifeline rates, PhilHealth benefits, free tuition and scholarship programs, and housing subsidies, ensuring that it supplements rather than replaces current entitlements. It introduces a national beneficiary registry, anchored on official statistics and interoperable government databases, to ensure accurate targeting, transparency, and protection against leakage. Recognizing the cyclical nature of inflation, the bill further provides for an automatic, time-bound expansion of benefits when inflation breaches defined thresholds, thereby avoiding the delays and uncertainty of ad hoc emergency legislation. To ensure fiscal sustainability, the measure adopts a cost-sharing mechanism with the private sector, requiring covered service providers to grant discounts upfront, while allowing reimbursement solely through tax credits and incentives, subject to fiscal ceilings, audit, and verification. No direct cash reimbursement is allowed, and no new or special appropriation is mandated. 3 Oversight is institutionalized through an inter-agency council attached to the Office of the President, supported by a permanent secretariat, and complemented by congressional oversight and sunset review provisions. The immediate impact of this measure is the protection of real household income. By reducing the price of essentials, the bill functions as a form of universal income stabilization, ensuring that earned income retains its purchasing power even during inflationary periods. Unlike cash transfers, which may be inflationary, this approach directly lowers effective prices and moderates second- round inflation effects. Economically, the measure is expected to stabilize consumption, particularly among low- and middle-income households with high marginal propensity to spend. This sustains local demand, supports small and medium enterprises, and mitigates economic contraction during periods of price volatility. Socially, the bill reduces the risk of preventable health crises, educational dropouts, housing insecurity, and debt accumulation. Over time, these effects translate into lower public health costs, higher educational completion rates, a more resilient workforce, and a broader tax base. From a governance perspective, the measure shifts social protection from discretion to design—from reactive relief to automatic response—thereby strengthening public trust and policy credibility. At its core, this measure affirms a simple but powerful idea: income is only meaningful if it can meet the cost of living. By institutionalizing a Maginhawang Buhay Support Framework, the State acknowledges that protecting dignity in times of economic stress is not charity, but responsibility. 4 This bill does not promise abundance. It promises stability. And in an economy shaped by uncertainty, stability is the foundation upon which opportunity, growth, and shared prosperity are built. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE

label: HB 11340
title: AN ACT PRESERVING AND PROMOTING THE INDIGENOUS GAMES OF THE PHILIPPINES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Culture shapes values. In this digital era, Filipino children spend most of their time with game consoles or mobile gadgets either at home or in internet cafés, in contrast with the children of the past who spent their leisure time interacting with other children and playing traditional street games. These games include patintero, tumbang preso, siato, and taguan, to name a few. These indigenous games have shaped generations of Filipinos and have imparted values of teamwork, resilience, and sportsmanship. They have been part of our childhood and our cultural heritage. This proposed measure seeks to preserve indigenous games to ensure that future generations of Filipinos can still enjoy them. This bill has been approved on third and final reading in the House of Representatives for three consecutive Congresses (17th, 18th, and 19th) but failed to be passed into law due to time constraints. We seek to revive efforts to make this worthwhile advocacy a law. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. title: AN ACT REQUIRING LAND, AIR, AND SEA TRANSPORT PROVIDERS TO PROVIDE PRIORITY SEATING FOR THE ELDERLY, FURTHER AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7432, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9257 AND 9994, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “EXPANDED SENIOR CITIZEN’S ACT OF 2010”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It is the duty of the State to ensure that public utilities and transportation services are accessible to all people, especially those in vulnerable groups such as senior citizens and persons with disabilities. In furtherance of this mandate, Batas Pambansa Bilang 344, or the Accessibility Law, and Republic Act No. 9994, or the Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010, were enacted to improve access to public transportation for persons with disabilities and senior citizens. Under these laws, public transport providers are required to designate seats for persons with disabilities, and the Department of Transportation is directed “to develop a program to assist senior citizens to fully gain access to public transport facilities.” Administrative issuances, including Department of Transportation Department Order No. 2014-013, likewise provide for reserved or priority seating for persons with disabilities, senior citizens, and pregnant women in certain public transportation facilities. However, existing law and regulations do not establish a comprehensive statutory requirement expressly prescribing priority seating for senior citizens across all modes of public transportation— land, rail, air, and sea—along with uniform standards on seat designation, labeling, reservation, enforcement, and penalties. As a result, senior citizens continue to experience difficulties in accessing priority seats. They often find themselves standing in cramped, moving vehicles while non-eligible passengers occupy seats that should be available to them. The lack of clear statutory rules and consistent enforcement undermines the intent of existing accessibility and senior-citizen laws. In recognition of the invaluable contributions of senior citizens to nation-building, it is only right and just to provide them with additional privileges, particularly in public transportation. By ensuring priority seating for the elderly, this measure promotes their mobility and access, enabling them to continue participating actively in the life of their communities. This bill seeks to strengthen the Expanded Senior Citizens Act by expressly requiring priority seating for senior citizens in land, air, and sea transport, including rail services. It further provides for appropriate penalties for public transport operators who fail to comply with this requirement. It is the hope of this measure to mainstream mobility and access for senior citizens in public transportation, so that we may continue to support them in their daily lives and in their ongoing efforts to contribute to nation-building. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11342
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE DISPLAY OF NUTRITIONAL INFORMATION ON THE MENU OF FOOD ESTABLISHMENTS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Good nutrition has been attributed to healthier food choices and, generally, a healthier diet. The presence of nutritional information on the food labels helps people maintain their healthy diet and nutrition because of informed choices. This, in turn, helps prevent the rise of various diseases attributed to an unhealthy diet. The World Health Organization indicates that 80 percent of premature heart disease, stroke, and Type II Diabetes and 40 percent of cancers can be prevented through a healthy diet. Thus, consumers have now become more discerning in their choice of food, always checking the nutritional information and calorie count on food labels. Filipinos, however, are not as informed when dining in restaurants. They are often unaware of the calorie and nutritional content of a meal, leading them or misleading them into an unhealthy eating pattern. This bill aims to mandate the disclosure and display of the nutrition content information on each standard menu in all types of restaurants, including fast food chains, in order to enable and empower consumers with the right to choose the food they want to eat without compromising their health. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11343
title: AN ACT ALLOWING AND REGULATING THE USE OF MOTORCYCLES AS PUBLIC UTILITY VEHICLES, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 4136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LAND TRANSPORTATION AND TRAFFIC CODE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State provides that it shall protect and promote the rights and obligations of commuters, drivers, and operators through an efficient and fair transport system for the commuting public. As such, Republic Act 4136, otherwise known as the “Land Transportation and Traffic Code,” was enacted, providing for the control, registration, and operation of motor vehicles and the licensing of owners, dealers, conductors, drivers, and similar matters. While the law covers relevant provisions for privately owned and for-hire motor vehicles, the law lacks coverage for motorcycles-for-hire which have become a growing mode of public transportation in recent years. In 2022, there were at least 682,000 registered motorcycles and tricycles for hire in the country. For many commuters, these motorcycle taxis are sometimes the better option of transportation because of their accessibility, efficiency, and reliability. The growing demand for motorcycles as public utility vehicles also led to the operation of non-registered motorcycles-for-hire, which in turn have posed risks for many commuters since riders do not necessarily have the proper training or insurance coverage to protect themselves and even their passengers. The proposed amendments to RA 4136 shall ensure that the law includes motorcycles-for-hire among the defined public transportation, and as such guarantee their roadworthiness while assuring the safety of the riding public. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of the bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11344
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A BILL OF RIGHTS FOR AIR PASSENGERS, PENALIZING VIOLATIONS THEREOF, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State has established that it shall protect the interest of all consumers, promote their general welfare, and establish standards of conduct for business and industry. With the vital role of the air transport industry in fostering inclusive economic growth, it is imperative to guarantee that the air transport sector operates effectively. The industry is experiencing phenomenal growth and has not only regained but, in some indicators, surpassed its pre-pandemic levels, as shown by the sustained rise in business and leisure travel since mobility limitations were relaxed. According to the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP), total passenger movements reached about 27.3 million in 2023, 25.2 million in 2024, and 24.5 million in 2025, reflecting robust recovery in domestic and international air travel.1 As the industry offers services to travelers from all socioeconomic backgrounds, issues looming in air travel have continuously affected many air passengers, including but not limited to flight delays, airline overbooking, baggage loss, the disappearance of bookings, and trouble with refunds, among many others. These concerns persist despite the existence of the DOTC-DTI Joint Administrative Order No. 1, series of 2012 (the Air Passenger Bill of Rights), which was further updated by the Civil Aeronautics Board through Economic Regulation No. 9 in January 2024 to strengthen carrier obligations and passenger entitlements for delays, cancellations, denied boarding, and baggage issues.2 1 Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP), “Aircraft, Passenger, and Cargo Movements” annual reports: 27,305,261 passenger movements in 2023; 25,194,580 in 2024; 24,450,723 in 2025, https://www.caap.gov.ph/aircraft-passenger-and-cargo-movements/; 2 DOTC-DTI Joint Administrative Order No. 1, series of 2012 (Air Passenger Bill of Rights), issued December 10, 2012; Civil Aeronautics Board, Economic Regulation No. 9 (updated Air Passenger Bill of Rights), effective January This proposed measure aims to focus on the right of air passengers to receive the full value of the service they have purchased and the convenience it offers. Consequently, it protects air passengers, especially during events when their flights are canceled or delayed, and their baggage is lost or damaged, to name a few. It establishes a mechanism to address the grievances of affected air passengers and maintains their right to full and truthful information regarding the contract of carriage. This bill institutionalizes and updates the Joint DOTC-DTI Administrative Order No. 1 issued on 10 December 2012, incorporating developments such as the CAB’s 2024 amendments, with the intent of ensuring the rights of air passengers in the country and promoting efficient air transport service. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11345
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE BILL OF RIGHTS OF COMMUTERS, PROMOTING EFFICIENT, SAFE, CONVENIENT, ACCESSIBLE AND INCLUSIVE PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Greater Manila Area is home to millions of commuters daily who need to move from their homes to their workplaces or schools by taking buses, jeepneys, taxis, trains, tricycles, and pedicabs. With the existing road-based public transport system, a regular commuter in Metro Manila will have spent about 15 to 59 minutes 1 on a regular day or worse, 3 hours for a 13-kilometer distance2 , and will have transferred from at least two modes of Public Utility vehicles before he or she gets to work. For those taking trains or buses, an additional of at least 30 to 40 minutes on average will be allotted for waiting time alone. A study on commuting in Metro Manila finds that Filipinos spend about 16 days a year stuck in traffic, costing them about 100,000 Philippine pesos ($2,000) a year in lost income 3 or an estimated economic loss of 4.6% of the GDP4. With the evident economic losses and the commuter’s daily ordeal, it is the State’s obligation to remedy the public’s outcry for better, efficient, and dignified transport system. 1 “Duration of daily Commute in the Philippines as of June 2022” https://www.statista.com/forecasts/1274764/philippines- duration-of-daily-commute Accessed on September 20, 2022 2 Metro Manila Development Authority 2019 3 Ana P. Santos, 2019. “Carmageddon: The indignity of commuting in Metro Manila” https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2019/10/24/carmageddon-the-indignity-of-commuting-in-metro-manila Accessed on September 21, 2022 4 Asian Development Bank, 2012 “ Transport Sector Assessment, Strategy and Roadmap” https://www.adb.org/sites/default/files/institutional-document/33700/files/philippines-transport-assessment.pdf Accessed on September 21, 2022 This bill seeks to promulgate and implement policies and programs that will ensure the welfare and dignity of the commuting public, address challenges of mobility amidst rapid urbanization, promote road safety, reduce road congestion and air pollution, mitigate transport-related health hazards, and improve access to services and markets, thereby fostering social equity, economic development, and ecological balance. When the system for mass transportation is efficient and effective, fewer people will take private cars, leading to less cost, less pollution, and a more dignified overall commute experience. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11346
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A MAGNA CARTA OF TRICYCLE DRIVERS AND OPERATORS, INSTITUTIONALIZING MECHANISMS FOR ITS IMPLEMENTATION AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Tricycles are considered the “vehicle of the masses”. It is often the transportation option of many low-income households to reach major thoroughfares, and a significant income source of many Filipinos displaced in the formal working sector due to a lack of employable skills. Oftentimes, driving a tricycle will be the only mode of livelihood until retirement. According to the 2023 Annual Report of the Land Transportation Office, there are more than 7 million registered private motorcycles and tricycles in the country. It is high time that we give value to our tricycles in the country. It is high time that we give value to our tricycle drivers and operators for their contribution to the daily life of the ordinary Filipinos and to economic development. This measure ensures the welfare of the tricycle drivers and operators for a more organized sector by defining the requirements for proper operation of tricycles and simplifying the registration system imposed in the application and issuance of motorized tricycle operator permit (MTOP). It also mandates the establishment of a one-stop shop in every local government unit to cater to all the transactions of tricycle drivers and operators. It advances the welfare of the tricycle sector by mandating the Social Security System and the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation to assure their provision of health care and social benefits. The measure outlines the significant role of the Local Government Units and other government agencies in supporting the sector. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11347
title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE PREVENTION OF ADOLESCENT PREGNANCY, STRENGTHENING THE FAMILY AND COMMUNITY SUPPORT FOR ADOLESCENTS, AND PROVIDING FOR A NATIONAL ADOLESCENT PREGNANCY PREVENTION AND EDUCATION PROGRAM
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Adolescent pregnancy remains a significant public health, education, and social protection concern in the Philippines. While recent data show encouraging improvements1, the persistence of pregnancies among adolescents, particularly among younger girls and those from disadvantaged households, demonstrates the need for a comprehensive and sustained national response. The figures reveal that teenage pregnancy is closely linked to socioeconomic disadvantage. The PSA's 2022 National Demographic and Health Survey reported that 10.3 percent of women aged 15 to 19 in the poorest wealth quintile had experienced pregnancy, compared with only 1.8 percent among those in the wealthiest quintile.2 These disparities demonstrate that adolescent pregnancy cannot be addressed solely as a matter of individual choice. It is also a question of unequal access to information, health services, education, protection, and opportunities. Of even greater concern are pregnancies involving very young adolescents. PSA data showed that registered births to mothers aged 10 to 14 increased from 1,903 in 2016 to 2,113 in 2020, an increase of 11 percent. During this period, an average of five to seven births each day were registered to mothers aged 10 to 14.3 Pregnancies at such young ages require particular attention from the State because they may be associated with abuse, exploitation, coercion, or other circumstances that compromise a child's safety and rights. 1 Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), 2025 National Demographic and Health Survey: Teenage Pregnancy. The 2025 NDHS reports that 4.9 percent of women aged 15–19 had ever been pregnant, compared with 5.4 percent in 2022. 2 Philippine Statistics Authority, 2022 National Demographic and Health Survey: Teenage Pregnancy. The PSA defines teenage pregnancy as the percentage of women aged 15–19 who have ever been pregnant. The survey reported a prevalence of 10.3 percent among women in the lowest wealth quintile and 1.8 percent among those in the highest wealth quintile. 3 Philippine Statistics Authority, Adolescent Pregnancy in the Philippines: 2016–2020, PSA Reference No. 2022-477, 8 December 2022. The report states that registered births to mothers aged 10–14 increased from 1,903 in 2016 to 2,113 in 2020, equivalent to an 11.0 percent increase. Page 1 The consequences of adolescent pregnancy can extend beyond pregnancy and childbirth. A young mother may face difficulty continuing her education, increased economic vulnerability, diminished employment opportunities, and greater dependence on her family or social protection programs. These consequences can, in turn, reinforce an intergenerational cycle of poverty. The response of government must never be to stigmatize adolescent parents. A young person who becomes pregnant remains entitled to education, health care, protection, and opportunities to build a productive and dignified life. Prevention and support must therefore go hand in hand. The proposed Adolescent Pregnancy Prevention Act seeks to adopt a prevention-centered, family-supported, values-based, and age- and development- appropriate approach to adolescent pregnancy. It recognizes that no single government agency, program, or intervention can adequately address the problem. The measure therefore establishes the Adolescent Pregnancy Prevention Inter-Agency Council which shall serve as the policy-making body responsible for the development of a national framework that shall be called the National Adolescent Pregnancy Prevention and Education Program. The measure shall strengthen, at the community level age, culturally-sensitive and responsive, and age- and development-appropriate education on responsible decision-making, healthy relationships, self-respect, self-discipline, personal boundaries, and the consequences of early and unplanned pregnancy and childbearing for all adolescents through the development and delivery of the Adolescent Pregnancy and Reproductive Health Education. The measure further recognizes the importance of parents, families, schools, communities, and local governments. Government programs will have limited impact if young people lack supportive environments in which they can ask questions, obtain reliable information, seek help, and make responsible decisions without fear of stigma. The bill therefore promotes stronger family and community engagement and clearer coordination among service providers. Education continuity shall be an important component of the national strategy through School-Based Programs to be implemented by the Department of Education which includes interventions such as educational, career, and life-planning support, and continuing educational support and reintegration of adolescent parents. The proposed Act shall likewise strengthen mechanisms for the early identification and referral of adolescents who may be at heightened risk of pregnancy, school disengagement, abuse, exploitation, or other forms of vulnerability. Particular attention shall be given to children and adolescents in communities with persistently high rates of adolescent pregnancy or other identified risk factors. label: HB 11350
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Sierra Madre Mountain Range is one of the Philippines’ most important natural ecosystems and a vital environmental and disaster-resilience asset. Stretching across eastern Luzon, it serves as a natural barrier that helps lessen the impacts of typhoons, heavy rainfall, flooding, landslides, and other natural calamities. In line with this, this measure seeks to strengthen the protection, conservation, restoration, and sustainable management of the Sierra Madre Mountain Range by establishing a dedicated Sierra Madre Mountain Range Authority and providing a comprehensive framework for its long-term management. Among its salient features are: (1) the creation of a dedicated authority to coordinate conservation, enforcement, restoration, climate adaptation, and disaster- risk reduction efforts; (2) the formulation of a 25-year Sierra Madre Master Plan integrating biodiversity conservation, watershed management, climate resilience, disaster risk reduction, sustainable livelihoods, land-use planning, and the rights and traditional knowledge of Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples; and (3) the establishment of landscape zoning, ecological corridors, restoration measures, and stronger enforcement against activities that degrade the mountain range. The measure is firmly anchored in Article II, Section 16 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution which declares the State’s duty to protect and advance the people’s right to a balanced and healthful ecology. It also advances the State’s responsibility to protect the nation’s natural resources for present and future generations. By treating the Sierra Madre as a critical natural foundation for disaster risk reduction, climate resilience, and public safety, the bill gives concrete effect to the constitutional mandate of environmental protection. The protection of the Sierra Madre is therefore not merely an environmental concern. It is a matter of public safety, national resilience, food and water security, and national survival. The mountain range functions as one of Luzon’s principal natural defenses against typhoons and extreme weather, while healthy forests and watersheds help reduce flooding and landslide risks. The bill accordingly recognizes the Sierra Madre as a critical natural foundation for national security, disaster risk reduction, and climate resilience, and directs government agencies to integrate ecosystem-based approaches into disaster and national security planning. label: HB 11352
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR FAIR TREATMENT OF CERTAIN SENIOR CITIZEN PENSIONERS BY GRANTING ANNUAL CHRISTMAS CASH GIFT, THIRTEENTH-MONTH PENSION, AND PENSION INCREASES TO PENSIONERS OF THE SOCIAL SECURITY SYSTEM AND GOVERNMENT SERVICE INSURANCE SYSTEM WHO ARE BENEFICIARIES OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7699, “AN ACT INSTITUTING LIMITED PORTABILITY SCHEME IN THE SOCIAL SECURITY INSURANCE SYSTEMS BY TOTALIZING THE WORKERS’ CREDITABLE SERVICES OR CONTRIBUTIONS IN EACH OF THE SYSTEMS”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 7699, otherwise known as the “Limited Portability Law,” allows workers who have rendered service or made contributions under both the Social Security System (SSS) and the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) to totalize their creditable periods for purposes of qualifying for benefits. This recognizes the contributions and years of service of workers who have moved between the private and public sectors. Despite this recognition, pensioners who qualify under the portability scheme have not always received benefits on the same basis as similarly situated old-age pensioners of the respective systems, particularly with respect to supplemental pension benefits and pension increases. This measure seeks to ensure fair and equal treatment by granting qualified pensioners under Republic Act No. 7699 the same annual Christmas cash gift, thirteenth-month pension, and pension increases granted to similarly situated pensioners of the SSS and GSIS. A pensioner receiving pensions from both systems shall be entitled to the applicable benefits from both systems, based on the pension payable by each. The measure further seeks to protect existing benefits and ensure that the implementation of the law shall not result in the diminution or reduction of benefits already enjoyed by portability pensioners. The passage of this measure will uphold the principle that workers who have contributed to both social insurance systems should not be placed at a disadvantage merely because their pension entitlement was established through the portability scheme. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11353
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING AUTISM CENTERS AND EARLY DETECTION PROGRAMS NATIONWIDE, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) affects many Filipino individuals and families who continue to face significant challenges in accessing timely developmental screening, diagnosis, intervention, therapy, healthcare, education, and community support services. These challenges are compounded by the limited availability of specialized facilities and trained professionals, financial barriers, and unequal access to developmental services, particularly in underserved and geographically disadvantaged areas. This proposed measure seeks to establish a nationwide network of accessible and affordable Autism Centers that will serve as regional hubs for developmental screening, diagnostic assessment, intervention, rehabilitation, family support, educational coordination, and referral services. It likewise seeks to strengthen early detection and intervention by integrating developmental screening into existing health and community-based programs and by training frontline healthcare, education, and community personnel to recognize developmental concerns and facilitate timely referrals. The measure further promotes inclusive education and community support, strengthens the capacity of healthcare professionals, therapists, educators, and other service providers, and encourages research and data-driven policymaking to improve the availability, quality, accessibility, and affordability of autism-related services. Recognizing that timely and continuous support is essential to improving outcomes, the bill provides for coordinated referral mechanisms among Autism Centers and relevant healthcare, education, social welfare, skills training, and employment institutions. It also encourages the expansion of appropriate health coverage and financial assistance for indigent and financially vulnerable families. Consistent with Republic Act No. 7277, otherwise known as the “Magna Carta for Persons with Disability,” as amended, Republic Act No. 11036, otherwise known as the “Mental Health Act,” Republic Act No. 11223, otherwise known as the “Universal Health Care Act,” Republic Act No. 11650, otherwise known as the “Instituting a Policy of Inclusion and Services for Learners with Disabilities in Support of Inclusive Education Act,” and other relevant laws, this measure adopts a rights-based, inclusive, family-centered, community-based, and evidence-informed approach to autism care and support. By establishing accessible Autism Centers and strengthening early detection, referral, intervention, and support systems nationwide, this measure seeks to reduce disparities in access to services and enable persons with ASD and their families to receive timely, appropriate, and continuing support regardless of their place of residence or economic circumstances. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L.
