label: HB 11452
title: AN ACT EXPANDING FRONTLINE SERVICE HOURS INCLUDING WEEKEND COVERAGE FOR VOICE AND NON-VOICE INQUIRIES AND IN-PERSON TRANSACTIONS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In the Philippines, both private employees and government offices essentially follow the same weekday work schedule. This presents a fundamental difficulty for working Filipinos who must process official transactions during business hours such as license applications, loan and benefits facilitation, or payment of taxes and fees. They are often left with an impossible choice: postpone essential transactions, use their vacation leaves or absent themselves from work at the cost of their daily wage. This burden falls heaviest upon our daily wage earners and frontline workers. Through the years, technology has been integrated into government services to assist citizens who cannot personally visit government offices. Various agencies such as the Social Security Service (SSS), Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth), and Home Development Mutual Fund (PAG-IBIG) have adopted digital solutions, including mobile applications, chat support services, and online portals. However, these advancements remain insufficient. Certain transactions inherently demand face-to-face processing and personal review, particularly those involving frontline services that require physical presence, identity verification, or the submission of original documents. This bill seeks to institutionalize accessible government service. Frontline services shall operate on extended working hours, including Saturdays or even Sundays if deemed necessary, with 24/7 availability for digital platforms, hotline, inquiries, appointments, and document submissions. By mandating extended operating hours across all covered agencies, we ensure that Filipinos can complete essential matters including urgent and emergency transactions without sacrificing their time and wages. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JANICE V. title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A PHILIPPINE PSYCHOLOGY PROFESSIONALIZATION ACT, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10029, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “PHILIPPINE PSYCHOLOGY ACT OF 2009”, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR 26 Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 29 Section 1. Short Title. This Act shall be known as the "Philippine Psychology Professionalization Act". ARTICLE Il STATEMENT OF POLICY SEC. 2. Statement of Policy. The State recognizes that psychologists have an important role in nation-building and development. It also acknowledges the diverse specializations of psychologists and the distinct functions specific to the varied specializations, including those that do not involve the professional practice of psychology or the delivery of psychological services. It further acknowledges the need to protect the public by preventing unqualified individuals from engaging in psychological practice or offering psychological services. Hence, it shall nurture competent, upright, and diligent registered professional psychologists whose standards of practice and service shall be excellent and globally competitive through the administration of inviolable, effective, and credible licensure examinations and the imposition and promotion of regulatory measures, programs, and activities that enhance their professional growth and well-being.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 When a Filipino seeks psychological help, the person should be able to find a professional who is properly trained for the kind of help that is needed. This need becomes more pressing in light of the limited number of mental health professionals in the country. The World Health Organization's Mental Health Atlas 2024 reports only 0.3 psychologists per 100,000 population, or approximately 3 psychologists for every 1,000,000 Filipinos. 28 With so few professionals available, it becomes even more important that the psychology profession is properly structured and that available professionals are able to perform the functions for which they are trained. 32 Republic Act No. 10029, or the Philippine Psychology Act of 2009, established the regulation of psychologists and psychometricians. Now, this proposed measure seeks to update this framework by replacing the psychometrician classification with the Registered Psychology Associate, giving it a broader and clearly defined scope of practice, while reserving specialized clinical assessment and intervention for Registered Psychologists. 39 The proposed measure also recognizes that psychology professionals should have a rightful place in the institutions where their services are needed. It mandates the creation of plantilla positions for Registered Psychologists and Registered Psychology Associates in local government units, hospitals, educational institutions, and workplaces, with appropriate job descriptions, ranks, and salary grades that reflect the training, responsibilities, and value of their work. 46 A stronger psychology profession means better protection for the people who need help and better support for those who provide it. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 2 3 4 REP. JERNIE JETT V. title: AN ACT INCREASING THE COMPULSORY AGE OF RETIREMENT FOR OFFICERS AND NON-OFFICERS OF THE BUREAU OF JAIL MANAGEMENT AND PENOLOGY (BJMP) FROM FIFTY-SIX (56) YEARS OLD TO FIFTY SEVEN (57) YEARS OLD, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6975, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT OF 1990," AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP), along with the Philippine National Police and the Bureau of Fire Protection, was created through the promulgation of Republic Act No. 6975, otherwise known as the “Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) Act of 1990.” Subsequently, some provisions of the said law were amended by Republic Act No. 9263, otherwise known as the “Bureau of Fire Protection and Bureau of Jail Management and Penology Professionalization Act of 2004.” With over thirty-five (35) years and twenty-two (22) years since these laws were passed, respectively, the BJMP has grown its personnel to a total of around twenty-six thousand (26,000). This annual increase is in response to the ever-increasing need for manpower to assist in the safekeeping and rehabilitation of persons deprived of liberty. Through its relevant programs, the Jail Bureau aims to reduce decreasing recidivism and ultimately provide an orderly, safe, and peaceful society for the general public. Given this number, there is a clear need to ensure continuity of leadership in the BJMP by raising the retirement age from fifty-six (56) to fifty-seven (57) years old. While this is only a one-year adjustment, it can help retain experienced senior officers and make better use of their leadership, expertise, and institutional knowledge. It also gives them more time to guide and mentor younger officers and personnel. At fifty-six (56), many jail officers remain physically fit, mentally sharp, and fully capable of performing their duties. Allowing them to serve for one more year will help the Bureau retain capable leaders and strengthen the continuity of its operations. 1 Likewise, the proposed age adjustment brings the BJMP in line with reforms affecting other uniformed personnel. This includes the Armed Forces of the Philippines under Republic Act No. 11939, as well as pending Senate and House measures seeking a similar adjustment for the Philippine National Police. The passage of this bill would therefore promote consistency in retirement policies across uniformed services and recognize the BJMP’s continuing role in public service. Raising the retirement age by one year will also support the fiscal sustainability of the government’s pension system. Extending the service of qualified personnel allows the State to defer pension obligations while continuing to benefit from the skills and experience of trained officers. This provides a practical balance between retaining capable personnel and managing long-term public expenditures. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is respectfully and fervently sought. BRIAN RAYMUND S. label: HB 11458
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE RANK CLASSIFICATION AND ORGANIZATION OF KEY POSITIONS IN THE BUREAU OF FIRE PROTECTION (BFP) AND THE BUREAU OF JAIL MANAGEMENT AND PENOLOGY (BJMP), AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9263, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "BUREAU OF FIRE PROTECTION AND BUREAU OF JAIL MANAGEMENT AND PENOLOGY PROFESSIONALIZATION ACT OF 2004", AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9592
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 6975, otherwise known as the DILG Act of 1990, laid the foundation for a more organized public safety and peace and order system in the Philippines. Among the agencies established under the law are the Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) and the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP)---agencies which have particularly important responsibilities in highly urbanized and densely populated cities. In communities where large numbers of people live and work within limited spaces, the risk of fires, emergencies, overcrowding, and other public safety concerns is greater. Hence, the effective performance of their respective mandates directly contributes to public safety, security, and the maintenance of peace and order. Given the increasingly complex demands placed upon these agencies, there is a need to strengthen their organizational structures and professional standards. In 2018, Republic Act No. 11200 was enacted to update the rank classifications of the BFP and BJMP. These reforms were intended to establish clearer lines of authority and responsibility, improve organizational efficiency, and address ambiguities in the existing rank structure. However, organizational reforms must be complemented by measures that strengthen the qualifications and capabilities of those entrusted with leadership and supervisory responsibilities. For this reason, this proposed measure seeks to prescribe higher educational qualifications for certain positions in the BFP and BJMP. Higher educational standards are expected to enhance the capacity of personnel to manage their 1 responsibilities, exercise sound judgment, and effectively lead uniformed personnel in the performance of their duties. The proposed measure recognizes that the BFP and BJMP are essential components of the country's public safety and peace and order framework. Strengthening their leadership and professional standards is particularly important in densely populated urban areas, where the demands on these agencies are greater and where effective coordination, supervision, and decision-making can have a direct impact on the safety and welfare of the public. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is respectfully and fervently sought. BRIAN RAYMUND S. label: HB 11459
title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE INSTALLATION OF BEHIND-THE-METER ELECTRICITY GENERATION AND ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEMS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines now has the highest residential electricity rates in Southeast Asia, surpassing Singapore.1 As of June 2026, the average residential electricity rate was at an average of P12.43 per kilowatt hour.2 With volatile global conditions affecting fuel prices and supply, Filipino households may have to pay even more for electricity.3 Faced with these issues, Filipinos are turning to alternative sources of energy, particularly solar power. A Pulse Asia survey showed that 93% of Filipinos believe that affordable rooftop solar panels are necessary due to the rising demand and prices of electricity.4 There is also strong public support for policies that make renewable energy more accessible, thereby lowering consumers’ electricity expenses.5 In fact, rooftop installations of solar panels have nearly doubled in the country since early 2025.6 However, our current laws and regulatory framework has yet to fully adapt to the increasing ability of ordinary consumers to generate and store electricity for their own use. Republic Act No. 9136, or the “Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001,” was enacted at a time when electricity generation was largely undertaken by power generation companies operating large-scale facilities and selling electricity to the grid. Since then, advances in technology have made small-scale electricity generation more accessible to households and end-users. 1 Lelis, Brix. (2026). DOE: Philippines power rates now highest in SEA. Philstar. Available at https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2026/07/21/2543545/doe-philippines-power-rates-now-highest-sea. 2 Id. 3 Id. 4 Arayata, Ma. Cristina. (2026). Survey: Most Filipinos want affordable solar power. Philippine News Agency. Available at https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1278589. 5 Id. 6 High bills, cheap panels drive a Philippine solar surge. (2026). Inquirer.net. Available at https://globalnation.inquirer.net/333757/high-bills-cheap-panels-drive-a-philippine-solar-surge. 1 This measure therefore seeks to promote the installation of behind-the-meter electricity generation and storage, to help Filipinos reduce their electricity expenses and improve the country’s overall energy security. Behind-the-meter refers to energy systems installed on the consumer’s side of the utility meter, including solar panels, home batteries, heat pumps, and EV chargers.7 This is distinguished from front-of-meter systems which are located on the utility side for large-scale generation and storage and supply to the power grid.8 This proposed bill aims to reflect this distinction in regulation. As such, end-users who generate and store electricity for their own use should not be subjected to the same regulatory requirements imposed upon generation companies and commercial power producers. Further, systems using equipment certified under standards recognized by the Energy Regulatory Commission to prevent electricity from flowing into the distribution grid would no longer need a certificate of compliance or prior ERC authorization. Finally, the Department of Energy is tasked to promote the widespread adoption of behind-the-meter electricity generation and energy storage systems and to coordinate the removal of national and local administrative barriers to their installation. With this measure, we hope to ease the burden on ordinary Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is respectfully sought. BRIAN RAYMUND S. label: HB 11460
title: AN ACT REQUIRING DISASTER-RELATED INFORMATION TO BE STATED IN ACCESSIBLE LANGUAGE TO ENSURE PUBLIC UNDERSTANDING THEREOF TO PROTECT PUBLIC HEALTH AND SAFETY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Disasters demand immediate action. When typhoons, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and other natural disasters strike, people must be able to quickly understand warnings, evacuation orders, safety instructions, and other information that may determine whether lives are saved or lost. Disaster preparedness, therefore, is not only about having plans and resources in place, but also about ensuring that critical information reaches people in a form they can readily understand and act upon. This is particularly important in the Philippines, one of the most disaster-prone countries in the world,1 and home to more than 175 living languages.2 While Filipino and English are our official languages, many Filipinos continue to use their regional languages and dialects in their homes and communities. Examples are Bicol, Samar, and Leyte, which are also communities that regularly face strong typhoons. In an emergency, a warning that is difficult to understand can mean the difference between taking immediate action and losing valuable time. As such, there have been some efforts to make disaster-related information more tailored to its intended recipients. For example, in Batanes, residents receive localized disaster information in Ivatan alongside national weather bulletins and government advisories.3 These experiences show that the language used to deliver a warning can be just as 1 Bündnis Entwicklung Hilft / IFHV (2025): WorldRiskReport 2025. Berlin: Bündnis Entwicklung Hilft. 2 Philippines: Ethnologue. Ethnologue (Free All). (n.d.). https://www.ethnologue.com/country/PH/ 3 Abuso, G. (2024). Living with Typhoons: Lessons from the Ivatans of Batanes, Philippines. https://th.boell.org/en/2024/11/18/living-ivatans-philippines 1 important as the warning itself, recognizing the simple reality that people are more likely to understand and act on warnings when they are delivered in a language familiar to them. Therefore, this bill mandates national government agencies, as well as local government units (LGUs), to make disaster- and emergency-related announcements, advisories, warnings, issuances, and other relevant information clear and easy to understand. Furthermore, it requires the translation of these information into Filipino and appropriate regional languages and dialects. In a country as diverse and disaster-prone as the Philippines, disaster preparedness must reflect the different realities of its communities. Ensuring that emergency information is available in languages that people understand is essential so that warnings can be heard, understood, and acted upon. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. BRIAN RAYMUND S. label: HB 11461
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE PROPER INSTALLATION, MAINTENANCE, MANAGEMENT, AND REMOVAL OF DANGLING AND NON-OPERATIONAL OVERHEAD UTILITY WIRES AND CABLES BY ALL ENTITIES AUTHORIZED TO INSTALL OR MAINTAIN AERIAL UTILITY CABLES, AND PRESCRIBING PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The fast-paced expansion of telecommunications, high-speed internet, cable service, and electric distribution networks has significantly driven the Philippines’ modernization and economic growth.1 However, this expansion heavily burdened major metropolitan areas because of dangling, sagging, and abandoned overhead wires, widely known as “spaghetti wires”. In 2023, one of the most prominent structural failures linked to “spaghetti wires” happened near the historic Binondo Church in Manila, where four consecutive electric poles collapsed simultaneously due to the weight of thousands of unmaintained communication lines.2 The incident left three people injured and several vehicles damaged. The continued accumulation of these overhead wires has created a dangerous and often neglected problem along public roads and in residential areas. These messy cables are more than just a form of visual pollution, but a critical threat to public safety as well.3 Dangling live wires may cause electrocution, sparks, and devastating structural fires, particularly in densely populated communities. Furthermore, around two million kilos of unutilized and unusable wires have been removed in Manila, highlighting how utility companies often abandon dead and non- 1 Dela Cruz, R. (2026). PH connectivity agenda gets boost with telco sector’s $2.2-B capex. Available at https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1283081 2 Philippine Daily Inquirer. (2023). Eyes on heavy cables after Binondo pylons’ collapse. Available at https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1812393/eyes-on-heavy-cables-after-binondo-pylons-collapse 3 Garcia, P. (2024). MMC to discuss moves vs 'spaghetti wires'. Available at https://mb.com.ph/2024/5/27/mmc-to-discuss-moves-vs-spaghetti-wires-1 1 operational cables instead of removing them before installing new ones.4 As a result, utility poles are left structurally overloaded, leaving them highly vulnerable to snapping or falling during typhoons. Currently, the country lacks a strict legal framework that clearly holds public utility entities accountable for the proper maintenance and removal of their infrastructure. The regulation of these wires and similar hazards are left to the local government units. Without clear responsibilities and enforceable standards however, the “spaghetti wires” will continue to accumulate, posing risks to both public safety and existing infrastructure. This proposed bill seeks to address this long-standing urban hazard by establishing clear standards for the installation, maintenance, identification, and removal of cables, while ensuring that utility companies will be held accountable for keeping their infrastructure safe and orderly. label: HB 11462
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE ELECTRONIC WASTE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM, MANDATING EXTENDED PRODUCER RESPONSIBILITY, PROVIDING INFRASTRUCTURE AND INCENTIVES FOR E- WASTE RECYCLING, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes that every Filipino has the right to health and to a balanced and healthful ecology. Specifically Section 15, Article II directs the State to protect and promote the right to health, while Section 16 mandates the State to protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology. This constitutional responsibility takes on particular importance as the Philippines becomes increasingly dependent on electronic devices and digital technologies. The growth of electronics, however, also means a growing stream of discarded computers, mobile phones, appliances, batteries, spare parts and other electronic products. In 2022 alone, the Philippines generated approximately 537,000 tonnes of e-waste, equivalent to 4.7 kilograms per capita.1 But the problem appears more urgent when viewed from a global perspective. Reports from the Global E-waste Monitor 2024 show that a record 62 million tonnes of e-waste were generated globally in 2022, representing an 82 percent increase from our generation in 2010.2 Without intervention, the volume is projected to reach 82 million tonnes by 2030. The scale is difficult to ignore: the 62 million tonnes generated in 2022 would fill an estimated 1.55 million 40-ton trucks, which are enough to form a bumper-to-bumper line around the Earth’s equator.3 Despite these, the Philippines has yet to enact a comprehensive law governing e- waste. Apart from environmental consequences, this gap also presents a pressing public health concern. Electronic products may contain lead, mercury, and other hazardous substances. When discarded, dismantled, or burned without appropriate safeguards, 1 Sumaria, M. G. C., & Sumaria, R. (2025). Waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) management and policy frameworks in the Philippines: A mini review. Annals of Tropical Research, 47(1), 17-33. 2 Balde CP, Kuehr R, Yamamoto T, McDonald R, D’Angelo E, Althaf S et al. The Global E-waste Monitor 2024. Bonn, Geneva: International Telecommunication Union, United Nations Institute for Training and Resources; 2024 (https://ewastemonitor.info/). 3 Id. 1 these substances can contaminate air, soil, water, and surrounding communities. The World Health Organization has identified associations between exposure to e-waste pollutants and adverse health outcomes, including impaired neurodevelopment, respiratory effects, adverse birth outcomes, and effects on the immune system.4 Children, adolescents, and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to such exposure, adversely affecting neonatal outcomes, neurodevelopment, learning and behaviour outcomes, and even causing reduced lung and respiratory function.5 Proper e-waste management therefore goes beyond environmental preservation. Rather, it is an urgent preventive public health measure and an investment in the health of the next generation. Existing environmental laws provide important foundations, but their scopes still leave a gap: Republic Act No. 9003 or the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000 primarily governs municipal solid waste, Republic Act No. 6969 or the Toxic Substances and Hazardous and Nuclear Wastes Control Act of 1990 addresses toxic substances and hazardous wastes largely in industrial and chemical contexts, while Republic Act No. 11898 or the Extended Producer Responsibility Act of 2022 established extended producer responsibility for plastic packaging but excludes electronics. The proposed National Electronic Waste Management Act fills that gap by providing rules specifically responsive to the distinct environmental and health risks and recovery potential of e-waste. Specifically, it creates a national framework for the proper segregation, collection, transport, storage, reuse, recycling, and disposal of e-waste; prohibits its mixed disposal with ordinary municipal waste; requires consumers and establishments to surrender e-waste through authorized collection and treatment channels; and assigns defined responsibilities to the DENR, DTI, LGUs, DOLE, TESDA, and other relevant agencies. The measure also recognizes that the government cannot address the e-waste problem alone. It institutionalizes Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) by requiring manufacturers, brand owners, and importers to establish or participate in systems for the recovery, recycling, or safe disposal of the electronic products they introduce into the Philippine market. Progressive recovery targets and Producer Responsibility Organizations provide a mechanism for producers to assume responsibility beyond the point of sale and encourage better product design, reuse, material recovery, and circularity. At the same time, the bill does not overlook the workers already engaged in informal recycling. It provides for their training, provision of appropriate safety equipment, accreditation, and integration into formal collection and recycling supply chains. Incentives for qualified enterprises and accredited facilities further support the development of a domestic e-waste recycling and resource-recovery industry. The proposed measure is, therefore, a whole-of-nation approach to a problem that will only grow with continued technological advancement. The national government will establish the standards and infrastructure; producers will share responsibility for the products they place in the market; LGUs and communities will participate in proper collection and segregation; and workers in the informal sector will be given a pathway toward safer and more formalized livelihoods. In doing so, the bill seeks to turn e-waste 4 World Health Organization, “Electronic waste (e-waste),” Fact Sheets, 1 October 2024, https://www.who.int/news- room/fact-sheets/detail/electronic-waste-(e-waste). 5 Id. 2 from a growing environmental and health liability into an opportunity for responsible innovation and a more circular economy. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought.

label: HB 11463
title: AN ACT UPGRADING THE SALARY GRADE OF DENTISTS EMPLOYED IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A person’s overall health and well-being includes oral health. However, for many Filipino families, dental care is not a priority. Oftentimes, people just go to the dentist when the pain is no longer bearable. When a family’s financial resources are limited, it is understandable that they would rather spend on food, medicine, and other basic needs rather than preventive dental care. This is the reason why affordable and accessible dental services in public health facilities are vital to the country’s healthcare system. The state of oral health among Filipinos shows the need to prioritize dental services in the country. According to the DOH, in 2023, about 3 out of 10 Filipino children aged 5 years and older have decayed, missing, or filled teeth.1 Meanwhile, the Philippine Dental Association estimates that 7 out of 10 Filipinos have dental caries or tooth decay, and this number includes school-age children.2 Oral health problems, when left untreated, can cause pain and infection, and interfere with one’s daily life. Despite the importance of oral health, the country faces a shortage of dentists within the public health system. This year, the DOH reports that the current dentist-to- population ratio is at 1 to 53,000, which is below the ratio of 1 to 7,500 as recommended by the World Health Organization.3 To bridge this gap, the government must be able to attract and retain qualified dentists. 1 Oral Health of Young Filipino. Facts in Figures. Congressional Policy and Budget Research Department House of Representatives, December 2024 (No. 67). Dentists' group says 7 of 10 Filipinos have tooth decay. Philippine News Agency. Available at https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1219293. 3 DOH flags critical shortage of dentists nationwide. (2026). GMA News Online. Available at https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/nation/976631/doh-flags-critical-shortage-of-dentists- nationwide/story/. 1 Currently, the entry level position for dentists (Dentist I) is classified as Salary Grade 14 while Dentist II is at Salary Grade 17.4 However, this compensation must be evaluated in light of the years of education, licensure requirement, and technical expertise required of dentists. The salaries for dentists must likewise be assessed against the opportunities available to them in private practice, where dentists have greater control over their professional fees and the volume of procedures performed. The adequacy of compensation is particularly important in ensuring that qualified dentists are encouraged to enter and remain in government service. When there are too few dentists serving in public health facilities, the burden of limited access to oral healthcare falls most heavily on communities that have fewer resources and fewer alternatives for obtaining dental services. Thus, addressing the shortage of public dentists is not only a matter of strengthening the public health workforce, but also of ensuring that underserved and low-income Filipinos have meaningful access to essential oral healthcare. With this measure, we hope to attract and retain qualified professionals in the public sector, and ultimately strengthen the government’s ability to deliver essential health services to the Filipino people. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this measure is earnestly sought. BRIAN RAYMUND S. YAMSUAN Representative 2nd District, Parañaque City 4 Index of Classes by Salary Grade. label: HB 11465
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTIONS 149 AND 150 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Tax systems should be designed to promote a fair, progressive, and efficient system that requires those with greater capacity to contribute a proportionately greater share toward the financing of government programs and public services. The present tax structure, however, does not fully capture consumption expenditures associated with luxury and other non-essential goods. Expanding the coverage and increasing the rate of excise tax on such goods will help address this gap while discouraging conspicuous consumption and generating additional revenues for national development. The proposed measure aims to achieve greater tax progressivity and promote a more equitable distribution of wealth since luxury and high-value goods are generally purchased by consumers with greater disposable income and capacity to pay. By raising the cost of high-value discretionary purchases, the measure may discourage conspicuous consumption and redirect part of household resources toward savings, investment, or socially productive expenditure. This bill amends Section 149 of the NIRC of 1997, as amended, to put a limit to the current ceiling whilst introducing a new bracket above the current ceiling: automobiles priced over Four Million Pesos (P4,000,000.00) up to Eight Million Pesos (P8,000,000.00) will be taxed at fifty percent (50%), while automobiles priced beyond Eight Million Pesos (P8,000,000.00) will be taxed at seventy-five percent (75%). It likewise amends Section 150 of the Tax Code to raise the excise tax rate on non-essential goods from twenty percent (20%) to twenty-five percent (25%), to expressly bring yachts, jet skis, speedboats, sailboats, and motorboats, aircraft, planes, jets, and helicopters within the coverage of non-essential goods when acquired for pleasure, private use, or sport, and finally to remove perfumes and toilet waters from the coverage of the tax altogether. Crucially, this measure touches no one who cannot afford it. The tax treatment of ordinary passenger vehicles, motorcycles, and commercial vehicles such as trucks and cargo vans remains entirely untouched. Its entire burden falls on a narrow slice of transactions at the very top of the market. By removing perfumes and toilet waters from the coverage of Section 150, it also lifts an existing tax on everyday personal-care purchases that has never meaningfully reached the wealthy segment the tax was intended to target. In exchange, it is expected to generate additional, sorely needed revenue to help fund government priority programs, without asking anything more from the ordinary Filipino taxpayer. The increase in automobile tax alone translates to an estimated annual revenue of ₱3.91 billion. Strengthening the taxation of luxury consumption constitutes a practical means of enhancing the progressivity of the Philippine tax system. It enables the Government to tap revenue sources that are readily identifiable and administratively accessible, while ensuring that goods and assets used for essential, livelihood, public transportation, or productive purposes are not unduly burdened. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is urgently sought. ATTY. MIRO S. label: HB 11467
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Sierra Madre Mountain Range is one of the Philippines’ most important natural assets. Stretching from Cagayan in the north to Quezon in the south, it forms a vast interconnected landscape of forests, watersheds, rivers, biodiversity areas, and coastal ecosystems. Its ecological functions extend far beyond the mountain range itself, providing essential services that sustain communities, agriculture, water systems, infrastructure, livelihoods, and economic activities in both upland and downstream areas. The Sierra Madre likewise serves as a critical natural defense against typhoons, flooding, landslides, storm surges, drought, and other climate- related hazards. Its forests, watersheds, wetlands, riparian areas, ecological corridors, and coastal ecosystems regulate water flows, store and sequester carbon, support biodiversity, and contribute to the resilience of communities and critical infrastructure. The protection and restoration of the Sierra Madre are therefore not merely matters of environmental conservation, but matters of national development, public safety, water security, climate resilience, and national security. Despite its importance, the Sierra Madre remains vulnerable to continuing degradation arising from illegal logging, destructive extraction, incompatible land conversion, habitat fragmentation, biodiversity loss, and other activities that undermine ecological integrity. Existing governmental mandates and management arrangements, while important, operate through different agencies, jurisdictions, plans, and regulatory systems. Such fragmentation makes it difficult to manage the Sierra Madre as one interconnected ecological system and to consistently account for impacts that cross administrative boundaries. 1 This proposed measure seeks to address this institutional and ecological gap by establishing the Sierra Madre Mountain Range Authority (SMMRA) as a government-owned or -controlled corporation with an original charter, attached to the Office of the President for policy coordination and administrative supervision. The Authority is envisioned as the lead policy, planning, coordinating, and regulatory body for range-wide ecological governance, while preserving the lawful mandates of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), local government units, Protected Area Management Boards, the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples, and other competent institutions. At the center of the proposed framework is the Sierra Madre Ecological Integrity and Sustainable Development Master Plan, a comprehensive, science-based, geospatially explicit, 25-year plan that will establish ecological limits, management zones, no-go areas, permitted and prohibited uses, restoration priorities, measurable outcomes, investment requirements, and implementation responsibilities. The Master Plan will provide a common framework for harmonizing national, regional, local, ancestral-domain, and sectoral plans affecting the Sierra Madre. The measure adopts a landscape-scale and ridge-to-reef approach to conservation. Rather than treating forests, watersheds, rivers, biodiversity areas, and coastal ecosystems as isolated units, the proposed framework recognizes their ecological and hydrological interdependence. It provides for the identification and protection of ecological corridors, riparian buffers, critical habitats, key biodiversity areas, and other connectivity systems necessary to maintain biodiversity and ecosystem resilience. The bill further advances a Nature-Based Solutions-First policy. Government interventions addressing flooding, landslides, erosion, watershed degradation, water insecurity, coastal hazards, and climate risks will be required to consider the feasibility of nature-based, green, or green-gray solutions before relying solely on conventional infrastructure. The proposed approach recognizes natural ecosystems as functional infrastructure capable of providing long-term disaster-risk reduction, water-security, and climate- adaptation benefits. Recognizing that conservation cannot be sustained without viable communities and economic incentives, the proposed measure promotes sustainable livelihoods, including agroforestry, ecotourism, and sustainable non-timber forest products. It also provides avenues for Indigenous Peoples, upland communities, and lawful tenure holders to participate in conservation and restoration activities and benefit from verified ecological outcomes. A significant innovation of the measure is the establishment of a Sierra Madre Nature Credit System. The system is intended to create a transparent and independently verified mechanism through which measurable protection, restoration, biodiversity, watershed, water-security, and climate-resilience outcomes may be recognized and financed. Covered enterprises that 2 materially depend upon Sierra Madre ecosystem services may be required to satisfy Nature Credit Purchase Obligations, thereby helping align economic activity with the ecological services upon which such activity depends. The system expressly does not authorize prohibited activities or substitute for environmental, tenure, protected-area, or Indigenous Peoples safeguards. To support the long-term implementation of the law, the bill establishes a Sierra Madre Fund and provides for lawful and transparent financing mechanisms, including national government appropriations, certain environmental charges, penalties and restoration recoveries when legally assignable, grants and technical assistance, and other lawful sources. The Fund is limited to the Authority’s statutory public-good and market- governance functions and is subject to government accounting, procurement, auditing, transparency, and disclosure requirements. label: HB 11468
title: AN ACT CREATING A DENTAL UNIT IN EVERY RURAL HEALTH UNIT AS PART OF THE PRIMARY HEALTH CARE APPROACH IN THE DELIVERY OF HEALTH SERVICES AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Oral health is an essential component of overall health and well-being. Access to basic dental services, however, remains a concern, particularly in rural and underserved communities where geographic, financial, and other barriers may limit access to regular dental care. The Rural Health Unit serves as an important primary health care facility within local communities. Integrating basic dental services into the Rural Health Unit will help bring preventive, promotive, and appropriate primary dental care closer to the people and facilitate the early detection and treatment of oral health conditions. This measure seeks to establish a Dental Unit in every Rural Health Unit, with at least one (1) public health dentist and one (1) trained dental aide, and to provide the Department of Health with the responsibility to establish appropriate standards, guidelines, and technical assistance for their operation. By strengthening dental services at the primary health care level, this Act will promote preventive oral health care, encourage early intervention, improve access to essential dental services, and strengthen the delivery of comprehensive primary health care in local communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11469
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH TO ESTABLISH A RESEARCH CENTER ON OBESITY PREVENTION”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Corpulence or obesity has become significant public health concern in the Philippines. The 2023 National Nutrition Survey of the Department of Science and Technology–Food and Nutrition Research Institute (DOST-FNRI) reported that 39.8% of Filipino adults aged 20 to 59 were classified as Obese I or II under the Asia-Pacific BMI classification. The survey also provides national data on anthropometry, blood pressure, blood glucose, lipid profiles, dietary intake, physical activity, and other factors relevant to nutrition and health. Despite the availability of national nutrition and health data, there remains a need for sustained and focused research on the prevention and management of overweight and obesity. Evidence on risk factors, effective interventions, treatment outcomes, costs, and the health and socioeconomic consequences associated with obesity can contribute to the development of effective and evidence-based public health policies and programs. This measure seeks to mandate the Department of Health to establish an Obesity Prevention Research Center that will conduct, support, coordinate, and promote research on overweight and obesity. The Center shall study their prevalence and determinants, evaluate preventive treatment interventions, assess their health and economic consequences, and generate evidence to guide the formulation and improvement of government policies and programs. The proposed Center shall also coordinate with existing government agencies, research institutions, academic institutions, local government units, and other stakeholders to maximize existing data and research resources and avoid unnecessary duplication of efforts. The collection and use of health information shall be undertaken in accordance with the Data Privacy Act of 2012 and applicable ethical standards for health research. Through a dedicated research mechanism, this measure seeks to strengthen the country's capacity to generate reliable evidence, evaluate interventions, and support informed strategies for the prevention and control of overweight and obesity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11470
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR FREE MAINTENANCE MEDICATIONS, VITAMINS, AND MINERAL SUPPLEMENTS FOR SENIOR CITIZENS”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE As the Filipino population ages, more senior citizens are living with chronic and age-related conditions that require continuous maintenance medications. The rising cost of medicines, vitamins, and other medically necessary supplements can place a significant financial burden on elderly Filipinos, particularly those who rely solely on pensions or have limited sources of income. While Republic Act No. 9994, otherwise known as the “Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010,” provides senior citizens with discounts and tax exemptions on medicines and other health-related goods, these benefits do not necessarily ensure that maintenance medications are available and affordable to all senior citizens. For many elderly Filipinos, even the remaining cost of regularly purchased medicines may constitute a substantial portion of their limited income. This measure seeks to establish a government program that will provide free maintenance medications and medically indicated vitamins and mineral supplements to qualified senior citizens, subject to an appropriate national formulary and prescription requirements. It also provides mechanisms for community-based access and delivery, particularly for the oldest- old, frail, homebound, and bedridden senior citizens. The measure further ensures coordination with the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation’s existing medication benefits, including the Guaranteed and Accessible Medications for Outpatient Treatment (GAMOT), to complement existing programs and prevent duplication of benefits. By reducing the financial burden of essential medicines and promoting continuity of treatment, this measure seeks to improve medication adherence, prevent avoidable complications and hospitalizations, and promote healthier and more dignified aging among Filipino senior citizens. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11471
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FRESH FILIPINO GRADUATES OF PHILIPPINE HIGHER EDUCATION AND TECHNICAL-VOCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS AND PROGRAMS WITH A ONE-TIME CASH GRANT OF FIVE THOUSAND PESOS (₱5,000.00)”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Entering the workforce after graduation is an important transition for young Filipinos, but it often comes with immediate expenses. Job applications, transportation, documentation, medical examinations, work attire, and other requirements can impose a financial burden at a time when many fresh graduates have yet to receive their first income from employment. For many young Filipinos, the lack of readily available funds can make the transition from education to employment more difficult. A modest and timely form of financial assistance can help bridge this gap and enable graduates to pursue employment opportunities without having to rely immediately on family members or incur debt for basic employment-related expenses. This measure seeks to provide qualified fresh Filipino graduates of duly recognized or authorized higher education institutions or duly registered technical-vocational programs in the Philippines with a one-time cash grant of Five Thousand Pesos (₱5,000.00). The proposed grant is not conditioned on unemployment or household income. Its purpose is to provide basic transition assistance to qualified graduates as they seek and commence employment. The measure likewise limits availment to one time per beneficiary and requires application within one year from graduation or completion of the program. The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) is designated as the lead implementing agency, in coordination with the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) for the verification and processing of applications of graduates and completers of technical-vocational programs. The measure further provides for electronic verification of graduation records and safeguards against duplicate availment, while requiring compliance with existing data privacy laws. The amount necessary for implementation shall be provided through the annual General Appropriations Act. The enactment of this measure will provide practical and immediate assistance to young Filipinos as they take their first steps toward employment and productive participation in the economy. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11472
title: AN ACT INTEGRATING PALLIATIVE AND HOSPICE CARE INTO THE PHILIPPINE HEALTH CARE SYSTEM”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Palliative and hospice care are essential components of a compassionate and comprehensive health care system. Patients suffering from serious, life-threatening, life-limiting, chronic, or complex illnesses often experience significant pain and other physical, psychosocial, and emotional burdens that require care beyond the treatment of the underlying disease. While the Philippine health care system has made significant progress in expanding access to health services, access to organized and affordable palliative and hospice care remains uneven. Many patients and their families continue to face difficulties in obtaining appropriate pain and symptom management, home-based care, psychosocial support, continuity of care, and end-of-life services. This measure seeks to integrate palliative and hospice care into the Philippine health care system and the framework of Universal Health Care, ensuring that such services are available across hospitals, primary care facilities, communities, and appropriate home-based settings. The bill establishes standards for quality and accreditation, strengthens referral and continuity-of-care networks, promotes education and training of health professionals and volunteers, supports continuing research, and directs the development of appropriate PhilHealth benefit packages for inpatient, outpatient, and home-based services. It likewise facilitates support for indigent patients and recognizes the important role of family caregivers. Ultimately, this measure seeks to ensure that every Filipino facing serious or end-of-life illness may receive accessible, affordable, quality, and compassionate care that protects dignity, relieves suffering, and improves quality of life for both patients and their families. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11474
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Sierra Madre Mountain Range (SMMR) makes up 40 percent of the forest cover in the Philippines. Its range starts at Cagayan in the north and extends to Quezon Province in the south of Luzon. The provinces that trail the SMMR also include Isabela, Nueva Vizcaya, Quirino, Nueva Ecija, Aurora, Bulacan, Rizal, and Laguna. The forest cover spanning 540 kilometers is not just home to 3.5 million species but also a significant carbon-sequestering spot.1 The rich biodiversity of the SMMR has undoubtedly supplied the people with ecosystem services that benefited multi-generations of Filipinos. But the mountain range that Filipinos are fond of referring to as the first line of defense against disasters is hounded with illegal activities such as encroachment and deforestation. The indispensable contribution of this major ecological system is crucial to the life of all organisms that depend on it—human and non-humans alike. The conservation, protection, and sustainable management of the SMMR increases the chances of a better biodiversity conservation, climate resilience, water security, and disaster risk reduction of the systems that depend and are interconnected to the forest cover. In line with the constitutional mandate to uphold every Filipino’s right to a healthful ecology by protecting the largest tropical rainforest in Luzon, this bill seeks to establish the Sierra Madre Mountain Conservation and Development Authority. ______________________________ 1. Climate Change Commission. 2024. Through this agency, a Nature-based solutions and resilient-investment approach shall be operationalized to protect and enrich the mountain range of Sierra Madre. The agency shall create an ecosystem-scale governance framework that will harmonize and integrate mandates and function of national agencies and local government units. In this regard, passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. ROY M. title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE IMPLEMENTATION, MANAGEMENT, AND UTILIZATION OF THE COCONUT FARMERS AND INDUSTRY TRUST FUND, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE CERTAIN SECTIONS OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11524, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE COCONUT FARMERS AND INDUSTRY TRUST FUND ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Since its enactment in 2021, Republic Act No. 11524 or the Coconut Farmers and Industry Trust Fund Act, has been regarded as the much-awaited hope for the coconut industry. With over 3.5 million coconut farmers in the Philippines and 14.5 million metric tons of coconuts produced in 2025, we are recognized as the second-largest coconut producer in the world. As such, it is imperative upon the government that we continue to improve and develop this industry. The Coconut Farmers and Industry Trust Fund (CFITF) established pursuant to RA 11524, aims to boost the coconut industry through programs geared towards development and sustainability. However, coconut farmers have yet to experience the benefits of the programs under this law as much of the fund remains unused. President Marcos himself sought for the amendment of the law in order to facilitate faster utilization and disbursement of the funds and ensure effective and responsive programs for the industry. This bill is thus filed to address these issues and strengthen its implementation. The bill provides for the creation of the Coconut Farmers and Industry Development Plan and identified the programs where the CFITF will be utilized. This includes the massive coconut planting, fertilization, and irrigation which ensures continuous planting of coconut trees to sustain production. This bill also includes the Phlippine Coconut Authority as part of the Trust Fund Management Committee to ensure that funds are properly managed to fund relevant programs for coconut farmers. Through this bill, it is hoped that the CFITF will be efficiently and effectively utilized to support the industry and adequately address their needs. The passage of this bill is thus earnestly sought. 1 NICANOR M. title: AN ACT TO PROMOTE THE DEVELOPMENT AND SUSTAINABILITY OF THE SEAWEED INDUSTRY IN THE PHILIPPINES, ENHANCING RESEARCH, SUPPORT, AND GLOBAL COMPETITIVENESS AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is a country rich in marine resources. With 1,065 seaweed species found in our waters, so far, only four are farmed. These are Eucheuma, Kappaphycus, Gracilaria, and Caulerpa1. The seaweed industry is one of the major contributors of our economy. In 20242, seaweed aquaculture accounted for an impressive 66% of overall fishery production and remains as one of the agriculture sector’s top export commodities. It sustains thousands of families in coastal communities and contributes significantly to national employment and aquaculture output. Beyond food, seaweed has diverse applications such as animal feed, fertilizer, cosmetic ingredient, and most recently, as raw material for bio-plastics 3 among others. However, the industry continues to face mounting challenges such as global warming, degradation, disease outbreaks like “ice-ice”, volatile market prices, and insufficient post-harvest infrastructure that significantly affect this industry. These challenges are no longer theoretical. Recently, the Philippine Statistics Authority logged a 3.3% production decline in seaweed for the second quarter of 2026.4 This bill seeks to strengthen and future-proof our seaweed industry by providing support in promoting sustainable farming practices to protect marine ecosystems and ensure long-term productivity, advancing research and technology to improve yield, disease resistance, and product development, expanding support for seaweed farmers, and strengthening market competitiveness to secure the sector's position in both domestic and international trade. 1 Philippine Seaweeds and Fishery By-Products are Raw Materials for Locally Made Bioplastics, National Academy of Science and Technology, 17 August 2026, https://nast.dost.gov.ph/index.php/13-news-press-releases/971-philippine-seaweeds-and-fishery-by- products-are-raw-materials-for-locally-made-bioplastics (17 August 2026) 2 Seaweed, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, https://www.fao.org/hand-in-hand/previous-editions/hih- investment-forum-2025/The_Philippines/en 17 August 2026 (last accessed 17 August 2026) 3 Experts Urge More R&D in Bioplastics From Seaweed To Help Reduce Plastic Pollution, Department of Science and Technology, 14 July 2026, https://dost.gov.ph/knowledge-resources/news/87-2026-news/4447-experts-urge-more-r-d-in-bioplastics-from-seaweed-to- help-reduce-plastic-pollution.html (last accessed 17 August 2026) 4 Fisheries output grows 2 percent in Q2, A. title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE RECLASSIFICATION AND CONVERSION OF CERTAIN PARCELS OF FORESTLAND IN THE PROVINCE OF NUEVA VIZCAYA INTO ALIENABLE AND DISPOSABLE PUBLIC LANDS Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Declaration of Policy. – It is hereby declared the policy of the State to conserve and protect the nation's forest lands as part of its patrimony, and, consistent with that duty, to determine by law the specific limits of such forest lands and to release from them only those areas which, by reason of long and actual human settlement, cultivation and use, no longer serve forest purposes. It is further the policy of the State to promote social justice and security of tenure for actual occupants and tillers of lands of the public domain, to respect the rights of indigenous cultural communities and indigenous peoples to their ancestral domains and ancestral lands, and to ensure that the reclassification of forestland does not impair watersheds, riverbanks, headwaters, or the ecological balance of the areas concerned. SECTION 2. Definition of Terms. – As used in this Act: (a) Alienable and disposable land refers to land of the public domain classified as agricultural land and declared available for alienation and disposition under Commonwealth Act No. 141, as amended, otherwise known as the Public Land Act; (b) Forestland refers to land of the public domain which has not been declared alienable and disposable, and which is subject to the system of land classification administered under Presidential Decree No. 705, as amended, otherwise known as the Revised Forestry Code of the Philippines; (c) Ancestral domain and ancestral land have the meanings assigned to them in Republic Act No. 8371, otherwise known as the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act of 1997; (d) Segregation survey refers to the ground survey conducted by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources to delimit,
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 4, Article XII of the 1987 Constitution directs that the Congress shall, as soon as possible, determine by law the specific limits of forest lands and national parks, marking clearly their boundaries on the ground, and that thereafter such forest lands may not be diminished except by law. That mandate is not merely an allocation of power; it is the only door through which the situation this measure addresses can be resolved. In the Municipality of Kasibu, Province of Nueva Vizcaya, communities have for generations built their homes, planted their rice, banana and citrus, and raised their children on land that the State still carries on its maps as forest. The Department's own field assessment describes the covered areas as occupied by the community for residential, agricultural and agro-forest purposes, containing scattered residential houses occupied by farmers, with actual use recorded as agricultural, agroforest, rice field, banana and citrus plantations. They cannot obtain a title. They cannot pledge the land for a loan, pass it to their children with certainty, or be secure against displacement. The local government cannot assess the land for real property tax, so the municipality earns nothing from land it must nonetheless serve with roads, water and schools. For the Province as a whole, the Forest Management Bureau records that the conversion proposed here would reduce forest land by about six hundredths of one percent, leaving the provincial forest estate substantially intact. This bill reclassifies two (2) parcels of forestland in the Province of Nueva Vizcaya, described by metes and bounds as certified by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources, into alienable and disposable public land, and opens them to disposition under the Public Land Act. It deliberately does three further things. It carries forward, as statutory exclusions, the protections of Section 16 of the Revised Forestry Code — the twenty-metre riverbank strips, the ridge tops and plateaus from which headwaters emanate, and the other areas needed for forest purposes — so that reclassification does not become deforestation. It excludes from coverage any land within an ancestral domain, ancestral land, Certificate of Page 1 of 9 Ancestral Domain Claim or Certificate of Ancestral Domain Title, and requires certification by the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples before any segregation survey may proceed, in recognition that land held by indigenous cultural communities under native title has never been public land at all. And it requires that the boundaries between the reclassified land and the forestland that remains be marked on the ground with concrete monuments and maintained there, which is what Section 4, Article XII actually commands and what decades of paper-only classification have failed to deliver. Considering the potential economic, social and developmental benefits of the proposed measure, its immediate passage is respectfully and strongly recommended. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A MINIMUM BASIC MONTHLY SALARY OF FIFTY THOUSAND PESOS (P50,000.00) FOR PUBLIC SCHOOL TEACHERS AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Tamang Sahod para sa Guro Act.” SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is hereby declared the policy of the State to assign the highest budgetary priority to education and to ensure that teaching attracts and retains its rightful share of the best available talents through adequate remuneration. SEC. 3. Coverage. – This Act shall cover all persons occupying teaching positions in public elementary and secondary schools, including those performing supervisory or administrative functions therein, as contemplated under Republic Act No. 4670, otherwise known as the “Magna Carta for Public School Teachers,” but excluding those in the professorial staff of state universities and colleges. As used herein, basic monthly salary refers to the compensation corresponding to the salary grade and step of the position, exclusive of allowances, bonuses, honoraria and other emoluments. SEC. 4. Minimum Basic Monthly Salary. – No public school teacher shall receive a basic monthly salary lower than Fifty Thousand Pesos (PhP 50,000.00), or the rate corresponding to the salary grade and step of the position under Republic Act No. 11466, otherwise known as the “Salary Standardization Law of 2019,” as amended, whichever is higher. SEC. 5. Preservation of Salary Differentials. – The Department of Budget and Management shall adjust the basic monthly salaries of public school teachers occupying positions higher than the entry-level teaching position so as to maintain the percentage differentials between successive salary grades and steps existing immediately prior to the effectivity of this
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 5(5), Article XIV of the 1987 Constitution commands that the State “shall assign the highest budgetary priority to education and ensure that teaching will attract and retain its rightful share of the best available talents through adequate remuneration.”1 Of all the professions in the public service, teaching alone is singled out in the Constitution for a guarantee of adequate remuneration. That guarantee remains unfulfilled. A Teacher I presently earns Thirty Thousand Twenty-Four Pesos (PhP 30,024.00) monthly,2 below the family living wage of Thirty-Six Thousand Five Hundred Ten Pesos (PhP 36,510.00) estimated for a household of five.3 Some eight hundred three thousand two hundred seventy-two (803,272) personnel occupy Teacher I to Teacher III positions. While officials in Salary Grades 31 to 33 receive between Two Hundred Ninety-Three Thousand One Hundred Ninety-One Pesos (PhP 293,191.00) and Four Hundred Thirty-Eight Thousand Eight Hundred Forty-Four Pesos (PhP 438,844.00) monthly, teachers were granted increases of only 4.95% to 5.6%. Many take on part-time work or leave for posts abroad. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. label: HB 11479
title: AN ACT UPGRADING THE LAND TRANSPORTATION OFFICE (LTO) DISTRICT OFFICE IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF BAYOMBONG, PROVINCE OF NUEVA VIZCAYA, FROM CLASS “C” TO CLASS “A,” AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Land Transportation Office (LTO) District Office in the Municipality of Bayombong, Province of Nueva Vizcaya, is presently classified as a Class “C” district office. Situated in the provincial capital, it delivers the core services of the Office within its jurisdiction, including motor vehicle registration, the issuance of driver’s licenses and permits, and the enforcement of land transportation laws, rules and regulations, to the municipalities of Bayombong, Bagabag, Diadi, Villaverde, Solano, Quezon and Ambaguio. The sustained growth in motor vehicle registrations and licensing transactions within this area of responsibility has correspondingly increased the responsibilities and workload of the office. The present Class “C” classification no longer reflects the expanding functions and service demands of the office. Its existing organizational structure and resource allocation limit its capacity to efficiently serve the increasing number of clients while maintaining the quality of public service. Upgrading the Bayombong District Office to Class “A” will provide the appropriate organizational structure, additional personnel, and operational resources needed to effectively carry out its mandated functions. It will likewise enhance service efficiency, strengthen enforcement activities, and improve the delivery of LTO services to the communities within its jurisdiction. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. label: HB 11480
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A MAGNA CARTA OF TRICYCLE DRIVERS AND OPERATORS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the "Magna Carta of Tricycle Drivers and Operators". SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is the policy of the State to promote the welfare of workers in the tricycle sector, to secure for them access to social security and health insurance commensurate to their capacity to contribute, to protect them against deprivation of their livelihood without valid cause and due process, and to ensure that the regulation of tricycles-for-hire is uniform, predictable, and free from exaction. SECTION 3. Scope and Regulatory Authority. – This Act applies to operators of tricycles-for-hire, to the drivers they engage, and to the local government units and national agencies named herein. It does not apply to tricycles used exclusively for private purposes or to two-wheeled motorcycles however used. The grant, amendment, renewal, suspension, and cancellation of the MTOP and the designation of zones, routes, and terminals are exercised by the Sanggunian under Sections 447(a)(3)(vi) and 458(a)(3)(vi) of Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, subject to guidelines issued by the Department of Transportation (DOTr). The registration of tricycles and the licensing of drivers remain with the LTO, and no LGU shall impose a requirement in the nature of either. SECTION 4. Operating Requirements. – No tricycle-for-hire shall operate on a national highway utilized by four-wheeled vehicles heavier than four (4) tons and on which the normal speed exceeds forty (40) kilometers per hour: Provided, That the Sanggunian may, by ordinance and with the approval of the DOTr, allow such operation where no other public transport services the route: Provided, further, That where allowed, the tricycle shall traverse only the outer right lane except when preparing to turn.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Tricycles carry passengers where jeepneys and buses do not go, and their regulation is devolved to cities and municipalities.1 Devolution supplied no national floor: each sets its own requirements, fees, and processing periods, and that variation produces the exactions and brokered permits the sector reports. The gap in social protection is contribution capacity, not coverage. Self-employed persons are already compulsorily covered by the SSS, and every Filipino by the National Health Insurance Program.2 But a driver on an irregular daily income must remit PhP 1,250.00 a month to keep both current.3 This measure sets uniform operating requirements, caps the permit fee, requires a one-stop shop with a definite processing period, replaces impounding for documentary lapses with citations, and establishes a Tricycle Sector Registry. On that Registry it builds a Contribution Support Program paying half of a qualified beneficiary's contribution at the statutory floor, matched by the member and capped by the annual appropriation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. Representative Lone District of Nueva Vizcaya 1 Rep. label: HB 11481
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROTECTION OF LOCAL HOG RAISERS, ENSURING FARMGATE PRICE TRANSPARENCY AND FAIR TRADING PRACTICES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. This Act shall be known as the “Local Hog Raisers Protection and Fair Pricing Act.” SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. It is the policy of the State to promote comprehensive rural development, to provide support to agriculture through adequate financial, production, marketing, and other support services, to promote the preferential use of locally produced goods, and to prohibit combinations in restraint of trade and unfair competition, consistent with Sections 1 and 5 of Article XIII, Sections 1, 6, 12, 13, and 19 of Article XII, and Section 21 of Article II of the Constitution. Nothing in this Act shall be construed to authorize the fixing of the purchase or selling price of any animal or animal product. SEC. 3. Coverage. This Act shall apply to farmgate transactions in swine throughout the country. SEC. 4. Livestock Transaction Reporting System. The Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI) shall establish and maintain a Livestock Transaction Reporting System. Every buyer covered by the implementing rules shall report the date, location, volume, price, and terms of payment of each farmgate transaction, without disclosing the identity of the selling raiser without the raiser's written consent. Reported information shall be published only in aggregate form and shall not be used as the sole basis for any tax assessment or admitted in evidence against the reporting party, except in a proceeding for violation of this Act. SEC. 5. Reference Farmgate Price. The Department of Agriculture (DA), in coordination with the Philippine Statistics Authority, shall compute and publish weekly a reference farmgate price for hogs, at the national and regional levels, derived from data collected under Section 4. The reference price shall be published on official websites and disseminated to local agriculture offices and accredited raisers' associations, and shall be clearly identified as an administrative indicator distinct from official statistical series.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Backyard and small- hog raising provides livelihood and income to thousands of Filipino families, including many households in Nueva Vizcaya. Small-hold farms accounted for 70.0 percent of the country’s swine inventory as of 1 January 2023, underscoring their importance to the domestic pork supply and rural economy.1 Yet local hog raisers remain particularly vulnerable to low farmgate prices, rising production costs, weak bargaining power, and an increasingly complex livestock marketing chain. The Department of Agriculture has acknowledged that farmgate prices had fallen sharply without corresponding relief to consumers.2 Even the existing law provides significant resources for animal industry development, including repopulation, disease response, credit, and related support,3 the core market is still facing challenges as local producers remain largely unresolved. The measure is anchored on the constitutional policies promoting agricultural support, reduction of economic inequalities, preferential use of locally produced goods, and regulation of unfair competition.4 For these reasons, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. label: HB 11483
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY PROGRAM, STRENGTHENING DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS, AND PREVENTING SCHOOL VIOLENCE, ACTIVE ASSAILANT INCIDENTS, AND OTHER SAFETY AND SECURITY THREATS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Schools must always remain places of learning, formation, and safety. Recent successive incidents and threats involving bullying and cyberbullying, bomb scares, deadly weapons, online threats, and other acts of violence have haunted our places of learning and peace. They have also exposed the evolving risks faced by learners, teachers, and school personnel. In response, the Department of Education has strengthened its policies on weapons and bomb threats and introduced school safety audits, active-threat preparedness exercises, confidential reporting mechanisms, and mental-health interventions. Existing laws address particular aspects of school safety, including bullying, mental health, and disaster risk reduction. Nevertheless, there remains a need for a unified and permanent framework covering the prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery measures necessary to address both natural hazards and intentional acts of violence across educational institutions. This bill therefore establishes a National Comprehensive School Safety Program. It mandates school-specific safety and vulnerability assessments, emergency plans and drills, reasonable security infrastructure, weapons-control measures, violence-prevention and mental-health programs, confidential reporting and threat assessment mechanisms, inter-agency coordination, and post-incident recovery and continuity-of-learning measures. 1 Through this measure, school safety shall no longer depend on isolated or reactive interventions but shall become a coordinated, preventive, and adequately supported national responsibility. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. BERNADETTE “DETTE” G.
