label: HB 11551
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A TEXTBOOK ASSISTANCE VOUCHER PROGRAM FOR STUDENTS ENROLLED IN PRIVATE BASIC EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Education remains one of the most effective means of promoting social mobility, strengthening human capital, and ensuring national development. While the State recognizes the complementary role of private educational institutions in the delivery of quality basic education, many Filipino families continue to struggle with the increasing cost of educational materials, particularly textbooks and learning resources. Although tuition and miscellaneous expenses are often the primary focus of educational assistance programs, the recurring cost of textbooks and instructional materials imposes a significant financial burden on parents and guardians, especially those belonging to low-income and middle-income households. In many cases, students rely on outdated, borrowed, or insufficient learning materials, adversely affecting learning outcomes and academic performance. This measure seeks to establish a Textbook Assistance Voucher Program that will provide qualified students enrolled in private elementary and secondary schools with targeted financial support for the acquisition of textbooks, workbooks, and other Department of Education-approved learning materials. The proposed voucher mechanism aims to promote equitable access to educational resources while supporting parental choice and the continued participation of private schools in the national education system. 1 The bill likewise ensures accountability and transparency through accreditation standards, digital tracking systems, and coordination with private schools, publishers, and authorized educational suppliers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 11552
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A COMPREHENSIVE, INTEGRATED, AND SUSTAINABLE REINTEGRATION PROGRAM FOR OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Overseas Filipino Worker (OFW) is an integral part of Filipino society and a significant contributor to our nation’s development. Yet, after years of working abroad and being separated from their families, many OFWs face another challenge upon returning home: rebuilding their livelihoods and reintegrating into their communities. This measure seeks to establish a comprehensive, integrated, and sustainable reintegration program for OFWs covering the entire migration cycle—from pre-departure, to on-site support, and upon return. It adopts a whole-of-government approach to provide returning OFWs with access to employment, entrepreneurship, education and skills development, financial literacy, psychosocial support, and other social protection services. The measure likewise seeks to strengthen coordination among government agencies and private sector partners, improve job matching and skills recognition, and ensure that undocumented OFWs are not excluded from reintegration assistance. It recognizes that effective reintegration requires not only financial assistance, but sustained support that enables OFWs to achieve economic self-sufficiency, social stability, and psychosocial well-being upon their return. 1 We owe it to our OFWs and their families to ensure that, when they return home, they are provided meaningful opportunities to rebuild their lives and contribute once again to the country’s development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 11553
title: AN ACT LOWERING THE OPTIONAL RETIREMENT AGE OF GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES FROM SIXTY (60) YEARS TO FIFTY-SIX (56) YEARS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 13-A OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8291, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE GOVERNMENT SERVICE INSURANCE SYSTEM ACT OF 1997
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Principle 3 of the 1991 United Nations Principles for Older Persons recognizes the right of older persons to participate in determining when and at what pace they withdraw from the labor force. Consistent with this principle, this measure seeks to lower the optional retirement age of government employees from sixty (60) years to fifty-six (56) years. Lowering the optional retirement age will allow government employees to enjoy their retirement benefits after years of dedicated public service and pursue other opportunities where their skills and experience may continue to contribute to the economy. At the same time, vacancies created by retirement will open opportunities for younger workers, bringing fresh skills and greater familiarity with emerging technologies into government service. This measure seeks to promote a more dynamic and responsive public service while expanding employment opportunities and supporting the financial independence of retiring government employees. Hence, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 11554
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE RIGHTS OF INFORMAL AMBULANT VENDORS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every day, informal ambulant vendors earn a living by selling food, goods, and other products, or by offering services, in streets, parks, terminals, and other public spaces. They are part of the daily life of our communities and contribute to our local economies. Yet, despite their important role, many of them remain outside the reach of government programs and social protection because they are not formally registered or recognized by the local government units where they operate. Being part of the informal economy should not mean being invisible to government. Informal ambulant vendors face unique challenges. They often have no permanent place of business, limited access to social protection, and little security in their livelihood. At the same time, their operations must also be balanced with the legitimate concerns of consumers, communities, and local governments, particularly on public safety, sanitation, traffic, and the proper use of public spaces. This bill seeks to address these concerns by recognizing informal ambulant vendors as legitimate participants in our local economy and by providing a clear and simplified framework for their registration and protection. 1 The proposed Magna Carta of Informal Ambulant Vendors seeks to protect and promote their rights to just and humane working conditions, social protection, access to justice, and workplace security. It likewise provides for a simplified registration process at the local level so that informal ambulant vendors can be properly identified and connected to government programs and services without being burdened by complicated procedures and unnecessary fees. By formalizing the informal ambulant vending sector, this measure seeks to ensure that these workers are no longer overlooked, but are instead recognized as part of our communities and included in the social protection and economic opportunities that government provides. In light of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 11556
title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the right to housing is a recognized fundamental human right ensuring that every person has access to a safe, secure, and affordable place to live. Adequate shelter means much more than just a roof and four walls. In keeping with international law, Article XIII, Section 9 of the Philippine Constitution mandates the State to undertake a continuing program of urban land reform and housing for the underprivileged and homeless in line with the policy of the State to promote a just and dynamic social order as enshrined in Section 9, Article II of our fundamental law. Despite the government's continuing efforts, however, millions of Filipinos remain without affordable, adequate, and secure shelter. This predicament is particularly significant among low-income families, informal settlers, and other vulnerable sectors who are unable to acquire or sustain homeownership due to the high cost of land, construction, and financing for housing. This bill seeks to establish a national policy providing qualified beneficiaries with free access to government-owned housing through usufruct. Under this arrangement, beneficiaries are granted the right to use and enjoy a government housing property for a specific period without transferring ownership of the property to the beneficiary. This approach allows the government to make productive use of its housing assets while providing qualified families with decent shelter. This bill proposes to accord underprivileged and homeless Filipino citizens who do not own any real property anywhere in the country. It shall also be extended to government employees under the auspices of Local Government units (LGUs) and other government agencies provided that the beneficiary does not own any real property within the territorial jurisdiction of the LGU where the employee is assigned or employed. This provision may help government institutions attract and retain personnel, particularly those assigned to areas where housing costs are beyond their means. To ensure that government housing resources remain available to future beneficiaries, the grant of usufruct shall not constitute a transfer of ownership and shall be subject to reasonable conditions on occupancy, maintenance, use, and termination. Beneficiaries are expected to use the property as their principal residence and to comply with the terms of the usufruct agreement. These safeguards will promote responsible stewardship of public housing assets and protect government property from unauthorized sale, transfer, or commercial use. The proposed policy is also intended to complement, rather than replace, existing national and local government housing programs. By introducing usufruct as an additional mechanism for providing secure housing, the government can expand access to shelter while maximizing the use of available public land and housing properties. It may likewise provide LGUs and government agencies with greater flexibility in addressing the housing needs of vulnerable communities and their qualified personnel. The urgency of this measure is underscored by the country's continuing housing deficit. Government estimates indicate that, without sustained intervention, the national housing backlog could reach approximately 22 million units by 2040. Addressing this gap requires not only the construction of additional housing units but also innovative approaches that make existing government resources more accessible to families who need them most. Free housing through usufruct offers a practical means of advancing the constitutional right to decent shelter while preserving public ownership of government housing assets. It places the State's existing land and housing resources at the service of Filipino families who have no adequate home of their own, while ensuring that these resources remain available for public benefit over the long term. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11557
title: AN ACT UPGRADING THE CLASSIFICATION OF TABACO DISTRICT OFFICE OF THE LAND TRANSPORTATION OFFICE (LTO) IN TABACO CITY, PROVINCE OF ALBAY FROM CLASS “D” TO CLASS “B” DISTRICT OFFICE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Province of Albay, where the world famous Mayon Volcano majestically sits, is the second most populous province in the Bicol region. The total population of the province stands at 1,379,398 distributed across 277,127 households (PSA Population Census 2024). Albay is accessible to tourists and other travelers via land, air or sea. A developing road network connects tourist destinations to urban centers and the countryside through public utility vehicles, i.e., buses, jeepneys, tricycles, padyaks (pedicabs) and privately owned motorcycles, cars and other conveyances. Expectedly, the rising vehicle density greatly contributes to traffic congestion – one of the critically urgent challenges to land transportation management. Albay is divided into three (3) Congressional Districts composed of fifteen (15) municipalities and three (3) cities. One of these three is Tabaco City, which together with the five (5) municipalities of Bacacay, Malilipot, Malinao, Sto. Domingo and Tiwi constitute the First District covering a population of approximately 433,349 (PSA Population Census 2024). The Land Transportation Office (LTO) Tabaco District Office hobbled by a meager workforce of only eight (8) plantilla positions as it is under the Class “D” category, provides the necessary major services. These include Licensing, Registration, Adjudication and Law Enforcement to a fast-growing population of road users. Despite human resource constraint, the LTO Tabaco District Office, although not without difficulty, has exhibited a commendable operational performance particularly for the period 2021-2025. An evidence-based analysis of the LTO Tabaco District Office’s overall performance for this five- year period reveals robust accomplishments in the delivery of the following services: • Motor Vehicle (MV) Registration: A total of 417,890 MV transactions were handled over the five-year period with an annual average of 83,578 transactions. Transactions increased significantly from 2021 to 1 2023, then declined in 2024 with a slight increase in 2025. This reduction may be attributed to the 2023 LTO policy extending the validity of initial registration for motorcycles to three (3) years, thereby decreasing the volume of annual renewal transactions in the succeeding years. • License and Permits: The office processed a total of 176,277 transactions, with an annual average of 35,255. The number of licenses and permits handled steadily rose from 2021 to 2024, before declining in 2025. The decrease may be partly due to the long- standing effect of the 10-year validity of driver’s licenses, which reduces the frequency of renewal activities, although overall figures remain higher compared to earlier years. • Apprehension Cases: A total of 4,367 apprehension cases were recorded over the five-year period, with an average of 873 cases per year. Cases gradually declined from 2021 to 2023, reflecting improved compliance with land transportation regulations. In 2024, apprehensions rose due to intensified enforcement operations; however, in 2025, the number decreased as motorists continued to adhere to traffic rules, demonstrating the positive impact of sustained enforcement and compliance efforts. • Revenue collection: The LTO Tabaco District Office generated a total revenue of P307,381,319.74, with an average annual collection of approximately P61.48 million. Despite the decline in some transaction volumes, revenue collection consistently increased from 2021 to 2023 and remained steady at a high level in 2024 and 2025, demonstrating sustained financial performance and efficiency in revenue-generating services. (Records of the Operations Division, LTO V) Needless to stress, the upgrade of the LTO Tabaco District Office from Class “D” to Class “B” is imperative. Hence, this proposed measure that seeks to implement the upgrade hopefully forthwith. The recommended upgrade shall necessarily increase the plantilla positions of the LTO Tabaco District Office to twenty (20), thereby creating an additional twelve (12) positions to its current eight (8) personnel complement. The change in classification and the consequent accompanying addition of personnel will indubitably benefit the patrons and clients from Tabaco City and nearby municipalities primarily through enhanced services and expedited transactions. These timely and much-needed reforms will trigger and promote higher revenue collection which in turn is expected to further expand and optimize provision of transport and allied public welfare services. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. CIELO KRISEL B. label: HB 11558
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE BED CAPACITY OF THE DRUG ABUSE TREATMENT AND REHABILITATION CENTER IN THE CITY OF LAS PINAS FROM ITS CURRENT CAPACITY TO ONE THOUSAND (1000) BEDS, UPGRADING ITS FACILITIES AND PROFESSIONAL HEALTHCARE SERVICES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XII, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development which shall endeavor to make essential goods, health and other social services available to all the people at affordable cost. The highly urbanized City of Las Pifias has seen continuous population growth and urban density, which brings a corresponding surge in demand for public health and social protection services, particularly in substance abuse treatment, mental health support, and community rehabilitation. While local health initiatives and outpatient drug treatment facilities exist in the city, the current physical capacity, medical infrastructure, and specialized personnel remain insufficient to meet the volume of individuals seeking residential rehabilitation and long-term recovery support. This measure seeks to expand and modernize the existing drug treatment and rehabilitation infrastructure in the City of Las Pifias by converting the existing locai facility into a high-capacity center named the Las Pifias City Drug Treatment and Rehabilitation Center. The bill explicitly mandates an increase in bed capacity to at least one thousand (1,000) beds, upgrades existing clinical, psychiatric, and vocational facilities to guarantee that the government provides adequate support to the city’s health sector. By enhancing the facility's bed capacity and integrating comprehensive medical, psychological, and vocational services, this Act ensures that residents of Las Pifias and neighboring localities in southern Metro Manila receive accessible, humane, and evidence-based rehabilitation without being displaced from their support systems. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MARK ANTHONY G. label: HB 11560
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE LOCAL HOUSING LAND BANK SYSTEM, MANDATING THE SUITABILITY ASSESSMENT AND PRIORITY RESERVATION OF TAX-DELINQUENT REAL PROPERTIES FOR SOCIALIZED HOUSING, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 264 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991," AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIII, Section 9 of the 1987 Constitution mandates the State to undertake, in cooperation with the public sector, a continuing program of urban land reform and housing that will make available affordable and decent housing and basic services to underprivileged and homeless citizens. Yet in many highly urbanized cities, one of the greatest obstacles to providing affordable housing is not merely the cost of construction, but the extreme scarcity and high market cost of available land. At the same time, local government units periodically acquire real properties as a consequence of unpaid real property taxes. Under Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, real properties may, after compliance with the required notice, levy, and public auction procedures, be acquired by the local government when there is no qualified bidder or when the highest bid is insufficient to satisfy the taxes and related charges due. The law likewise preserves the property owner's statutory right of redemption before ownership finally vests in the local government unit. Once ownership has lawfully and finally vested in the local government, however, existing law generally allows the property to be subsequently disposed of through public auction. This measure seeks to introduce a more socially productive alternative. Before an LGU-owned property acquired through tax delinquency proceedings is resold, the property should first be evaluated to determine whether it can be utilized for socialized or public housing. Properties that are safe, accessible, appropriately located, and economically feasible for housing development may be placed in a Local Housing Land Bank rather than immediately returned to the private real estate market. This policy complements Republic Act No. 7279, otherwise known as the Urban Development and Housing Act of 1992, which recognizes land banking as a mode of acquiring land for socialized housing and accords priority to government-owned, abandoned, and idle lands. The proposed Local Housing Land Bank will provide LGUs with an VX YS Zz additional mechanism to address their housing requirements, particularly in highly urbanized areas where land prices frequently make in-city relocation difficult. The measure expressly protects property owners. Mere tax delinquency shall never be sufficient to place privately owned property in the Local Housing Land Bank. No property may be included until all procedures required by law have been completed and the owner's statutory right of redemption has fully expired. The measure further promotes in-city and on-site development whenever practicable so that families receiving government housing are not unnecessarily displaced far from their employment, schools, health facilities, transportation, and established communities. Housing should not merely provide a roof over a family's head. It should provide security of tenure while keeping families connected to their livelihoods and communities. label: HB 11564
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A COMPREHENSIVE NATIONAL HEALTH PROGRAM FOR THE PREVENTION, EARLY DETECTION, DIAGNOSIS, TREATMENT, AND MANAGEMENT OF SYSTEMIC LUPUS ERYTHEMATOSUS (SLE), PROVIDING SUPPORT FOR PERSONS LIVING WITH LUPUS AND THEIR FAMILIES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Lupus is a serious and lifelong illness that affects many Filipinos, yet it remains poorly understood by the general public. Its symptoms can differ from one person to another and may resemble those of other illnesses. As a result, some patients spend considerable time and resources seeking medical attention before their condition is properly identified. For an ordinary Filipino family, this delay has real consequences. Repeated consultations, laboratory tests, medicines, and continuing treatment can become a significant financial burden. More importantly, when the disease is not detected and properly managed early, the patient's condition may worsen and affect his or her ability to study, work, earn a living, and care for a family. Government intervention should therefore focus on a simple objective: help Filipinos recognize lupus earlier and make proper care more accessible and affordable. This bill seeks to establish a comprehensive national program for lupus under the Department of Health. It provides for greater public awareness, early detection and proper referral, training of health workers, improved access to appropriate treatment and medicines, patient and family support, and the collection of reliable information necessary for government planning and research. The measure also recognizes that detecting an illness is only the beginning. A person diagnosed with lupus may require continuing care and regular monitoring. Thus, the bill directs the 1 Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) to provide appropriate coverage for lupus screening and early detection and to develop and periodically review an appropriate benefit package for medically necessary diagnostic procedures, laboratory monitoring, treatment, and other health services for persons living with lupus. Access to proper care should likewise not depend on where a Filipino lives or how much a family earns. The bill therefore strengthens the referral system among primary care facilities, government hospitals, specialists, and other health facilities, while giving particular attention to indigent and financially incapacitated patients and those living in underserved communities. No Filipino suffering from lupus should have to endure years of uncertainty before receiving proper care, nor should a family be left to face the financial and emotional burden of the disease on its own. Through greater awareness, earlier detection, accessible treatment, and continuing support, government can help persons living with lupus lead healthier and more productive lives. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. R. label: HB 11565
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A NATIONAL PLAN OF ACTION FOR THE CARE, SUPPORT, DEVELOPMENT, AND INCLUSION OF PERSONS WITH AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER, PROVIDING SUPPORT FOR THEIR FAMILIES AND CAREGIVERS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Filipinos with autism and their families face challenges that extend far beyond obtaining a diagnosis. Many families struggle to find affordable assessment, therapy, education, health services, and other forms of support. These difficulties become even greater for families with limited financial resources or those who do not have ready access to specialists and appropriate facilities. For parents and caregivers, raising and supporting a person with autism can be a lifelong responsibility. During childhood, families must navigate health care, education, therapy. and social services. As the child grows older, new concerns arise, including further education, skills development, employment, independent living, and continued care and support. Government assistance should therefore not end with diagnosis or childhood intervention. This bill seeks to establish a comprehensive National Plan of Action for the Care, Support. and Inclusion of Persons with Autism Spectrum Disorder. It brings together the programs and responsibilities of government agencies involved in health, education, social welfare, employment, skills development, and local government services so that persons with autism and their families can receive more coordinated support. The measure promotes early identification and appropriate intervention, accessible health and rehabilitation services, inclusive education, skills development and employment opportunities, support for parents and caregivers, and greater public awareness and acceptance. It likewise 1 strengthens referral systems so that families can more easily determine where and how to obtain appropriate government services. More importantly, the measure recognizes that persons with autism have different needs at different stages of their lives. Government programs must therefore provide continuity of support from childhood and education to adulthood, employment, community participation, and, when necessary, continuing care. Persons with autism are members of our families and communities who deserve the same opportunities to learn, work, participate, and live with dignity. A more inclusive society requires not only awareness and acceptance, but also accessible services and concrete opportunities that allow every Filipino to reach his or her potential. label: HB 11567
title: AN ACT DECLARING AUGUST 25 OF EVERY YEAR AS ILOILO CITY CHARTER DAY AND DECLARING THE SAME AS A SPECIAL NON-WORKING HOLIDAY IN THE CITY OF ILOILO
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 15 The City of Iloilo is one of the oldest and most historically significant urban centers in the Philippines and has played an important role in the political, economic, cultural, and social development of the country. The legal foundation for the establishment and organization of the City of Iloilo is found in Commonwealth Act No. 57, otherwise known as the Charter of the City of Iloilo, as subsequently amended by Commonwealth Act No. 158 and other amendatory laws. Commonwealth Act No. 158, approved on November 9, 1936, amended the Charter and provided for the organization and administration of the City of Iloilo. The inauguration of the city was originally scheduled by the President for July 16, 1937. On January 23, 1937, President Manuel L. Quezon issued Proclamation No. 133, entitled “Setting Aside July 16, 1937, as a Day for the Inauguration of the City of Iloilo, and Declaring It a Special Public Holiday for the Province of Iloilo.” The inauguration date was subsequently changed. On August 20, 1937, President Quezon issued Proclamation No. 172, expressly amending Proclamation No. 133 and setting aside August 25, 1937 as the day for the inauguration of the City of Iloilo. The same proclamation declared August 25, 1937 a special public holiday for the Province of Iloilo. Project - Proclamations Series of Thus, August 25, 1937 represents the date officially designated by the national government for the formal inauguration of the City of Iloilo. The date consequently acquired historical significance as the city's Charter Day. The establishment of the City of Iloilo was likewise part of the transformation of several historic communities into a unified urban political jurisdiction. The Charter was subsequently amended to further define the territorial jurisdiction of the city. Among these later developments, Commonwealth Act No. 604, approved on August 22, 1940, provided for the inclusion of the territory of the municipality of Jaro into the City of Iloilo. The national government has, on various occasions, continued to recognize August 25 as a significant date for the City of Iloilo through presidential proclamations declaring the date a special non-working day in the city. A permanent declaration by Congress will ensure that the historical significance of August 25 is recognized every year and will provide the people of Iloilo City with an opportunity to commemorate the city's beginnings, celebrate its heritage, and reflect upon its continuing contribution to the development of Western Visayas and the Philippines. 48 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. 50 51 52 53 54 HON. label: HB 11568
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING AN ELECTRIC VEHICLE FIRE SAFETY AND EMERGENCY RESPONSE SUPPORT PROGRAM, REQUIRING MANUFACTURERS, ASSEMBLERS, IMPORTERS AND, WHERE APPLICABLE, DISTRIBUTORS OF ELECTRIC VEHICLES TO PROVIDE THE BUREAU OF FIRE PROTECTION WITH ELECTRIC VEHICLE FIRE RESPONSE SAFETY EQUIPMENT FOR EVERY TEN (10) COVERED ELECTRIC VEHICLES INTRODUCED INTO THE PHILIPPINE MARKET, STRENGTHENING FIREFIGHTER TRAINING AND INDUSTRY COOPERATION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 15 Republic Act No. 11697, otherwise known as the “Electric Vehicle Industry Development Act” (EVIDA), established the national policy for the development and adoption of electric vehicles in the Philippines. 19 As electric mobility expands, the emergency-response capability of government must develop alongside it. 22 Electric vehicles equipped with rechargeable traction batteries present emergency-response considerations different from those encountered in conventional vehicle fires. Battery thermal runaway may involve extreme heat, hazardous gases, prolonged incident management, and the possibility of reignition even after visible flames have been controlled. 27 Republic Act No. 9514, otherwise known as the “Revised Fire Code of the Philippines of 2008”, mandates the Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) to prevent and suppress destructive fires and enforce appropriate fire-safety standards. 31 Republic Act No. 11589, otherwise known as the “Bureau of Fire Protection Modernization Act”, further strengthens the capabilities of the BFP through the acquisition of modern fire suppression, rescue, hazardous-materials, specialized equipment, training, research and other resources necessary for effective emergency response. 36 There is therefore a need to ensure that the continuing growth of the electric vehicle industry is accompanied by a corresponding strengthening of the capability of the BFP to respond to electric vehicle fires and battery-related emergencies. 40 This measure establishes a statutory public-safety responsibility requiring manufacturers, assemblers, importers and, where applicable, distributors that first introduce covered electric vehicles into the Philippine market to provide the BFP with one (1) approved Electric Vehicle Fire Response Safety Set (EVFRSS) for every ten (10) covered electric vehicles introduced into the Philippine market. 46 Each EVFRSS shall include an appropriate BFP-approved Electric Vehicle Fire Containment Device (EVFCD) and such complementary equipment as may be required by the BFP. 50 The measure adopts technology-neutral terminology and does not mandate any particular brand, design or proprietary product. Technical requirements shall be determined and periodically reviewed by the BFP, in coordination with concerned government agencies, based on prevailing fire science, applicable safety standards and technological developments. 56 The measure likewise provides safeguards against double counting, establishes reporting and accountability mechanisms, requires proper government inventory and accounting of equipment received, mandates technical cooperation and firefighter training, and provides administrative due process. 61 As the number of electric vehicles on Philippine roads increases, the country’s capacity to safely respond to electric vehicle emergencies must increase with it. 64 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. 66 67 68 69 70 HON. label: HB 11569
title: AN ACT AUTHORIZING THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH (DOH) TO SET AND APPROVE THE BED CAPACITY AND SERVICE CAPABILITY OF ALL DOH HOSPITALS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution mandates the State to protect and promote the right to health of the people (Article II, Section 15) and to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development that makes essential health services available to all at affordable cost (Article XIII, Section 11). Republic Act No. 11223, or the Universal Health Care Act, builds on this mandate by requiring a responsive network of public health facilities guided by a national facility development plan. Hospitals under the Department of Health (DOH) form the backbone of this public network, particularly for patients who cannot afford private care. Yet the authorized bed capacity and service capability of most DOH hospitals are fixed by statute, so any increase or change, however urgent, must pass through the full legislative process. As a result, Congress each term considers numerous local bills seeking to raise the bed capacity of individual hospitals. The process takes time, and in the interim hospitals operate beyond their authorized capacity, patients are placed in hallways and shared beds, and the plantilla positions, budget, and equipment that should accompany expansion lag behind actual demand. This bill proposes a more responsive arrangement. It authorizes the DOH, through an administrative issuance, to adjust and approve the bed capacities and corresponding service capabilities of hospitals under its supervision and control. Such decisions must be grounded on objective considerations, namely each hospital’s development plan, catchment population, burden of disease, available human resources, and health care provider networks, together with other standards the DOH may set. The DOH is directed to continue updating and implementing the Philippine Health Facility Development Plan (PHFDP) to 1 guide the modernization of government health facilities, and to include in its programs the funding requirements for each approved adjustment. Importantly, the measure preserves the constitutional power of the purse. Funding for bed capacity adjustments remains subject to the regular budget process and must be included in the annual General Appropriations Act. The DOH is likewise required to submit an annual report to the Committee on Health of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Health and Demography of the Senate on hospitals with approved bed capacities and the corresponding funding requirements, ensuring that Congress retains effective oversight. This measure adopts as its reference Senate Bill No. 1508, entitled “An Act Authorizing the Department of Health (DOH) to Set and Approve the Bed Capacity and Service Capability of All DOH Hospitals,” the substitute bill recommended for approval of the Senate of the Twentieth Congress. Filing a counterpart measure in the House of Representatives is intended to facilitate the timely enactment of this legislation and its harmonization with the Senate version. For communities such as Marikina and its neighboring localities, which rely on DOH hospitals like the Amang Rodriguez Memorial Medical Center, the ability of the health system to expand capacity promptly where the need is greatest is not an administrative detail but a matter of timely and dignified care. Rationalizing how DOH hospital capacity is set will allow resources to follow patients, rather than wait for a separate law for every hospital. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MARCELINO “MARCY” R. label: HB 11570
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A NATIONAL PLAN OF ACTION FOR THE CARE, SUPPORT, AND INCLUSION OF PERSONS WITH AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution directs the State to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development and to give priority to the needs of, among others, the disabled and children (Article XIII, Section 11). It further mandates the establishment of a special agency for persons with disability for their rehabilitation, self-development, and self- reliance, and their integration into the mainstream of society (Article XIII, Section 13). The Philippines, as a State Party to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, has likewise committed to ensure the full and equal enjoyment of all human rights by persons with disability. Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition that affects how a person communicates, interacts with others, and experiences the world. Advocacy groups such as the Autism Society Philippines have long estimated that more than a million Filipinos may be on the autism spectrum, yet the country still lacks a dedicated national framework to guide how government responds to their needs. Families commonly face late or costly diagnosis, a shortage of developmental specialists outside major urban centers, expensive and hard-to-access therapies, limited inclusive learning environments, and few pathways to meaningful work once formal schooling ends. Existing laws provide important but general protections. Republic Act No. 7277, or the Magna Carta for Persons with Disability, as amended, sets out the rights and privileges of persons with disability; Republic Act No. 11228 provides for mandatory PhilHealth coverage of all persons with disability; and Republic Act No. 11650 institutes a policy of inclusion and services for learners with disabilities. None of these, however, establishes a single, coordinated plan that ties together screening, intervention, education, employment, and social protection specifically for persons with ASD across the life course. This bill seeks to close that gap. It mandates the formulation of a National Plan of Action for Autism Spectrum Disorder, to be led by the National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA) through existing inter-agency mechanisms and in consultation with local government units, civil society, autism self-advocates, and parents’ groups. It assigns clear responsibilities: the Department of Health for integrating ASD screening, referral, and diagnostic protocols into primary and maternal and child health care; the Department of Health and PhilHealth for the progressive availability of evidence-based interventions in 1 public facilities; the Department of Education, the Commission on Higher Education, and the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority for inclusive education and transition pathways; the Department of Labor and Employment and the Civil Service Commission for equal and supported employment; and the Department of Social Welfare and Development and local government units for social protection and community-based support. The bill also declares discrimination against persons with ASD unlawful, requires sustained public awareness campaigns, and provides for funding through the General Appropriations Act. This measure adopts as its reference Senate Bill No. 1822, entitled “An Act Instituting a National Plan of Action for the Care, Support and Inclusion of Persons with Autism Spectrum Disorder and Appropriating Funds Therefor,” the substitute bill recommended for approval of the Senate of the Twentieth Congress. Filing a counterpart measure in the House of Representatives is intended to facilitate the timely enactment of this legislation and its harmonization with the Senate version. Local government units are often the first point of contact for families of children with ASD, whether through barangay health centers, child development programs, or local social welfare offices. A national plan that equips and connects these frontline services with national agencies will allow every Filipino with ASD, wherever he or she lives, to receive timely support and to take part in community life with dignity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MARCELINO “MARCY” R. label: HB 11571
title: AN ACT EXPANDING DEPOSIT INSURANCE COVERAGE AND STRENGTHENING THE INDEPENDENCE, MANDATES, AUTHORITIES AND FINANCIAL CAPABILITY OF THE PHILIPPINE DEPOSIT INSURANCE CORPORATION AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 3591, AS AMENDED, AND OTHER RELATED LAWS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation (PDIC) was created under Republic Act No. 3591 in 1963 to insure bank deposits and help maintain a sound and stable financial system. Since then, its Charter has been amended only twice in over sixty years — through Republic Act No. 9302 in 2004 and Republic Act No. 9576 in 2009 — even as the Philippine financial system has grown substantially more complex, more digital, and more interconnected with non-bank deposit-taking channels. This bill seeks to enact the Responsive Deposit Insurance Act (ReDI) to modernize and strengthen the country’s deposit insurance framework. It expands deposit insurance coverage beyond traditional banks to include other deposit-taking institutions, subject to appropriate regulatory safeguards, thereby extending protection to a broader segment of the depositing public. The measure also empowers the PDIC to adopt a more responsive insurance system by allowing periodic adjustments in deposit insurance coverage based on economic conditions, implementing risk-based premium assessments, and enhancing its capacity to monitor and manage risks to the Deposit Insurance Fund. It further institutionalizes mechanisms to address systemic risks and ensure the sustainability of the deposit insurance system. To improve operational efficiency and financial resilience, the bill strengthens the PDIC’s fiscal and administrative autonomy, enhances its governance structure, expands its investment and resolution authorities, and authorizes the creation of a subsidiary to manage and dispose of assets acquired from closed banks. These reforms are intended to maximize asset recovery, reduce resolution costs, and improve the Corporation’s overall effectiveness. Ultimately, this measure aligns the Philippines’ deposit insurance regime with evolving financial sector realities and international best practices. By enhancing depositor protection, strengthening financial safety nets, and promoting confidence in the financial system, the proposed legislation will contribute to a more stable, resilient, and inclusive financial sector. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought REP. MARCELINO “MARCY” R. label: HB 11572
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE FILIPINO FAMILY MAINSTREAMING FRAMEWORK, ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR THE FILIPINO FAMILY (NCFF), MANDATING FAMILY IMPACT ASSESSMENTS IN PUBLIC POLICYMAKING AND GOVERNANCE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution gives the Filipino family a place of special constitutional protection. Article II, Section 12 recognizes the sanctity of family life and directs the State to protect and strengthen the family as a basic autonomous social institution. Article XV further recognizes the Filipino family as the foundation of the nation and mandates the State to strengthen its solidarity and actively promote its total development. This constitutional command is now confronted by measurable social and demographic realities. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) reported that registered marriages decreased from 414,213 in 2023 to 371,825 in 2024, while the crude marriage rate declined from 3.7 to 3.3 marriages per thousand population. The 2025 National Demographic and Health Survey reported a total fertility rate of 1.7 children per woman aged 15 to 49 for the three-year period preceding the survey, down from 1.9 in 2022 and below the replacement fertility level of 2.1 children per woman. PSA likewise recorded 1,358,989 registered live births in 2024, 6.2 percent fewer than the 1,448,522 registered in 2023. Of the 2024 registered live births, 808,965, or 59.5 percent, were non-marital births. This last figure does not, by itself, establish poor family functioning; rather, it underscores the range of family circumstances in which government must support children, parents, and caregivers. These demographic figures describe changing patterns of marriage, fertility, and childbearing; they do not, standing alone, measure family functioning or parental care. The case for family mainstreaming rests on the fact that child welfare and family resilience are shaped across multiple policy domains. A child’s welfare is affected by health, education, housing, labor, digital safety, local government capacity, and household economic resilience. A parent’s ability to raise and protect a child is likewise affected by employment conditions, childcare support, public safety, social protection, transport systems, housing affordability, and access to reliable services. The condition of the Filipino family is therefore a governance issue that cuts across agencies and sectors. The risks facing Filipino children further demonstrate the need for a coordinated family policy framework. UNICEF Philippines, citing the 2022 Disrupting Harm study conducted by UNICEF Office of Research, INTERPOL, and ECPAT International, reported that two in ten, or around two million, internet-using children aged 12 to 17 in the Philippines had experienced online sexual abuse and exploitation in the preceding year, while fewer than three percent reported such incidents to authorities. This study- based estimate highlights the need for stronger coordination among family support, child protection, law enforcement, education, digital safety, and community-based intervention systems. The proposed Filipino Family Mainstreaming Act responds to these realities by making family well-being a deliberate and measurable consideration in governance. It does not create a new large bureaucracy. Instead, it establishes the National Commission for the Filipino Family (NCFF), attached to the Office of the President for policy coordination, with the Department of Social Welfare and Development serving as Secretariat. It requires agencies to designate existing senior officials as Family Mainstreaming Focal Points, thereby avoiding unnecessary creation of new plantilla positions. It also integrates family mainstreaming into existing planning, budgeting, monitoring, and performance systems. The measure also introduces Family Impact Assessments (FIAs) as a policy discipline. Under Section 11, an FIA is mandatory for covered Executive department and agency measures, including nationally significant executive issuances, development plans, regulations, and major government programs reasonably expected to have substantial effects on Filipino families. For proposed legislation, however, the NCFF is directed to develop and make available an FIA methodology and technical assistance which either House of Congress, its committees, or legislative offices may use in accordance with their respective rules. FIAs are not another permit or clearance; they are intended to help decision-makers assess effects on child welfare, parental responsibilities, caregiving, household resilience, work- family balance, vulnerable family sectors, implementation costs, measurable outcomes, and less adverse policy alternatives. The proposal also addresses a recurring weakness of social legislation: the absence of measurable outcomes. It directs the National Commission for the Filipino Family, in coordination with the Philippine Statistics Authority and concerned agencies, to adopt National Family Well-being Indicators covering child development, educational participation and completion, family economic resilience, health and nutrition, housing conditions, caregiving, child protection, violence affecting family members, and work-life balance. These indicators will allow Congress, the Executive, local governments, researchers, and the public to evaluate family policy on the basis of evidence and measurable results. The bill also contains targeted obligations intended to give practical effect to the mainstreaming framework. In basic education, it requires advance curriculum transparency for defined Sensitive Topics, parental opt-out procedures, and specified parental consent and notification rules. In government procurement, it disqualifies natural or juridical entities with final administrative, civil, or judicial convictions for violations of specified laws protecting life, women, children, and family welfare, consistent with Republic Act No. 12009 or the New Government Procurement Act.
